en: Saṃjaya said:
To him who was thus overcome with compassion, his eyes filled and clouded with tears—
To him who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words.

Śrīdhara: In the second chapter, having awakened Arjuna—who was tormented by grief—by means of the knowledge of Brahman, Hari described the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established. When there arises the expectation as to what occurred thereafter, Sañjaya said: "To him [the Lord] who said 'So be it,'" and so forth.
To him whose eyes were thus filled and agitated with tears, Madhusūdana spoke these words to Arjuna in the manner described above. //1//

Madhusūdana, having heard Arjuna’s reluctance to fight— characterized by the thought that non-violence is the supreme dharma and that one should subsist on alms— and having ascertained that the kingdom of his sons was unshakable, addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose heart was now at ease.
Then Vaiśampāyana said that Sañjaya spoke to him, wishing to dispel the expectation of what had happened next after that occasion of joy:
"Compassion for these" refers to a particular kind of affection caused by delusion.
"Pervaded" means permeated by its inherent nature.
By stating that Arjuna is the object (*karman*) and compassion is the agent (*kartṛ*), the adventitious nature of that [compassion] is excluded.

Therefore, "despairing" refers to one who has fallen into a state of mental agitation—synonymous with grief—caused by the apprehension of separation from his own kin who have become objects of his affection.
Here, by treating dejection (*viṣāda*) as the object and Arjuna as the agent, its adventitious nature is indicated.

For this very reason, [he addresses] him whose eyes were filled with tears, agitated, and incapable of seeing due to the power of compassion and dejection. Thus, to that Arjuna—who was distressed by compassion and dejection, which had reached their full development by producing two effects known as the shedding of tears and agitation—[the Lord spoke] this following argumentative discourse.
He spoke these words and did not disregard him;
the sense is that Madhusūdana will likewise speak even to Arjuna, who himself acts as the punisher of the wicked. //1//
Viśvanātha:

Dispelling grief, delusion, and darkness through the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, Kṛṣṇacandra here, in the second [chapter], has declared the characteristics of the liberated one. //1//
Baladeva:
In the second [chapter], he taught the knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul, its means [of attainment], Hari,
action free from desire, and the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established.

Having thus heard of Arjuna’s dispassion, and perceiving Dhṛtarāṣṭra rejoicing at the prospect of his own son losing the kingdom, Sañjaya said to him, "So be it. The implication is that Madhusūdana will destroy even his grief, just as he destroyed the demon Madhu.
The Blessed Lord said: Whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis?
O Arjuna, it is practiced by the ignoble, does not lead to heaven, and brings about infamy. //2//

Śrīdhara: He speaks that very same statement; the Blessed Lord said, "From where?"—from what cause has this delusion come upon you, this auspicious [opportunity] which has presented itself in this crisis and difficulty, and which is not practiced by the noble ones?
It leads neither to heaven, nor is it righteous, and it brings about infamy. //2//
Madhusūdana introduces that very statement of the Blessed One with the words "But whence [is this]? [referring to]:
"Of complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, and fortune..."
The term "Bhaga" is a designation for detachment (*vairāgya*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), as well as for the six [perfections]. The word "of" (*iti*) is to be connected with each [term individually].
"Of liberation" refers to the knowledge that is the means to achieve it.
*Inganā* means intention (*saṃjñā*).
The Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is he in whom such complete sovereignty and so forth exist eternally and without obstruction;
the suffix *-matup* is used here in the sense of eternal possession (*nitya-yoga*). Likewise—
"He who knows the origin and destruction, the coming and going of beings,
as well as knowledge and ignorance— he is to be called Bhagavān.
Here, the term "of beings" (*bhūtānām*) is connected with each [pair of terms].
The terms "origination" and "destruction" also imply their causes;
likewise, "coming" and "going" refer to future prosperity and adversity. Since the meaning of the word *bhagavat* culminates in Śrī Vāsudeva alone, he is described in such a manner.

Why has this dejection— which turns one away from one's own duty, which is preceded by compassion, delusion, and the shedding of tears, and which is defiled because it is censured by the virtuous— come upon you, the foremost of all Kṣatriyas, at this uneven and perilous place? Is it out of a desire for liberation?
Or is it from a desire for heaven? This is what is raised by the word "what" (kiṃ).
He refutes all three reasons with the three qualifiers in the second half of the verse.
"Not resorted to" means not practiced by noble seekers of liberation.

The meaning is: how can those seekers of liberation whose passions (*kaṣāya*) are not yet matured abandon their own duties (*svadharma*), since they desire liberation through the purification of the inner disposition (*āśaya*) by means of their own duties?
It will be explained later that one qualified for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), however, is one whose passions have reached maturity.

That which leads away from heaven (*asvargya*) should not be practiced out of a desire for heaven, because it is contrary to the dharma that is the cause of attaining heaven. That which causes ill-repute (*akīrtikara*)—meaning either the absence of fame or the production of infamy—should not be practiced out of a desire for fame.
Thus, it must be avoided by those who desire liberation, those who desire heaven, and those who desire fame.
"Therefore, you should indulge in desire alone"—the sense is: "Alas! Your conduct is most improper. //2//
Viśvanātha:
*Kaśmala* means delusion. *Viṣame* refers here to the perilous crisis of battle.
For what reason?
Because it occurred that you were approached by that which is not frequented by the noble ones and is practiced by those well-established in the world.
"Not conducive to heaven" and "bringing ill-repute" means that it is unfavorable to happiness both in the next world and in this one. //2//
Baladeva: The Blessed Lord repeats those words: "The term *bhaga* is a designation for the six attributes: complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, splendor, dispassion, and liberation" (ViP 6.74).
Thus, He is eternally distinguished by the six qualities—sovereignty and the rest—as spoken of by Parāśara.
The phrase "of the complete" is to be applied to each of these six. O Arjuna!

Why has this dejection—a turning away from one’s own duty (*svadharma*), a stain because it is censured by the cultured—come upon you, the crest-jewel of Kṣatriyas, at this critical moment of battle? Nor is this renunciation of battle for the sake of liberation, heaven, or fame; thus he says, "O ignoble one."
It is not enjoyed—that is, not practiced—by the noble ones who seek liberation.
Indeed, the noble ones practice their own duties for the sake of purifying the heart. It is not conducive to heaven; it is contrary to those dharmas that bring about the attainment of heaven.
It causes ill repute and destroys one's fame. //2//
Do not yield to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe! (2.3)
Śrīdhara: "Do not yield to unmanliness.
Therefore, O Pārtha, do not succumb to unmanliness—that is, to cowardice.
Do not attain it;
for this is not appropriate or fitting for you.
[Abandon] this base, trivial weakness of heart and cowardice; arise for battle!
O scorcher of enemies, O tormentor of foes! //3//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: "What can be done by me, who, having become disheartened by the sight of my kinsmen's army, was unable even to hold my bow? To this he says, "Do not yield to unmanliness. Do not go toward *klaibyam*—the state of being unmanly, a lack of fortitude consisting in the collapse of vigor, splendor, and so forth. Do not succumb to it.
"O Pārtha, son of Pṛthā"—

the meaning is that because it is well known that an extraordinary degree of heroism resides in you, who are merely the son of Pṛthā obtained through the grace of the gods, you are unfit for cowardice by virtue of being Pṛthā’s son.
He further states that you are unfit for it even by virtue of being Arjuna, saying "not this."

"In you, Arjuna—who have fought even with Maheśvara himself and who possess renowned great majesty—this weakness is neither fitting nor appropriate"; thus he indicates his unfitness through this extraordinary description. Anticipating the objection, "But I have already said, 'I am unable to stand and my mind seems to wander,'" he says, "It is trivial. Abandoning this weakness of heart—this lack of fortitude consisting of mental wandering and the like—which is called "trivial" because it is the cause of triviality or because it is easily cast off, and having removed it through discernment, arise and prepare yourself for battle.
"Bhava! O scorcher of enemies!"—he is thus addressed with an epithet containing a reason, for he is one who torments the supreme enemy. //3//
Viśvanātha:
*Klaibyam* means the nature of a eunuch, that is, cowardice.
"O Pārtha," [he says], even though you are the son of Pṛthā, you are retreating.
Therefore, do not go;
do not attain this boon for another Kṣatriya.
"But this [compassion] is not appropriate for you, my friend.
Do not suspect that this is cowardice characterized by a lack of heroism;

rather, it is because of the vision of righteousness (*dharma*) toward teachers such as Bhīṣma and Droṇa, whereas regarding the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—who are weak and are now preparing to die after being struck by my weapons—this is simply compassion. To that, he says:
"Trifling" means:
these two, discernment and compassion, do not belong to you; rather, they are merely grief and delusion.
And those two manifest the weakness of the mind;
therefore, casting off this weakness of heart, arise,
O scorcher of the foe!
Fight, scorching your enemies. //3//
Baladeva said: If you should think, "What must I do now that I am shaken by the fault of my resolve to destroy my kinsmen?"— to that he says, "Cowardice," O Pārtha,
born of Pṛthā through the grace of the King of the Gods!
"Do not fall into unmanliness; attain [courage].
Such unmanliness is not fitting for you, O Arjuna, my friend, who are a conqueror of the universe, nor for one born of the kṣatriya lineage.
Surely this unmanliness of mine is not a lack of heroism, but rather a discrimination based on the sense of dharma toward venerable persons such as Bhīṣma."
If you think, "What compassion this is," regarding Duryodhana and the other brothers who are about to die from the blows of my weapons, to that he says: "It is base.
These are not instances of your discernment or compassion; rather, they are merely a base, most trivial weakness of heart.
Therefore, abandoning that, arise for battle and prepare yourself, O scorcher of foes! Do not become an object of ridicule for your enemies. //3//
Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, how could I [strike] Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle?
O slayer of enemies, I shall fight back with arrows against those two who are worthy of worship.
Śrīdhara: Arjuna said, "How? to show that he has not withdrawn from battle out of cowardice, but rather because of its injustice and unrighteousness:
"How shall I fight against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are worthy of honor—that is, fit and deserving of veneration?"
In that case as well, where it is improper even to speak with words, saying "I shall fight," what need is there to mention how one would fight with arrows?
O Ari-sūdana, O crusher of enemies! //4//
Madhusūdana [says]:

"Indeed, this is not a renunciation of one's own duty (svadharma) due to being under the sway of grief, delusion, and so forth; rather, it is because this battle lacks the nature of dharma and is unrighteous that its renunciation is performed by me"—this is the intention of Arjuna, who has not yet grasped the Lord’s intended meaning.
"How shall I bring about [this]?"—how shall I fight against, that is, strike with arrows and shafts in battle (saṅkhye), my grandfather Bhīṣma and my teacher Droṇa?
The meaning is: "not in any way at all."

The meaning is this: since those two are worthy of worship and fit to be honored with flowers and other offerings, even a playful battle— which results in joy— would be improper for them even in a place of play, let alone a strike with arrows on a battlefield that results in the loss of life, even if performed merely in words.
The two vocatives "O Madhusūdana" and "O Arisūdana" [occur] due to the agitation of grief, which results in a lack of coherent reflection on what precedes and follows.
Therefore, there is no fault of redundancy regarding the meaning of the phrase "Madhusūdana-Arisūdana.
By the words "I shall fight," it is indicated that even mere combat would be inappropriate in this situation, let alone killing.
Alternatively, how shall I fight against those two who are worthy of worship?
The phrase "Bhīṣma and Droṇa" is an elaboration of "those two who are worthy of worship.
The connection is like [the sentence]: "O King, feed two Brāhmaṇas, Devadatta and Yajñadatta."
The point is this: Duryodhana and the others will not prepare for battle without placing Bhīṣma and Droṇa at their head.
In that case, fighting with them is not righteous (*dharma*), because it has not been prescribed as such, unlike acts of worship and the like.
Nor can it be argued that this is not unrighteous (*adharma*) simply because it is not prohibited.

Since even verbal acts such as addressing a guru with "huṃ" or "you" (tvaṃ) are prohibited as offenses against the guru because they are shown to yield undesirable results, what need is there to mention that engaging in combat with them is unrighteous and forbidden? //4//

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "Indeed, the neglect of the worship of those worthy of worship obstructs one's spiritual welfare"—so says the Dharmaśāstra. Therefore, he asks "How? meaning, "Why should I desist from battle?"
"I shall fight back; I shall fight back.
[The opponent asks: "In that case, these two are indeed fighting; why are you unable to become their opponent?
[Arjuna replies: "It is true, I am indeed unable," and he says this because they are worthy of honor.
The sense is: "Out of devotion, I ought to offer only flowers at their feet, and not sharp arrows out of anger.
O friend Kṛṣṇa, you too kill only enemies in battle, and not your own teacher, Sandīpani.
Nor [should you abandon] your kinsmen, the Yadus; thus he says, "O Madhusūdana.
But surely Mādhava is indeed a Yadava;
to this he replies, "O Ari-sūdana."
"There is a Daitya named Madhu, whom I tell you is your enemy. //4//
Baladeva: [Objection: "But since Bhīṣma and others are there as opponents, why should you not fight?

For it is prescribed as the duty of a Kṣatriya that 'one who is challenged should not turn back'. To this he replies with the word "How" (katham), referring to Bhīṣma, his grandfather, and Droṇa, his preceptor in learning.

How shall I fight with arrows those two who are worthy of worship and should be honored with flowers and other offerings, and with whom even war is not fitting, even if they should speak words of jest?
How could it be appropriate for him to act together with those two and their arrows?

For the *Smṛti* states: "The transgression of failing to honor those worthy of honor obstructs one's spiritual welfare. Furthermore, there is a repetition in the vocatives "O Slayer of Madhu" and "O Slayer of the Enemy."
Because one who is overwhelmed by grief lacks the connection between preceding and succeeding thoughts;
and this state applies to you as well, for you kill only enemies in battle, but not venerable ones such as Ugrasena and Sāndīpani. //4//
For it is better in this world even to eat the food of begging than to slay these high-souled teachers.
But having slain my elders for the sake of wealth and desire, I would enjoy pleasures right here, stained with blood. (5)
Śrīdhara: If it is argued that "in that case, even your own bodily sustenance would not be possible without killing them," he says in response: "gurūn" (the teachers).

It is better and more appropriate to subsist here in this world even on alms-food—*bhaikṣya*, the food of mendicants—without killing the teachers, such as Droṇācārya and others, and thus without committing the murder of a teacher, which is contrary to the next world.

But regarding the opposite case, he says "having killed" (hatvā) to show that not only would there be suffering in the next world, but one would also experience the sufferings of hell right here in this world:
"Having killed my gurus, I would enjoy— that is, consume— those pleasures consisting of wealth and desire, which are smeared— that is, thoroughly stained— with blood, right here in this very life."
Alternatively, "those who desire wealth" (*artha-kāmān*) is an epithet for the elders.
The meaning is that because they are agitated by thirst for wealth, they might not desist from battle; therefore, their slaughter would inevitably follow.
And so it was said by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one"—this is the truth, O Great King; I am bound by wealth for the sake of the Kauravas. (MBh 6.41.36) //5//
Madhusūdana:
But surely the worthiness of Bhīṣma and Droṇa to be honored is due solely to their status as teachers,
and the same applies to others such as Kṛpa and the rest.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate at present to accept them as one's teachers—for it is ordained that even a teacher who is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, and who has set out upon a wrong path, must be abandoned:
"Even a teacher who is conceited, who does not know what is to be done and what is not to be done, and who has taken to a mistaken path—his abandonment is prescribed. (Manu Smṛti 5.178.24)

Thus says the Smṛti. Therefore, considering that for these men—who are arrogant with the pride of war, who have seized the kingdom unjustly, who have committed treachery against their teacher, who are devoid of discrimination between right and wrong action, and who are established on a path of deviation—slaughter alone is better, [the Lord], anticipating this doubt, said: "Without slaying the teachers," etc.
By not slaying the teachers, the next world certainly exists.

But in this world, for us—kings and others whose kingdoms have been seized by them—even eating alms-food is better, more praiseworthy, and appropriate; it is not better to have a kingdom through their slaughter. Thus, even regarding the duty of war, having taken it to result merely in a livelihood and having attributed sin to the vow [of fighting], [the opponent argues].
Anticipating the objection that their lack of guru-hood was stated due to their being conceited and so forth, he says "of great majesty" (mahānubhāvān).
This means those whose majesty is based on sacred learning, study, austerity, conduct, and the like.

Thus, the meaning is that for those endowed with such excellence of merit, who have even Time, Desire, and the rest brought under their control, there can be no contact with base evils such as conceit.
"Himahānubhāvān" may be taken as a single compound word.

"Himaha" refers to the sun or fire, so called because it destroys (*hanti*) cold (*hima*), which is to say, dullness (*jāḍya*); those whose majesty (*anubhāva*) or power (*sāmarthya*) is that of Himaha are "himahānubhāvān.
Thus, because of their extreme brilliance, they are entirely free from defects such as arrogance (*avaliptatva*).
"Transgression of dharma and recklessness are seen even among lords;
for those who are most powerful, these do not constitute a fault, just as fire consumes everything.
[BhP 10.33.30] Now, one might object: when they were greedy for wealth and engaged in battle, how could these men—who had sold their very selves—possess the aforementioned greatness?
And so it was said by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one;
this is the truth, O Great King, for I am bound by wealth to the Kauravas. (MBh 6.41.36)
Anticipating this objection, he says, "having killed.
Even those who are greedy for wealth would surely become venerable by virtue of their regard for me; thus, the word "guru" is used again.
The particle *tu* has the sense of "even": even having killed such venerable persons, I might enjoy only worldly pleasures (*bhoga*), but I would not obtain liberation (*mokṣa*).
They are called "enjoyments" (*bhoga*) because they are enjoyed; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Furthermore, these enjoyments exist only in this world and not in the next world.
Moreover, even in this world, they are utterly loathsome, being as if smeared with blood due to their pervasion by infamy—this is the meaning.
The sense is: "If this is so even here [in this world], then how much more must the suffering of the next world be described?

Alternatively, Viśvanātha should be seen as offering another interpretation by taking the compound *artha-kāma* as a qualifier of *bhoga*, meaning: "Having killed my elders, I would enjoy only pleasures consisting of wealth and desire, but not dharma or liberation."

"Now, if you have no desire to seize this kingdom of yours, then by what means will you live? To this he replies: "Without killing my teachers. Without committing the murder of one's teachers, it is better—even though begging for food is censured by Kṣatriyas—to subsist on alms-food.
The sense is that even if there is the acquisition of ill-repute in this world, there shall certainly be no misfortune in the next life.
Furthermore, teachers who are arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, and who follow unrighteous men such as Duryodhana, must indeed be abandoned. As it has been said:
"Even a teacher, if he is arrogant and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done..."
The abandonment of one who has set out upon a wrong path is ordained.
Thus it should be said.
To this he replies: "of great majesty" (*mahānubhāvān*).
The sense is: how could those faults possibly arise in Bhīṣma and the others, by whom even Time, Desire, and the like have been brought under control? But surely—
"A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one"—this is the truth, O Great King; I am bound by wealth on account of the Kauravas.
Since this was said by Bhīṣma himself to Yudhiṣṭhira, has their former greatness now vanished because they are currently driven by the desire for wealth?

True; yet even that would result only in sorrow for me, having slain these [kinsmen]. Thus he says: "Even if I were to enjoy pleasures after slaying these Kurus—who are greedy for wealth and lustful for gain—[I would do so] only while being smeared and stained with their blood.
The meaning is this: although they are greedy for wealth, my status as their elder (guru) remains indeed intact.
Therefore, if this [deity] were to be slain, my enjoyment—being that of one who has betrayed my guru—would surely be mixed with evil karma. //5//
Baladeva: If it is objected, "If you have no desire for sovereignty, then how will your maintenance of the body be accomplished? he says in response, "gurūn" and so forth.

For me, who remains without having slain my gurus—that is, without committing the murder of my elders—it is better and more praiseworthy to subsist on food obtained by begging, even though such food is censured for Kṣatriyas; for although it may cause ill repute in this world, it does not obstruct one's progress in the next world.

But surely these elders, Bhīṣma and the others, though they are gurus, must now be abandoned because of their association with Duryodhana and his followers— who, out of the arrogance of war and pride, have deceitfully seized your kingdom and committed treachery against you— and because they lack the discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done.
For even a guru who is haughty and ignorant of what is right and wrong [should be avoided].
The abandonment of one who has set out upon a wrong path is prescribed.
Because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), he says in response to that objection: "of great majesty" (*mahānubhāvān*).
This means those whose majesty (*anubhāva*)—the power caused by such factors as the study of the Vedas and the practice of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*)—is great, being preeminent among all.
The meaning is that even time, desire, and the like are subject to them; therefore, they have no connection with those defects.
Now, it may be objected:
"Man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one."
"Thus it is true, O Great King, that I am bound by wealth through the Kauravas.
Since they have sold themselves out of greed for wealth, as stated by Bhīṣma, how can they possess any greatness?
If you argue that they must therefore be slain in battle, he says in response: "Having slain those who are driven by wealth and desire."
Even by killing my elders who desire wealth and pleasure, I would enjoy these very enjoyments in this world alone, and not in the next world;
and I would enjoy them while they are smeared with blood, indeed mixed with their very blood.
But one should not consume them even if they are pure, for that would involve injury to them and result in the acquisition of that [sin].
Likewise, even when they are intoxicated by pride and arrogance regarding battle and so forth, their status as gurus remains intact; this is indicated by the repetition of the word "guru. //5//
And we do not know which of these two is better for us: whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us.
Those very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having slain whom we would not wish to live, stand arrayed before us.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, even if we were to accept unrighteousness, it is not known whether victory or defeat would be more significant for us; thus he says, "If not," and so forth. Between these two, we do not know which indeed will be *garīyaḥ*—that is, greater or more significant for us.
He shows those very two options: [if we fight, there is death; if we do not, there is the loss of our lineage].

"Either we shall conquer them, or they shall conquer us; even as for victory, what will it be for us? Among these two—victory and defeat—which indeed will be the weightier, the more significant? This we do not know.
He shows those very two sides: "We shall conquer them," [and so forth].
"Lest they should defeat us";
furthermore, he says "whomever [they choose]" to show that even victory for us is in effect a defeat. //6//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might object that since eating alms is forbidden for a Kṣatriya and fighting is prescribed as his own duty (*svadharma*), fighting alone is more beneficial in this case; anticipating this, he says, "And not this... and so forth.

We do not even know which of these two is weightier or better for us: begging for alms, because it is free from violence, or fighting, because it is our own duty. Nor do we know this: even if the battle were commenced, whether we might conquer and prevail, or whether the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would conquer us.
The position of equality between the two sides must also be understood by implication.
Furthermore, even if victory were achieved, it would result in defeat for us;
for we do not wish to live even after killing those kinsmen, much less enjoy the objects of the senses.
"Those very ones"—namely, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the kinsmen of Dhṛtarāṣṭra such as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the rest—are standing arrayed before me.
Therefore, the meaning is that the superiority of battle over mendicancy is not established.
Thus, by means of the preceding section, the qualifications of the qualified seeker have been stated through the delineation of the defects of saṃsāra.

In this context, regarding the statement, "And I do not see any good in slaying my own kin in battle," the text asserts that one slain in combat possesses the same spiritual status (*samāna-yoga-kṣema*) as a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*). Thus, the "good" (*śreya*) known as liberation (*mokṣa*), established by such Vedic scriptures as, "The good is one thing, and the pleasant is another" (*KaṭhU* 2.1), is presented. By implication, everything other than that is "not-good" (*aśreya*); thus, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities (*nityānitya-vastu-viveka*) is demonstrated.

In the passage, "I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa" (Gītā 1.32), there is detachment from fruits pertaining to this world (*aihika*). In the passage, "even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds" (Gītā 1.35), there is detachment from fruits pertaining to the next world (*pāralaukika*).
In the passage, "residence in hell is certain" (Gītā 1.44), there is the [realization of] the self as distinct from the gross body (*sthūla-deha*).

Peace (*śama*) is indicated by the path explained in the verse, "What have we to do with the kingdom? (*Gītā* 1.32); self-restraint (*dama*) is indicated by "What have we to do with enjoyments? (*Gītā* 1.32);
and freedom from greed (*nirlobhatā*) is indicated in the verse, "Even if these do not see... (*Gītā* 1.38).
"In that case, it would be more secure for me" (Gītā 1.46)—herein lies *titikṣā* (forbearance).
Thus, the meaning of the first chapter is an indication of the means for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
In this chapter, however, renunciation characterized by the practice of begging is established in the verse: "It is better to eat even alms-food" (Gītā 2.5). //6//
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, even for me who am intent upon hostility toward my guru, it is not even known whether victory or defeat will occur; thus he says, "Nor this," and so forth.
Nevertheless, we do not know which of the two—victory or defeat—will indeed be the more significant (*garīyaḥ*) for us.
He shows those very two positions: "May we conquer them, or may they conquer us.
Furthermore, he says "whomever [we conquer]," indicating that even victory for us is, in effect, defeat. //6//

Baladeva: If it is argued, "But surely subsisting on alms is censured for a Kṣatriya, and though you know that fighting is your own duty, you speak [of renouncing it]," he says in response, "And this we do not know. We do not know this.
Between begging for alms and fighting, which of the two is weightier—that is, more praiseworthy—for us?
Is begging weightier because it is free from violence, or is fighting weightier because it is our own duty?
This we do not know.
"When war has begun, we might defeat the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or they might defeat us.

If it is argued that victory will surely belong to you—who possess great prowess and are most righteous—then he says: "whichever" (yān eva). This refers to all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, beginning with Bhīṣma.
"We do not wish to live" means that we do not even desire to remain alive, much less to enjoy worldly pleasures;
thus, even victory for us would result in defeat in effect.
Therefore, your claim that war is superior to begging is unestablished.

Thus, by this much of the text, Arjuna’s qualification for knowledge—well-known from the Śruti that "one who knows thus, having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and endowed with faith, should see the Self in the very Self"—has been demonstrated. In that regard, [the verses beginning with] "What have we to do with the kingdom? [Gītā 1.32] indicate tranquility (śama) and self-control (dama).
"Even for the sovereignty of the three worlds" (Gītā 1.35) refers to *uparati*, characterized by indifference toward worldly and otherworldly enjoyments.
*Titikṣā*, characterized by endurance of the pairs of opposites (*dvandvas*), is expressed by "it is better to eat alms.
*Śraddhā*, characterized by firm conviction in the words of the Guru, will become manifest in the subsequent verse.
Indeed, one who is devoid of tranquility and the other [virtues] has no qualification for knowledge, just as a cripple or the like has no qualification for ritual action. //6//
My nature overwhelmed by the defect of compassion, my mind confused about duty, I ask you.
Tell me decisively that which would be the highest good; I am your disciple, instruct me who have taken refuge in you. //7//
Śrīdhara: By the words beginning with "kārpaṇya," he indicates his own qualification for receiving instruction.

That is to say, my nature is afflicted by the defects of miserliness (*kārpaṇya*) and the fault [of family destruction]; "miserliness" is the fear of death, and the "fault" is that caused by the destruction of one's own lineage.
My nature—characterized by valor and other virtues—is afflicted and overwhelmed by these two; as such, I ask you.
Likewise, he whose mind is deluded regarding dharma—
meaning one whose mind is in doubt as to whether for a Kṣatriya abandoning battle and wandering for alms is dharma or adharma— tell me that which is certain to be my welfare and appropriate.
Moreover, I am your disciple and worthy of instruction;
therefore, please instruct and teach me, who have approached you and taken refuge in you. //7//
Madhusūdana:

Now, approaching a teacher (*gurūpasadana*) is being expounded. For one who has fully understood the multitude of defects inherent in saṃsāra and is consequently deeply disenchanted, there is qualification for receiving knowledge only through having approached a teacher according to the prescribed rule;
thus it is, on account of the crisis involving Bhīṣma and others.

Having shown Arjuna’s desire for the practice of begging as established by the Vedic scripture, "Then, having risen, they wander for alms" (BAU 3.5.1), he demonstrates his formal approach to a teacher (*gurūpasatti*) under the very pretext of that distress with the word "kārpaṇya.
In the world, one who cannot endure even the slightest injury to the mind is well known as a "miser" (*kṛpaṇa*).
Because he is of that nature, every one who does not know the Self becomes miserable due to the non-attainment of the goal of human life;
for the Śruti says: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable" (BAU 3.8.10).
The state of being that is *kārpaṇya*—the condition of possessing the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the non-Self—and caused by that, [one thinks]: "In this very birth, these alone are mine..."

When they have been slain, what is the use of life? Thus, his nature—characterized by the duty of a warrior (*kṣātra*) and consisting of the exertion for battle—is impaired and eclipsed by that defect which takes the form of attachment (*abhiniveśa*) and is marked by possessiveness (*mamatā*).

He is utterly bewildered regarding the matter of *dharma*, because he sees no authoritative means of discernment (*nirṇāyaka-pramāṇa*): "Is the slaughter of these men *dharma*, or is their protection *dharma*?"

Likewise, his mind was pervaded by such doubts as whether the duty (*dharma*) consists in the protection of the earth, or whether it is rather the dwelling in the forest exactly as it is, and so forth; he who is thus [doubtful] says: "We do not know which of these two is weightier for us"—this has been explained here [in the previous verse]. Being in such a state, I now ask you, "what is the good" (*śreyaḥ*)—this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
Therefore, tell me that which is certain, absolute, and ultimate well-being—the fruit that constitutes the supreme goal of human life.
Certainty (*aikāntikatva*) is the state of being necessarily present immediately after the means; absoluteness (*ātyantikatva*) is the non-destruction of what has been attained.

For just as when a medicine has been administered, the cessation of disease may sometimes not occur, or even if the cessation of disease has occurred, it may be destroyed again by the recurrence of the disease; so too, even when a sacrifice has been performed, heaven may not occur due to the influence of obstacles, or even if heaven has been attained, it perishes when overcome by suffering. Thus, there is neither certainty nor finality regarding those two.
As it has been said:
"Because of the affliction by the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the means for its removal.
If it is argued that this [desire] is useless since [a remedy] is seen [in the world], we say no, because that [remedy] is neither certain nor final.
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 1) "That which is heard from tradition (the Veda) is like that which is seen; for it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess."
"The opposite of that is superior, through the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 1).
Now, you are my friend and not my disciple; therefore, he says, "I am your disciple.
Because I am fit for your instruction, I am indeed your disciple and not a friend, owing to the inferiority of my knowledge.

Therefore, instruct and teach me, who have approached you and sought refuge in you, out of compassion; the meaning is that I am not to be neglected on the grounds of my being unfit as a disciple. By this, [the following is implied]: "For the sake of knowing That, one should go to a guru alone, with fuel in hand, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12); and "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).

He approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Blessed One," and so forth; thus has the meaning of the Śruti, which demonstrates the approach to a teacher (gurūpasatti), been shown. //7//
Viśvanātha:

[Objection: "In that case, being a Kṣatriya who proclaims the meaning of the scriptures with supporting arguments, you are now determining to wander for alms; therefore, enough of my words. To this he replies with the word *kārpaṇya*: "It is precisely my abandonment of innate valor that constitutes my wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*)."
"The course of Dharma is subtle; therefore, even regarding the determination of Dharma, I am indeed of deluded intellect. Thus, you yourself must decide and tell me what is best.
If, however, you are merely refuting my words out of a sense of pride in your own scholarship,"
How could I speak? To that he says: "I am your disciple. The implication is: "I shall not pointlessly destroy what has been understood. //7//

Baladeva: Furthermore, by the word "kārpaṇya," he demonstrates the approach to a guru as established by such scriptural passages as, "Then, for the sake of that knowledge, one should go to a teacher alone, with fuel in hand, one who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12) and, "A person possessing a teacher knows" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).

For it is heard in scripture: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10); thus, "kārpaṇya" refers to the state of not knowing Brahman.

For that reason, I am one whose nature is impaired by that very fault which arises from killing those who are my own kin—a fault characterized by ignorance—and whose own duty (*svadharma*) is characterized by a longing for battle.
My mind is thus deluded regarding duty, being in doubt whether battle is my *svadharma* as a Kṣatriya or whether wandering for alms is.
Being in such a state, I now ask you: therefore, tell me that which is certain, absolute, and final—the good (*śreya*) that would be for me.
Necessity is the state of being necessarily established by the superior proof; certainty is the non-perishing of what has come to be; and absoluteness is the state of being ultimate.
[Objection: But surely instruction should be given to one who has come for refuge, according to such Vedic texts as, "To understand that, one should approach a guru alone. [Reply:
If you ask, "How then can I instruct you, my friend? he says in response, "I am your disciple. "Instruct" means "teach. //7//
Indeed, I do not see what could dispel this grief of mine that withers the senses.
Having obtained on earth a prosperous kingdom without rivals, and even sovereignty over the gods. //8//
Śrīdhara: If it is argued, "You yourself should deliberate and do whatever is appropriate," he replies to that with the words, "Indeed, I do not perceive [any such thing].
I do not perceive any action that would dispel—that is, remove—my grief, which causes the drying up, the extreme desiccation, of the senses.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Even if I were to obtain a prosperous kingdom on earth free from thorns, and likewise even if I were to attain the sovereignty of the gods (*surendratva*), although I might thus acquire all those desired things, I do not perceive any means for the removal of my grief. (8)
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: "Surely you yourself should deliberate upon what is beneficial; you are endowed with sacred learning (*śruta*), so why [seek it] by being a pupil of another? To this he says: "Not indeed... That welfare which, once attained, would remove—that is, dispel or ward off—my grief, I do not see such a thing.

"Indeed, because of this, instruct me"—thus he said, "O Blessed One, I am grieving; may the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of this grief. This is the meaning of the Śruti that has been shown.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the harm in not removing grief?", he provides a qualification for it, saying: "the withering of the senses."
The meaning is that it causes suffering at all times.

Now, one might object: "If you exert yourself in battle, your grief will cease; for if you are victorious, you will obtain the kingdom, according to the Dharma-śāstras which state, 'There are these two persons in the world,' and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says, beginning with the words "Even having obtained," etc.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "I do not see anything that could dispel the grief of one like me, who, even after having attained a kingdom free from enemies and abundant with crops, and having reached the sovereignty of the gods and even the status of Hiraṇyagarbha, remains [in this state].
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Just as in this world the world won by action perishes, even so in the next world the world won by merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).

The meaning is this: because of the inference that "whatever is created is impermanent," and because the destruction of worldly things is seen even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), neither worldly nor otherworldly enjoyment can remove sorrow.

Rather, enjoyment produces sorrow precisely because it involves dependence on external factors even during its own existence, and because it is severed at the time of destruction. Therefore, battle should not be undertaken for the sake of removing sorrow.
By this, detachment from enjoyments both here and hereafter is shown as a qualification of the candidate. //8//
Viśvanātha:
But surely you have only a sense of friendship toward me, not respect.

Therefore, how can I make you my disciple? Consequently, seek out someone else, such as Dvaipāyana or another, in whom you have respect. To this he says: "Not indeed... [I do not see] anyone who could dispel—that is, remove—my grief; I do not clearly perceive even one such person in the three worlds apart from you.
The sense is: "I do not know even Bṛhaspati, who is superior to me in intelligence; therefore, being truly afflicted by grief, whom indeed shall I take refuge in?
For from this grief comes the withering of the senses, just as small ponds are completely dried up by a great heat.
[Arjuna said: "Well then, you are indeed afflicted by grief right now; fight!"

Therefore, he says "avāpya" (having obtained), meaning: even for one like me who has conquered these [senses] and obtained a kingdom, grief would depart only through attachment to the enjoyment of that kingdom;
however, even having obtained a kingdom on earth free of thorns, or sovereignty over the gods in heaven, this very drying up of my senses remains. //8//
Baladeva said: "Surely you are learned in the scriptures; having reflected upon your own welfare, act accordingly.
If it be asked how you can be a disciple of my friend, he replies with the words 'Not indeed' (na hi):
I do not perceive any action whatsoever that would remove—that is, drive far away—my grief."
He specifies grief as "the drying up of the senses.
Therefore, [he says], "I have taken refuge in you for the destruction of that grief.
Thus, the meaning of the Vedic text—"O Blessed One, I am grieving; may you carry me across to the further shore of this grief"—is demonstrated.

If you object: "Are you not now overwhelmed by grief? Once you have attained the acquisition of happiness and prosperity through war, you will become free from sorrow," he says in response: *avāpya* (having obtained).

The meaning is: if I should be victorious in battle, then having obtained a kingdom on earth without rivals or thorns; and if I should be slain there, then having obtained sovereignty over the gods in heaven—while established therein—there would still be no freedom from sorrow for me.
"Just as in this world the world won by action perishes, even so in the next world the world won by merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).

According to this Vedic scripture, the happiness obtained through battle—whether of this world or the next—is not capable of removing grief; therefore, please tell me of that very excellence which truly dispels sorrow, for battle does not remove grief.
Sanjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes, [remained silent].
Having said to Govinda, "I will not fight," he became silent. //9//
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry as to what Arjuna did after speaking thus, Sañjaya said "evam" and so forth.
The meaning is clear. //9//
Madhusūdana:
When Dhṛtarāṣṭra inquired what Arjuna did immediately after that, Sañjaya said, "Thus," and so forth.
Guḍākeśa—meaning one who has conquered sloth—the scorcher of enemies (parantapa), Arjuna, addressed Hṛṣīkeśa, the inner controller (antaryāmī) by virtue of being the impeller of all the senses.
By the etymological derivation that Govinda "finds" (vindati) the cow, which is speech characterized by the Vedas, He is omniscient as the source of all the Vedas.

Having first stated His own unfitness for the nature of battle with the words "How shall I [fight] Bhīṣma? and so forth, and subsequently having stated the absence of any fruit of battle with the words "I will not fight," he became silent, [abandoning] the activity of his external senses for the sake of war.
The meaning is that by the cessation of what was previously done, He has become inactive.
The word *ha* is used to indicate that neither adventitious laziness nor a lack of scorching power will find a footing in Him, who is by nature victorious over sloth and the scorcher of all enemies.
This is further emphasized by the two terms *Govinda* and *Hṛṣīkeśa*, which signify His omniscience and omnipotence.
It is indicated that for the Blessed One, the removal of that delusion is accomplished without effort. //9//
Viśvanātha: [Silence].
Baladeva: Then, in response to the expectation of what Arjuna did next, Sañjaya said, "Having spoken thus," and so forth.

Having stated to Hṛṣīkeśa that war does not remove his grief by saying, "Indeed, I do not see... and so on, even he, the scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, the knower of all Vedas, "I will not fight."
And having said this, [the word] "thus" (iti) should be supplied.

In that regard, because he is Hṛṣīkeśa, he will impel Arjuna’s intellect toward battle; and because he knows all the Vedas, he will cause him to grasp that battle is his own duty (svadharma). By making this manifest, the hope for the kingdom for his own sons, which had arisen in Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s heart, is dispelled. //9//

O descendant of Bharata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies: bhagavadgītā 2.10: tam uvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasann iva bhārata / senayor ubhayor madhye viṣīdantam idaṃ vacaḥ //10//
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry as to what occurred thereafter, he says, "He spoke to him.
The meaning is that he spoke while appearing as if smiling, with a serene countenance. //10//
Madhusūdana said:
"He spoke to him"—this was said to dispel Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s false hope that even though Arjuna had thus neglected the battle, the Blessed Lord had not neglected him;
[he spoke] to him who, having come between the two armies with the intent to fight, was falling into despondency and delusion which oppose that [resolve].

Hṛṣīkeśa, the Blessed Lord who dwells within all, spoke these words beginning with "Do not grieve for those who should not be grieved for," which possess a most profound meaning and reveal Arjuna's improper conduct; the sense is that He did not overlook him, as if smiling at him while immersing him in an ocean of shame by exposing his unseemly behavior.
*Prahāsa* (derision) is the production of shame by making manifest an improper action;

and since shame consists of suffering, it is primarily an object of *dveṣa* (aversion). However, because Arjuna is an object of the Lord’s compassion, and because making manifest his improper action is a cause for the arising of discernment (*viveka*), this *prahāsa* is merely secondary due to the absence of one of its two constituent parts. This is what is intended to be stated.
The word "iva" (as if):
the Lord reveals Arjuna’s improper conduct as if to produce shame or as if to produce embarrassment.
The sense is that whether the arising of shame actually occurs as an inevitable consequence or not is not intended to be emphasized.

For if he had remained indifferent to the battle even before its commencement, then he would not have acted improperly; however, having arrived on the battlefield with great excitement, his neglect of it is extremely improper—this is what is intended by the qualifying description "of the two armies" and so forth. This will become clear in the passage beginning with "those who are not to be grieved for. (10)
Viśvanātha:

"Oh, even you have such a lack of discernment!"—thus, by joking with him in a spirit of friendship, he seems to plunge him into an ocean of shame by exposing his impropriety; for at that moment, since he has assumed the status of a disciple, laughter is inappropriate.
The meaning is that he concealed his smile by contracting his lower lip.

By the term *Hṛṣīkeśa*, the sense is that although previously he was restrained by Arjuna’s speech through affection alone, he now likewise becomes the restrainer of Arjuna’s mind through affection, because he acts for Arjuna’s welfare. The meaning is that both Arjuna’s despondency and the Lord’s awakening are perceived equally by both armies standing between the two. //10//

Baladeva, elucidating the meaning of the deficient [text], says: "He spoke to him"—the Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa spoke these words of exceedingly profound meaning, beginning with "Do not grieve for those who should not be grieved for," to Arjuna, who was despondent;
doing so while smiling out of a sense of friendship, as if saying, "Oh, what a discernment this is!"

The meaning is that [the Lord] causes [Arjuna] to sink into an ocean of shame by speaking what is improper. The word "as if" (iva) means that, since Arjuna had just attained the status of a disciple, the Lord slightly parted his lips to manifest a smile because of the impropriety of laughing [at him]. The phrase "of both armies" is used to make known that Arjuna’s despondency and the Blessed One’s instruction to him were witnessed by everyone. //10//
The Blessed Lord said:
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom.
The wise do not grieve for those whose life has departed nor for those whose life has not yet departed. //11//

Śrīdhara: Because of the failure to discriminate between the body and the self, this grief arises for him; therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating that discrimination, the Blessed Lord said, "Aśocyān" and so forth. You have grieved—indeed, you have lamented—over those very kinsmen who are not objects of grief, by saying, "O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these my own people," and so on. Although I have awakened you with such words as, "Whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis? and so forth, you again [cite] the discourses—the spoken words—of the wise, the learned, such as, "How shall I [fight against] Bhīṣma? and so on.
You merely speak such words as "in battle" and so forth,
but you are not a wise man; for [you disregard] both kinsmen whose life-breaths have departed and those whose life-breaths have not yet departed, even while they are alive.
The wise and discerning do not grieve, thinking, "How will these people, deprived of their kinsmen, survive? //11//
Madhusūdana:
Here Viśvanātha says: O Arjuna, this grief of yours, caused by the slaying of your kinsmen, is rooted solely in delusion.
Likewise, he states "aśocyān" and so forth to show that even such discernment as "How shall I [slay] Bhīṣma in battle? is rooted solely in a lack of wisdom.
You have grieved for those who are "aśocyān"—those who truly do not deserve grief.

Furthermore, you speak words of wisdom—"How shall I [slay] Bhīṣma in battle? and so forth—toward me while I am attempting to awaken you, even though such statements are only possible when wisdom is absent.
The sense is that no wisdom whatsoever exists within you;

for the wise, those possessed of wisdom, do not grieve for the departed—the gross bodies from which the vital breaths (asus) have departed—because their nature is perishable. This is the underlying meaning.
They do not grieve for those whose life-force has departed, whose breath has not yet issued forth, even though they possess subtle bodies;
for these are indeed perishable prior to liberation,
since the respective natures of both are impossible to avoid.
The foolish, however, grieve only when the vital breaths have departed from the bodies of the ancestors and others,
but not for their subtle bodies.
Therefore, they are generally perceived as such, and thus enough with them;

for all these, Bhīṣma and the others, together with their gross and subtle bodies, are indeed the Self (ātman). Since the Selfs are eternal, there is no occasion for grief regarding them; therefore, that which you previously [derived] from the Arthaśāstra—
It has been stated that the *dharma-śāstra* is more powerful; however, my intention here is to say that even more powerful than the *dharma-śāstra* is the *jñāna-śāstra*. //11//
Baladeva: When Arjuna remained thus silent, the Blessed One, challenging his understanding, said, "Aśocyān" (Those not to be grieved for).
O Arjuna, you have grieved—indeed, you have lamented—over the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who are themselves "aśocyān," unworthy of being grieved for.

The sense is this: having seen such "words of wisdom" directed toward me— utterances like "this kinsman" and so forth, as well as "how [could you kill] Bhīṣma" and so forth— which resemble the speech of those possessed of wisdom, yet you do not possess even a trace of wisdom yourself.

But those who possess wisdom do not grieve over those whose life-breath has departed— the gross bodies— nor over those whose life-breath has not departed— the subtle bodies— neither on account of sound nor with regard to the Self.

The meaning is this: grief [is appropriate] for gross bodies because they are perishable; it is not [appropriate] for subtle bodies because they are non-perishable prior to liberation; and likewise, for the selves that possess them—which are devoid of the six modifications of being—it is not a cause for grief because of their eternity.
For those who know the true nature of the body and the self, there is no cause for grief whatsoever.
That which is stated regarding the superior authority of the *dharma-śāstra* over the *artha-śāstra* is,
it is said, countered by the *jñāna-śāstra*, which possesses even greater authority than that.
Therefore, the delusion of grieving for that which is not to be grieved for is common to the vulgar; it is not fitting for you, a wise man—this is the intended meaning. //11//
But indeed, I was never non-existent, nor were you, nor these lords of men; and none of us shall ever cease to be hereafter. (2.12)
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for the state of not being subject to grief in the verse beginning with "But never was I.

Just as I, the Supreme Lord, was never—at any time—non-existent due to the manifestation and disappearance of my play-forms (*līlā-vigraha*), so indeed was I always existent because of my beginninglessness.
And it is not that you did not exist—that you were not; rather, you certainly did exist.
Nor is it the case that these lords of men, these kings, did not exist.
Rather, because they are portions of My own self, they are indeed near [to Me].

Thus, neither is it the case that "henceforth, from this point upward, we shall not come into being nor shall we remain," but rather, because they are devoid of birth and death, they simply *shall remain*; such is the meaning of their being beyond grief. //12//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha—
or rather, my friend, I ask you this very thing.
Furthermore, when the death of one who is an object of affection is seen, sorrow arises;
in that case, here, is the object of affection the self (*ātman*) or the body?
According to the words of Śuka, "O King, for all beings, their own self alone is dear" (BhP 10.14.57), it is the self alone.

If it is argued that [the self] is the locus of joy, then, since the self—being of two kinds through the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—is eternal and thus devoid of death, the self cannot be an object of grief; to this he says: "But verily, I was not... That is, it is not the case that I, the Supreme Self, did not exist at any time whatsoever in the past.
But rather, it was indeed so; likewise, you too were indeed a living self (jīvātman),
and likewise these lords of men, the kings, were indeed living selves— thus the absence of prior non-existence has been demonstrated.

Thus, the statement "all of us—myself, you, and these lords of men—shall not exist nor remain hereafter" is not [the case]; rather, it is shown that there is indeed persistence (dhvaṃsābhāva). Since the Supreme Self and the individual selves (jīvātman) are eternal, it is established that the Self is not an object of grief. Regarding this, the scriptural authorities (śruti) begin with: "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13). //12//

Baladeva: Having thus established Arjuna’s lack of wisdom due to his misplaced grieving, and having directed him—who now desires to know the truth—with palms joined in reverence, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All, declares the ultimate ontological distinction between Himself and the individual souls (jīvas), as established by the Śruti in the verse: "The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13), by saying: "But never am I... and so forth.
O Arjuna,
I am the Lord of all, the Blessed One; it is not that at any time whatsoever in the past, in the beginning, I did not exist.
Rather,
you certainly were; it is not that you were not Arjuna, but indeed you were.

It is not that these kings, the lords of men, did not exist; rather, they certainly did exist. Likewise, it is not that at the end of time beyond this, we all—myself, you, and these others—will not exist.
"But we shall indeed exist," [is the thought].
The meaning is that since both the Lord of All and individual souls possess existence throughout the three periods of time, grief concerning them is not appropriate.
Nor is this distinction merely conventional, as it is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is because [such a view] would apply even to the omniscient Blessed One due to his connection with ignorance;
and because, by the statement beginning "having relied upon this knowledge," his non-distinction [from all beings] will be declared even in the state of liberation.

Nor should it be argued that even for Hari—who knows there is no difference—this perception of difference in Arjuna and others occurs according to the principle of the persistence of the sublated (bādhitānuvṛtti-nyāya).

This being so, since the instruction would not be established, [your argument is] trivial: for even though the cognition of water in a mirage and the like is sublated, it continues to persist and, because its object is determined to be false, it does not lead one to act toward fetching water; likewise, although the cognition of non-difference is sublated, it will not lead one to act toward instruction and the like because its reality is determined. Thus, this is nothing at all.

Now, one might object: since the purport of the scripture is observed to lie in an unknown object that possesses a fruit, such non-difference (abheda) must be the object of that purport because difference is fruitless and already known;

thus, difference cannot be its object, but rather, like the meaning of such scriptural passages as "He indeed rises from the waters in the morning and enters the waters in the evening," it is merely something to be restated (anuvādya). This is weak.

For, from such passages as "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one then attains immortality" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.6), difference alone is heard to be the fruit of immortality;
and because that [difference] is unknown in the world due to its having as its counter-correlate that which is delimited by contradictory attributes.
Those attributes—such as omnipresence and atomicity, lordship and servitude, and so forth—are to be understood as mutually contradictory and knowable solely through the scriptures.
Non-difference, however, is fruitless in that context, because no fruit is admitted there;
and it is unknown, because it lacks existence, like a hare's horn.
Therefore, its ultimate difference is established. //12//
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this. 2.13
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "It is indeed true that for You, the Lord, there is an absence of birth and so forth; however, birth and death are well-known for living beings (jīvas).
To this, He says: 'Of the embodied one' (dehinaḥ), etc."

Just as for the embodied soul (jīva), who possesses the conceit of being the body, the states such as childhood and so forth in this gross body are dependent solely upon that body and not inherent to itself, since the previous state has perished.
Because there is recognition in the form "I am that very same person" even when a different state arises;
likewise, upon the destruction of this body, the attainment of another body is also dependent solely on the subtle body (liṅga-deha).
There is, for the time being, no destruction of the self.
Because it is observed that immediately upon birth, an infant engages in activities such as suckling milk due to past impressions (*pūrva-saṃskāra*),
the wise and intelligent person is not deluded regarding those two— the destruction of the body and its rebirth—
and does not think, "It is the very self that has died and been born. //13//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha:
But surely, by virtue of its connection with the self, the body too would be an object of affection?
If it is argued that even sons, brothers, and so forth exist through their connection to the body,
and their sons and so forth likewise through their connection to them—
and therefore grief would certainly arise upon their destruction— the author says "of the embodied" (dehinām) to address this.

Just as for the embodied soul (*dehin*) in this body there is the attainment of childhood— meaning the arrival at the state of childhood— and following the destruction of that childhood, the attainment of old age occurs, in exactly the same way does the attainment of another body occur.

Therefore, just as grief is not felt when childhood and other such states related to the self— which are objects of affection— are destroyed, so too should no grief be felt upon the destruction of the body, which is also related to the self and an object of affection.
It should not be done.

If you argue that sorrow arises when youth perishes and old age is attained, then joy also arises when childhood perishes and youth is attained; therefore, upon the destruction of the worn-out bodies of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others, and the attainment of new, different bodies, [sorrow is indeed inappropriate].
The sense is: "In that case, let joy be felt.
Or rather, just as one obtains the states of childhood and so forth within a single body, so too does a single embodied soul, the *jīva*, obtain various bodies. //13//

Baladeva: If it is argued that although the selves (ātman) delimited by the bodies of Bhīṣma and others are eternal, grief is nevertheless appropriate upon the destruction of those bodies which serve as the seats of their experience, he says in response: "Of the embodied one in this...
He who possesses many bodies throughout the three periods of time is the "embodied one" (dehin).
For that embodied soul (jīva) in this present body, there occur three successive stages: childhood, youth, and old age.

Just as one feels no grief when these stages—belonging to the self and conducive to its experience—are reached one after another through the destruction of each preceding state, so too, upon the destruction of this body, the attainment of another body is a cause for joy, according to the principle of King Yayāti’s acquisition of youth.
The sense is that grief caused by the destruction of that body is not appropriate for you.

"The wise one" (dhīra) means one who is intelligent and who knows the true nature of the body, the self, and the ripening of karma. Here, the singular form "of the embodied one" (dehinaḥ) should be understood as intended generically, because the plurality of selves was previously mentioned.
On this point, they say: there is only one pure Self; its state as manifold arises either because it is delimited by ignorance or because it is reflected therein.
And scripture says thus: "Just as the one space appears divided within jars and other vessels, so the one Self, though abiding in many places, is like the sun in various reservoirs of water."
Pārthasārathi says that when that [intellect] is destroyed by the cognition of it, its unity is established through the cessation of its manifoldness;
however, this is weak, because it is impossible for that inert [intellect] to cut through a mass of consciousness,
and because those [cognitions] themselves do not admit of being objects of that [intellect].

In reality, if there were actual cutting, it would entail the consequence of undergoing transformation, like a stone split by a chisel; furthermore, because a reflection is impossible for that which is formless and all-pervading, otherwise [if it were possible], such a consequence would apply to space and so forth as well.

Nor is the "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti) of perception the sole proof for a reflection in space, since the orb of light from the planets and stars situated therein is perceived as appearing within the water.
The scriptural statement, "For space is indeed one," refers to the Supreme Self; it is not contradictory, as it declares that [the Self] possesses manifold functions like space and like the sun.
Furthermore, no teacher of the identity of the self is possible.

For is he a knower of reality or not? In the first case, for one who knows the non-dual Self, there is no manifestation of anyone to be instructed. In the latter case, however, precisely because of his ignorance, he cannot be an instructor of the knowledge of the Self.
But resorting to the persistence of what has been sublated has already been refuted previously. //13//
But the contacts with the senses, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata. (2.14)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "Indeed, I do not grieve for them, but rather for myself, who must endure the suffering of separation from them and so forth. To this he says: "The contacts of the senses... (mātrā-sparśāḥ). They are called *mātrās* because objects are measured (*mīyante*) or perceived through them; thus, they are the functions of the senses.
Their contacts, bound to sense objects, produce cold, heat, and so forth;
yet these are impermanent and unstable because they are subject to coming and going.
Therefore, endure them and withstand them.

Just as contact with water, sunlight, and so forth, produced at their respective times, naturally yield cold, heat, and the like, so too do the union with and separation from the desired yield pleasure and pain.
Since these are unstable, it is fitting for you, who are steadfast, to endure them; the meaning is that you should not fall under the sway of joy or dejection caused by them. //14//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha: But surely, reality is indeed the truth.
Even that [pleasure] causes suffering to my mind, which lacks discrimination, as if it were enveloped by grief and delusion.

In this regard, it is not only the single mind that is so, but all the modifications of the mind as well—those consisting of the senses such as the ear and so forth—which, by making their respective objects experienced, act for one's harm. He says: "The *mātrās* are the objects perceivable by the senses; their *sparśas* are the experiences thereof."

Regarding the statement "cold and heat are subject to coming and going": that very same thing such as cool water which gives pleasure during the hot season becomes a source of pain during the cold season; therefore, because they are unstable and subject to coming and going, endure—that is, bear with—those experiences of sense objects. Enduring them is precisely the duty prescribed by the scriptures.
For one does not abandon the religious duty (dharma) in the form of bathing prescribed in the scriptures during the month of Māgha simply because of the perception that the water is painful.
Indeed, it is dharma itself that, when practiced at the proper time, becomes the remover of all misfortunes.

In the very same way, those very things—such as sons, brothers, and so forth—which provide pleasure at the time of their birth and at the time of acquiring wealth and the like, become the givers of pain at the time of death; they are subject to coming and going.
"Endure even those who are constant [in their hostility].

However, one must not abandon one's own duty (svadharma) as defined by the scriptures in the form of battle out of compliance with them; for the meaning is that the non-performance of prescribed duties at the proper time indeed brings about great calamity. //14//
Baladeva: [Objection: "But Bhīṣma and others have died; how will they come back? Let there be no grief caused by sorrow for them.

However, the grief caused by the pain of their separation burns my mind and other faculties. To this, he says: "The *mātrās*... The *mātrās* are the functions of the senses, such as the ears and so forth, based on the etymological derivation that they are those by which objects (*viṣayas*) are measured (*mīyante*) or delimited.
Indeed, through those sensations, the experiences of objects result in the giving of cold, heat, pleasure, and pain.

Just as water that is cool and pleasant in the summer becomes painful in the winter, you must endure and bear these things because they are uncertain and subject to coming and going; they are impermanent and unstable. What is meant by this is that just as the ritual bath in the month of Māgha—though it causes suffering—is performed because it is ordained by Dharma, so too the battle with Bhīṣma and the others, though it causes suffering, is likewise ordained.
It is indeed the duty [to act].
However, the experience of suffering therein is adventitious; since it is established by *dharma*, it must be endured.
But when liberation is attained through the arising of knowledge from *dharma*, subsequently—
There is no persistence in that [state], nor is there the culmination of knowledge; indeed, the abandonment of dharma without the ripening [of wisdom] is a cause of misfortune.
By the two words "O Kaunteya" and "O Bhārata," it is indicated that for you, whose lineage on both sides is pure, a fall from dharma is not fitting. //14//
For that steadfast man, O bull among men, whom these do not afflict, who is equal in pleasure and pain— he is fit for immortality. (2.15)
Śrīdhara: Even more than making an effort to counteract them, it is appropriate to endure them because of their great fruit; thus he says, "yaṃ hi" (for whom).
Those contacts with the objects of the senses (*mātrā-sparśāḥ*) which do not cause distress—that is, do not overcome—a certain person, for whom pleasure and pain are equal, him [they do not affect].
Not being distracted by those [defilements], he becomes fit—that is, capable—for immortality and liberation through the gateway of knowledge of the Dharma. //15//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha:
Thus, when through such inquiry there is the practice of enduring each of those [experiences], those experiences of sense objects will indeed, in time, no longer cause pain.
And if they do not cause suffering, then liberation for oneself is indeed very near; thus he says "yam" (whom). "For immortality" means for liberation. //15//
Baladeva: Demonstrating that the practice of enduring suffering for the sake of dharma and artha serves as a cause for future happiness, he says, "He whom...

These contacts with the senses (*mātrā-sparśāḥ*), which are the experiences of pleasant and unpleasant objects, do not afflict—that is, they do not overwhelm with pleasure and pain—the wise man (*dhīram*) who is established in dharma, based on the etymology "one who impels the intellect (*dhiyam īrayati*) toward duties."
He is fit for immortality and liberation;
the meaning is that he is not one who is thus stupefied by suffering and pleasure.
Clarifying the stated point, [the author] qualifies the person with the word "sameti" (he attains).

Because the practice of dharma is difficult to accomplish, suffering is its inherent consequence; yet, for one whose happiness derived from such consequences is equal to that suffering—meaning they are free from the fading of the face due to distress or the brightening of the face due to joy—this is the intended sense. //15//
The unreal has no being, nor does the real have non-being;
the truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality. (2.16)

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "Even so, how can cold, heat, and the like—which are extremely difficult to endure—be tolerated? And if they are endured to the extreme, could there not sometimes be the destruction of the body? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Of the non-existent, no being exists," with the intention that everything can be endured through the investigation of reality (*tattva-vicāra*). Because it is a property of the non-self (*anātma-dharma*), the non-existent—such as cold, heat, and so forth—has no existence (*bhāva*) or presence (*sattā*) within the Self.
Likewise, for the Self, which is existent and possesses the nature of existence, there is no non-existence or destruction.
Thus, the conclusion regarding the end of both the existent and the non-existent has been seen by those who perceive reality— those who know the true nature of things.
The meaning is: "Dwell together with such a state of seclusion. //16//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha:
And this has been said with reference to those who have ascended to the stage of discrimination (viveka).

In reality, however, according to the scriptural text, "For this person is indeed unattached," there is no connection whatsoever between the individual self (jīvātman) and the gross and subtle bodies, nor with their attributes such as grief, delusion, and so forth;
for that connection is merely imagined through ignorance (avidyā). Thus he says, "No.

Because they are unreal and are not attributes of the Self, grief, delusion, and the like—which do not exist in the individual self—possess no existence or reality, nor does the body which is their locus.
Thus, for the living self (jīvātman), which is existent and of the nature of truth, there is no non-existence or destruction.
Therefore, this is the observed conclusion regarding both of these—the unreal and the real.

Consequently, since the living selves in Bhīṣma and others, as well as in you and others, are real and therefore imperishable, there can be no grief, delusion, or the like arising from the failure to distinguish between the body and the embodied; how then could Bhīṣma and the others perish?
Or rather, the sense is: "Why do you grieve for them? //16//
Baladeva: Thus, the Blessed Lord has refuted Arjuna’s wisdom by showing that his grief was misplaced.

He has taught that the remover of grief is His own worship, and since that worship is constituted by the distinction between the object of worship and the worshiper, He has taught a real duality between Himself—the part-whole (the possessor of parts) who is the object of worship—and the worshipers who are His partial selves.
This is according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (2.15): "But he who, endowed with the lamp-like knowledge of the Self-principle, perceives here the Brahman-principle..."

Since it is heard in such passages that knowledge of the nature of the parts is useful for knowledge of the nature of the whole, that [knowledge] should be taught at the outset without distinction to all, including those established in devotion (sanniṣṭha) and others; and since that would not occur without the cognition of the difference between the body and the self, the difference between them is begun to be understood through the verses beginning with "Not of the non-existent" (nāsataḥ).
The existence—meaning non-transformability—of that which is non-existent and subject to transformation, such as the body and so forth, does not exist;
likewise, the non-existence—meaning transformability—of that which is existent and non-transformable, namely the Self, does not exist.
Thus, the body and the Self possess the natures of transformation and non-transformation, respectively.

Thus, the end— the final determination— of both the body and the self, which are respectively designated by the terms "non-existent" (asat) and "existent" (sat), has been seen and experienced by those who perceive reality and who know the true nature of both.
Here, the term "non-existent" refers to the perishable, insentient body and so forth, while the term "existent" refers to the imperishable consciousness of the Self.

In the same way, it is also determined in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
