Beginning with the verse, "The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu," and continuing with, "Whatever exists and whatever does not exist, O best of Brahmins," the nature of both the conscious and the insentient—denoted by the words "exists" and "does not exist"—is established through such statements as, "Is there any reality anywhere? and so forth.
In this regard, that which is denoted by the word "is not" is the insentient;
however, that which is denoted by the word "is" is consciousness—this has been explained by [the author] himself.

As for the claim that this verse is intended to establish the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*sat-kārya-vāda*), that is inattentive; for its purpose is to dispel the delusion of one who is bewildered by ignorance regarding the true nature of the self as distinct from the body, by making known that very nature.
Because it is the subject under discussion. //16//
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable.

Śrīdhara: Here, the indestructible entity whose nature is real has been described in general; it is "pervaded" (tataṃ), meaning it is pervaded as its witness. Know—that is, understand—that very Self-nature to be indestructible, devoid of destruction.
He states the reason for this with the words "destruction" (vināśam). //17//
Madhusūdana:
[The Lord] clarifies the meaning of the statement "there is no non-existence of the existent" by saying "indestructible."
That which is the nature of the individual soul (jīvātman) by which this entire body is pervaded and permeated.
Now, one might object: "If consciousness pervades only the body, then because the individual soul would possess an intermediate dimension, it would follow that it is non-eternal. Not so;
for the Lord has stated, "I am the individual soul," even though souls are subtle.
"This subtle self is to be known by the mind, in which the vital breath has entered fivefold";
and "The individual soul (jīva) should be understood as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundred times. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9]
For from such scriptural passages as "another [atom] is seen to be the size of the tip of a goad," its dimension is indeed that of an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Yet, even so, its possession of power pervading the entire body is not inconsistent; it is like the power of a great jewel or a piece of potent medicine embedded in lac, which, when worn on the head or the chest, possesses the power to nourish the entire body.
And its wandering through heaven, hell, and various wombs occurs precisely due to its subjection to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
This was stated by Dattātreya with reference to the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "That by which the person transmigrates.
For this very reason, its all-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*), which will be described in the following verse, is not inconsistent.

For this very reason, the Śruti declares: "The Imperishable, the Eternal among eternals, the Consciousness among conscious beings, the One who ordains the desires of the many" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13).
Alternatively, one might object: "Indeed, this triad of entities—the body, the individual self (jīvātman), and the Supreme Self—is observed everywhere among humans, animals, and so forth;
of these, the reality of the first two, namely the body and the individual self, has been stated by the verse: 'There is no being of that which is non-existent'."
To the question, "What is the true nature of the third reality, the Supreme Self (paramātman)? he says: "But [it is] indestructible" (*avināśi tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) marks a distinct beginning.
Because the Supreme Self is by its very nature distinct from both Māyā and the individual soul (jīva), this world [is not its essence]. //17//
Baladeva: With two verses beginning with "indestructible" (avināśī), he clarifies the nature of the individual soul and the body.
Know that reality of the individual soul to be indestructible and eternal, by which—through its attribute of knowledge—all this body is pervaded and permeated.

No gross object whatsoever is capable of bringing about the destruction of this immutable [Self], which—being of the nature of an atom—is incapable of destruction, just as the body cannot destroy the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Here, the living self (*jīvātman*) is not to be understood as being limited in size to the body;
for its atomicity is heard of in such passages as: "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind, into which the vital breath has entered fivefold" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.9).
The pervasion of such a self throughout the entire body, however, must occur through knowledge that has become an attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*).
Thus the Blessed Lord, the author of the Sūtras, stated: "Or [it is] due to its quality, like light" (VS 2.3.26).
Here too, he himself will say: "Just as one [light] illuminates... (Gītā 13.33), and so forth. //17//
These bodies are said to have an end, whereas the embodied self is eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable; therefore, fight, O Bhārata! (2.18)
Śrīdhara: [The Lord] demonstrates that [the body] has the nature of coming and going by saying, "they have an end.
Those for whom an end—that is, destruction—exists are "those who have an end" (antavantaḥ).
Of the embodied one (śarīriṇaḥ), that is, of the possessor of a body, who is eternal and whose form is always one and the same.

Therefore, by those who perceive the truth, these bodies characterized by attributes such as pleasure and pain have been described as belonging to the Self— which is indestructible, devoid of destruction, and immeasurable, being unlimited.
Since the Self is thus without destruction and has no connection with pleasure, pain, and the like, [it remains eternally unchanged].
Therefore, having abandoned this grief born of delusion, fight;
the meaning is: do not abandon your own duty (svadharma). //18//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: But how can that which is of the nature of manifestation (sphuraṇa) be indestructible, given that it is an attribute of the body and the body perishes moment by moment? Thus, refuting those who maintain the doctrine of elemental consciousness (bhūta-caitanya-vādin), he explains the statement "the being of the non-existent exists" with the words "they have an end."
These directly perceived bodies are finite and perishable because they consist of forms that are accumulated and dissipated;
by virtue of the plural number, they include the gross, subtle, and causal forms known as Virāṭ, Sūtra, and Unmanifest (avyākṛta), comprising both the collective and individual selves.
All these belong to the one eternal and imperishable embodied Self, which possesses a body through an illusory superimposition (ādhyāsika-sambandha).
The Śrutis and the proponents of Brahman have declared that which is of the nature of self-luminous manifestation to be the object of perception and the object of enjoyment for its correlate.

Thus, in the Taittirīyaka, having postulated the five sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* and ending with the *ānandamaya*, it is stated that the unpostulated Brahman, which is their substratum, is "the tail, the support" (*taittU 2.5*).
This has been shown.

Therein, the aggregate of the gross body (*virāṭ-mūrta-rāśi*), consisting of the five gross elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) and their products (*tat-kārya*)— the fivefold-composed (*pañcīkṛta*) ones— is the sheath made of food (*anna-maya-kośa*), which is the gross totality (*sthūla-samaṣṭi*).

Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the cause of that [universe], consisting of the five unquintuplicated great elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañca-mahābhūta*) and their effects, is the thread, the formless mass, and the subtle aggregate; he is the triad described in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (1.6.1) as "these three: name, form, and action," and being essentially all action, he is said to be the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*), taking up only the power of activity (*kriyā-śakti*).
Taking up that which consists of name as mere power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti-mātra*), it is called the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kośa*).
Taking up agency as the basis for both of those by way of its consisting of form (*rūpātmakatva*), it is called the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*).
Thus, the single sheath of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) known as Hiraṇyagarbha consists of the vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), the mind (*manomaya*), and consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).

But its cause is the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa), known as the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which has consciousness conditioned by māyā as its essence and in which all latent impressions (saṃskāra) remain.
And it has been stated that all these are the bodies of one and the same Self;
of that [Self], this very [sheath] is the embodied one.
Regarding the phrase "the self which belongs to the former" (TaittU 2.3.4):

this very one who exists within the body is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of that *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath), which is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, and was described as being hidden in the cave of the heart in relation to the preceding *annamaya* (consisting of food).
This same principle should be applied accordingly to the *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*.
Alternatively, the construction is as follows: all these bodies belonging to every living being existing in the three worlds are said to belong to one and the same Self.
And so says the Śruti:
"The one God is hidden in all beings."
Pervading all, the inner self of all beings,
the supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the sole one within the heart, and devoid of qualities. [ŚvetU 6.11]

Thus, he shows that there is one eternal and all-pervading Self related to all bodies. Now, one might object: "Eternality consists in persisting as long as time exists; therefore, even if it were destroyed along with time—as in the case of ignorance (avidyā) and the like—such [eternality] would still be possible. To this he says: "indestructible" (anāśin).

For while ignorance and the like, being limited by space, time, and substance, are impermanent due to their being merely imagined (kalpita), the nature of the Self persists for as long as time exists.
The permanence [of the self] is spoken of only figuratively, according to the maxim: "But as long as there is modification, there is division, as in the world" (VS 2.3.7).

However, for the Self—which is devoid of the three kinds of limitation and is unconstructed—there is no cause for destruction; therefore, its permanence is primary, being immutable (*kūṭastha-nityatva*), and not a permanence consisting of transformation (*pariṇāmi-nityatva*) or mere endurance for a certain duration.
This is the intended meaning.

Now, in the case of such an embodied being, some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily be stated; otherwise, lacking a means of valid cognition, it would follow that he is non-existent, and the commencement of the scripture would also result in futility.
This is also because of the logical principle: "And because [the Veda] has its source in the determination of reality" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3).
Therefore, he says: "of the unmeasurable."
"This alone should be seen as one; it is immeasurable and eternal. "Immeasurable" means unmeasurable. "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars;
these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. (Katha Upanishad 5.15)

And according to the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10), the Self is indeed of the nature of self-luminous consciousness. Therefore, for that which illuminates everything, there is no dependence on anything else to be illuminated for the sake of its own manifestation.
However, for the sake of the cessation of imagined ignorance and its effects, there is a requirement for a specific imagined mental modification (*vṛtti*),
because only that which is imagined can oppose what is imagined, according to the maxim:
"The offering must correspond to the spirit."
And thus, the commencement of the treatise is for the purpose of producing a specific mental state (*vṛtti*) that removes all conceptual constructions (*kalpita*),
since its [realization] depends solely on sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*). Furthermore,

because it manifests at all times by itself, because it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all conceptual constructions, and because it illuminates everything that is perceived, it does not incur the status of being a non-entity (*tucchatva*).

And thus, the very scripture stating "Brahman is one only, without a second, truth, knowledge, infinite," and so forth, by virtue of its own object of cognition, leads to the conclusion that it itself is also imagined; for otherwise, its own validity would be untenable.
Furthermore, it has been established previously that what is imagined cannot be the determiner of what is unimagined.
Moreover, the self-luminosity of the Self has been demonstrated through reasoning by the venerable Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
For instance, it is observed everywhere that where an inquirer possesses none of the three—doubt, error, or the absence of valid cognition—there exists a cognition contrary to them;
otherwise, one of these three would necessarily occur.
Furthermore, no one ever has a doubt regarding the self in the form of "Is this 'I' or not?"

Nor can it be said that the misconception "I am not" is either a negative cognition (*vyatireka*) or a valid cognition (*pramā*), for there is always a valid cognition of its own nature; this is because it serves as the substratum (*dharmin*) for all doubt and misconception, according to the principle that "in the aspect of the substratum everything is non-erroneous, but in the aspect of the qualifier (*prakāra*) there is misconception.
Therefore, it has been said:
Since valid cognition, invalid cognition,
and even fallacious cognition alike produce valid knowledge in that regard, how could there be any doubt regarding its possibility?
[Br̥had-vāmanaP 1.4.874] "Apparent valid cognition is doubt.
The meaning is that, regarding a subject (*dharmin*) which is self-luminous and of the nature of existence (*sat*), there is no distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge.
Furthermore, if the self were not manifest, there would arise doubts such as, "Has the cognition of a jar arisen in me, or has it not?
Nor is it the case that for an internal object, the object itself possesses the nature of being an obstacle to doubt and so forth;

for while in the case of external objects the obstruction of doubt and so forth is possible through a contradictory cognition, it is inappropriate to postulate a difference in intrinsic nature for an internal object.
Otherwise, the consequence would be a total collapse of all [cognition].
Furthermore, the mere conjunction of the self and the mind is the cause for the direct perception of the self.

And since that [conjunction] is the cause for cognition in general, the manifestation of the self would also necessarily occur even when a jar or similar object is perceived—according to the logic of a "collective apprehension" (*samūhālambana*)—a conclusion which is difficult to avoid even for the most eminent of logicians.
Furthermore, there is no confusion (saṅkara) between being visible to the eye, being an object of valid cognition, and being existent;
for this is logically consistent through a distinction of parts, just as in the case of being worldly and being transcendental.
Alternatively, such confusion is not a fault, or because visibility and the like are not admitted to be universals (jāti).
Since the causal complex for the manifestation of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) itself is present, even the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is discarded;
nor is it required for the manifestation of the primary cognition, because, like a lamp, it does not depend on another of its own kind for its own operation.

For there is no distinctness (*vaijātya*)—apart from the difference in individual entities—that establishes the relationship of objecthood and subjecthood between the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) and the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), just as it exists between a jar and the cognition of that jar; this is because you do not admit any dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) other than the difference in individuals.

Furthermore, if you admit that subjecthood is characterized by the very same form that delimits objecthood, then the same would apply to the jar and its cognition, as there is no distinction between the two cases.

[Objection: Just as the cognition of a jar is admitted for the sake of the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the jar, so too [is the subsequent cognition admitted] for the sake of the practical usage regarding the cognition of the jar.

If it is argued that "the cognition whose object is the cognition of a jar must be admitted [as self-luminous], because linguistic usage is accomplished by the cognition of the object of that usage," then what inconsistency has been pointed out by the "Beloved of the Gods" (the opponent) against the proponent of self-luminosity?
For even the qualification of "being distinct from the object of usage" is not the delimitor of the causal efficiency for linguistic usage, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

Likewise, just as the knowledge of Īśvara and the knowledge of a yogi are objects of cognition (*prameya*), and just as [the object] is known by its own [cognition], when the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of a thing is established by that very [cognition] itself, there is no room for postulating another cognition.

It must be examined whether the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) serves as the cause for the practical usage of the cognition of a jar by virtue of being a "cognition of the cognition of a jar," or rather by virtue of being simply the "cognition of a jar";
for both [conditions] exist therein.

In that regard, since the causality for the conventional usage of "pot" is established solely by way of being a cognition of a pot, it is possible for the cognition of a pot to function as a cause for the conventional usage of "cognition of a pot" in that very same form; therefore,
the property of being a cognition of the cognition of a pot is not the delimiting factor of causality, due to both complexity and a lack of evidence.

And thus, there is no establishment of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), because it is possible for a single determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) to produce linguistic usage with respect to the cognizer, the object cognized, and the cognition itself; so say the Prābhākaras, who maintain that perception consists of a triadic form.

The followers of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadas*), however, hold that the self is of the very nature of self-luminous knowledge and is not the substratum of self-luminous knowledge, because its manifestation as such would be impossible due to the contradiction between being an agent and being an object.
Furthermore, if it were distinct from knowledge, it would follow that it is insentient and thus imagined as being like a jar or other such objects.
Although the Self is by nature pure self-luminous knowledge alone, when conditioned by ignorance (avidyā), it is called the Witness (sākṣin);
when conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possessing mental modifications (vṛtti), it is called the knower (pramātṛ).
The eyes and so forth are its instruments.
By means of the transformation of the internal organ through the doors of the eyes and so forth, it pervades jars and other objects and assumes their form.
Thereupon, consciousness delimited by the jar, by virtue of its non-difference from the knower, destroys its own ignorance and becomes directly manifest.
And the jar manifests its own delimiting adjunct through the superimposition of identity with itself.

Furthermore, the modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), called a "cognitive state" (vṛtti), being extremely transparent, is manifested by consciousness delimited by itself alone; thus, there is the immediacy (aparokṣatā) of the internal organ, its cognitive state, and the jar.
This constitutes the threefold form [of cognition]: "I know the jar."

Although the consciousness that illumines is of a single nature, it is designated as the "knower" (pramātṛ) with respect to an object such as a jar because it requires a mental modification (vṛtti); however, with respect to the internal organ and its modifications, it is designated as the "witness" (sākṣin) because it does not require a modification— this is the distinction.
The details are found in the *Advaitasiddhi* and the *Siddhāntabindu*.
Since, by the reasoning previously stated, the Self is thus eternal, omnipresent, free from saṃsāra, and always of one uniform nature,
it is therefore not proper for you— who have already engaged in battle as your own duty— to desist from it out of fear that it might perish.
With the permission for battle, the Blessed One said, "Therefore, fight, O Bhārata.
For Arjuna, who was engaged in battle as his own duty (*svadharma*), the causes of desisting from it were grief and delusion;

since these two have been sublated by the higher knowledge born of inquiry, the statement "fight" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) rather than an injunction (*vidhi*), according to the maxim that when an exception (*apavāda*) is itself sublated, the general rule (*utsarga*) remains established.
Just as *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) is a general rule (*utsarga*),
and *ubhaya-prāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66) is its exception (*apavāda*),
so too the statement "it should be stated that [the sixth case ending is not used] when feminine suffixes other than *kā* and *ikā* are employed" is an exception to that [latter rule].

And thus, in the phrase "the desire to know Brahman for one seeking liberation" (*mumukṣor brahmaṇo jijñāsā*), since the general rule is reinstated after the exception has been set aside, the genitive case is applied by the very rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65].
Consequently, because the prohibition [*karmaṇi ca*] does not apply here, the compound *brahma-jijñāsā* is established as a genitive-case compound denoting the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
However, someone might prattle on that from this very injunction there is a combination of knowledge and action for liberation;
but that is not so, because from the command "fight," it is not understood that liberation is to be accomplished through a combination of knowledge and action.
We shall refute this at length later on, precisely by showing its contradiction with the words of the Bhagavad Gītā. //18//
Viśvanātha:
He clarifies the meaning of the statement "the non-existent has no being" with the words "having an end," etc.
This refers to the embodied soul (jīva), who is immeasurable, extremely subtle, and therefore difficult to know.
Therefore, the sense is that it is improper to abandon one's own duty (svadharma) as ordained by the scriptures, [expressed in the words] "fight. //18//
Baladeva: "Finite" means having a perishable nature;
[they belong to] the embodied beings, the individual souls (*jīvātman*).
"Of the immeasurable" means that which is impossible to measure due to its extreme subtlety and because its essential nature consists of consciousness and the knower of consciousness.

Thus, because they possess such a nature, the living self and its body are not objects of grief; rather, the body is created by the Supreme Lord for the sake of the soul's experience and liberation through the performance of dharma. That [body] exists by means of dharma; therefore, fight, O Bhārata! (18)
He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks this is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain. (2.19)
Śrīdhara: Thus, grief caused by the death of Bhīṣma and others has been dispelled;

as for the sorrow mentioned on account of one's own agency in killing, expressed in the words "I do not wish to kill these," etc., he says "ya enam" (he who [kills] this) to show that even that is likewise without a real cause.
"This self"—the meaning is that this self possesses neither the state of being the object (*karman*) nor the state of being the agent (*kartṛ*) in the act of its own killing.
The reason for this is stated as "for it is not this [self]. (19)
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: But even if grief arising from the separation from kinsmen such as Bhīṣma has been removed by the passage beginning with "Yet you grieve for those who should not be grieved for," there is still no remedy for the sin arising from being the agent of their slaughter.
There is no rule that wherever there is no sorrow, there is no sin;
for otherwise, it would follow that there is an absence of sin in the killing of a Brahmin who is hated.
Therefore, this [position] is untenable, as both—the one who acts and the one who instigates—would incur the sin caused by violence.
Anticipating the objection that one should therefore fight, O Bhārata, the Blessed One refutes it with the verse recited in the Kaṭhaka Upaniṣad beginning with "He who...
He who knows this aforementioned embodied being—characterized by qualities such as invisibility—as the slayer, that is, as the agent of the act of killing, thinking "I am his slayer";
and he who thinks otherwise of him, considering him slain—that is, perceiving him as the object of the act of killing, thinking "I am killed" because the body has been killed.
Both of them, due to their identification with the body, do not know this Self—which is changeless and non-agential by nature—through discernment as taught in the scriptures.
Why? Because "this one neither kills nor is killed," meaning that it is neither an agent nor does it experience the fruit of action.
Although it would have been sufficient to say simply, "he who knows this one as the killer or the slain," the repetition of these words serves as an ornament for the verse.
Alternatively, it should be construed thus: "Both he who knows him as the slayer— the logician and others, because they admit the self's agency—
and likewise he who thinks him slain— the Cārvāka and others, because they admit the self's perishability—
neither of these two understands."

The separate presentation is for the purpose of indicating the distinction between the disputants; or, the separate instruction is given because they are subjects who are either exceedingly brave or excessively timid.
As for the first half-verse, "If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain" (KaṭhU 1.2.19), this is the Vedic reading. //19//
Viśvanātha:
O friend Arjuna,
you are the Self.
He says "he" (yaḥ) to indicate that [the Self] is neither the agent of killing nor the object of killing;
the meaning is: he who perceives this individual soul (jīvātman) as the killer, thinking "Arjuna kills Bhīṣma and the others."
"He is slain" refers to Bhīṣma and others; "Arjuna slays" refers to Arjuna. Both of these [views] belong to the ignorant.
Therefore, what fear do you have regarding the ill repute sung by the ignorant world that "this Arjuna is killing his elders"? This is the intended meaning. //19//
Baladeva: This verse confirms the previously stated indestructibility.

He who perceives this Self—the individual soul (*jīva*)—which possesses the nature just described, as a slayer who harms it with a sword or other weapons, and he who thinks that it is slain or injured by such means, both of them do not know its true nature;
for since that consciousness is extremely subtle, its cutting or destruction is impossible. Thus, "this Self neither kills nor is killed."
The meaning is that one becomes both the agent and the object of the act of killing (*han*).
Since "killing" signifies the separation from the body, one should not consider it to be the destruction of the selves (*ātman*).
And the Śruti says thus: "If the killer thinks he kills, or if the killed thinks he is killed... (KaṭhU 1.2.19), and so forth.
By this, the statement "one should not harm any living beings," and so forth, is explained as referring to the separation from the body.
Nor should it be said that the self's agency is not established here; for that [agency] exists in the self with respect to the separation from the body. //19//
It is never born, nor does it ever die; nor, having come to be, will it ever cease to be again.
Unborn, eternal, ever-lasting, and ancient, this [Self] is not slain when the body is slain. //20//
Śrīdhara: The phrase "it is not killed" is strengthened by the fact that it is devoid of the six modifications of being, beginning with "it is not born.
"It is not born" is a negation of birth.
"It does not die" is a negation of destruction.
The two particles "vā" are used in the sense of "and.
Nor, having come into being—that is, having arisen—does it become something that will exist; it does not partake in existence.

However, since it is inherently of the nature of existence even prior [to manifestation], there is a negation of the second modification, characterized by existence in another birth. The reason for this is that it is "unborn" (*aja*).
For that which is not born does not partake in existence in another birth.
The meaning is that that which exists by itself does not further partake of another existence.
"Eternal" (*nitya*) means always of one and the same form; this is a negation of increase (*vṛddhi*). "Constant" (*śāśvata*) means existing perpetually; this is a negation of diminution (*apakṣaya*).
"Ever-new" (*purāṇa*) is a negation of transformation;
the meaning is that it is ever-new even from of old, and does not become new by attaining another form through transformation.
Alternatively, by supplying the word "not" (*na*) to connect with "will come to be" (*bhavita*), it means it does not come to be further or more; thus, it is a negation of increase.
The statements "unborn" (*aja*) and "eternal" (*nitya*) serve as the reasons for the absence of both growth and the other [stages of change]; thus, there is no tautology.

In this way, the six transformations of being (*ṣaḍ-bhāva-vikāra*)—namely, "it is born," "it exists," "it grows," "it transforms," "it declines," and "it perishes"—as taught by Yāska and others who follow the Vedic tradition, have been refuted.
He concludes with the verse, "It is not slain when the body is slain," summarizing that very absence of destruction which was the subject of these refuted transformations. //20//
Madhusūdana:
Why is this Self neither the agent nor the object of the act of killing?
He states the reason—namely, because of its changelessness—in the second mantra.
The etymologists (nairuktāḥ) maintain that Vārṣyāyaṇi stated there are six modifications of being: "it is born, it exists, it grows, it transforms, it declines, and it perishes.
Among these, a negation is made regarding the first and the last: "it is not born, nor does it die.
The word "vā" has the sense of conjunction.
The meaning is that it is neither born nor does it die.
Why is this self not produced?
Because this self, having never previously existed at any time whatsoever, shall not come into being again.
For that which comes into being after having not existed undergoes the modification characterized by origination;
but this [Self], because it exists even prior [to its manifestation], does not originate, and is therefore unborn (*aja*).
Likewise, this Self, having once existed previously, will never again cease to exist.
The word "or" (vā) does not imply a reversal of the sentence.
For that which, having existed previously, does not exist at a later time, undergoes the transformation characterized by death;
however, this [subject] at a later time...

The meaning is that since beings do not perish from this [state], they are eternal, in the sense of being incapable of destruction. Here, even in the absence of a compound in the phrase "not having come into being" (*na bhūtvā*), there is no logical inconsistency, just as in the case of *na-anuyojyeṣu*.
This is because the Blessed One Pāṇini included the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) within the section on the *Mahā-vibhāṣā* [of the *Vārttika*].

As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana—namely, "The word 'or' (vā) is redundant because [the compound] is established by its own nature"—this is not to be accepted, as it contradicts the statement of the venerable Pāṇini.
This was said by the teacher Śabarasvāmin: "Kātyāyana is indeed a proponent of non-existence.
In this context, the thesis is: "It is neither born nor does it die."
The analysis is as follows: "Never having been, shall he not be again" is the proof (*upapādana*) of that [immortality], while "unborn and eternal" is its conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).

Although by the negation of the first and last modifications (*vikāra*), the negation of the intervening modifications—which are subsumed under them—is already established, the mention of "decay" (*apakṣaya*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other unmentioned modifications such as motion (*gamana*) and so forth.
Furthermore, increase is also refuted by the very word [used].

In that regard, because the Self is immutable and eternal, and because It is devoid of qualities, neither decay nor diminution is possible either in Its essential nature or in Its attributes; thus it is said to be "eternal" (śāśvata).
The meaning is that It exists eternally—that is, at all times—and does not diminish, nor does It waste away.
If it does not diminish, then let it increase—this is denied by the word "purāṇa" (ancient).
Even in the past, it was new, being of a single uniform nature; it does not, however, now experience any newly acquired state.
For in common worldly usage, that which experiences some newly acquired state of growth is said to "increase."
But this [Self], because it is always of one and the same nature, neither decreases nor increases; such is the meaning.
As for existence and transformation, they are not separately negated because they are included within birth and destruction.

Since the self (*ātman*) is thus devoid of all modification, therefore, even when the body is being slain, that which is connected to it is not slain by any means; it cannot be killed—this is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
Viśvanātha:
He clearly establishes the eternity of the individual self (*jīvātman*), negating the occurrence of birth and death through the words "is not born, does not die."

The phrase "having been, it will not be" is a negation of its pastness and futureness. For this very reason, it is called "unborn" (*aja*); because there is no birth for the unborn throughout the three periods of time, it has no prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*).
It is "eternal" (*śāśvata*), meaning it exists perpetually at all times; thus, it has no destruction even throughout the three periods of time.
For this very reason, it is eternal.
If it is argued that because it persists for a long time, it must be seized by old age, we say no;
for it is "ancient yet ever-new"—meaning that even though it is old, it remains as if fresh—because it is devoid of the six modifications of being. This is the intended meaning.
[Objection: "But surely, since the body has died, let there be a figurative death for this [self]?
To that he says: "No," because there is no connection with the body, there can be no figurative usage. //20//

Baladeva: Now, by means of the absence of the six modifications of being (bhāva-vikāra) mentioned by Yāska and others—namely, "it is born, it exists, it grows, it transforms, it declines, and it perishes"—he confirms the previously stated eternity [of Brahman] with the words "it is not born.
The two particles *vā* and *ca* are used in the sense of conjunction (*cārthe*).
"This self, this living being (jīva), is never at any time born nor does it die"—this is the negation of birth and destruction.
"Nor does this self, having come into being, come to be [again]"—this is the negation of the existence of another birth.
"No more"—this is the negation of the notion that this self exists further or in addition.
Regarding the question "From what does one not become [again]?", the reason is given as "unborn" (aja) and "eternal" (nitya).
For indeed, things such as trees, being subject to arising and destruction, arise, undergo growth, and then perish;
however, since the self lacks both of these, it does not grow—this is the meaning.
"Everlasting" (*śāśvata*) is the negation of decay;
its meaning is that it exists eternally at all times, it does not diminish, and it does not undergo decay. "Ancient" (*purāṇa*) is the negation of transformation; [it means] ancient...
The meaning is that even in the past he was not new; no novel form whatsoever has been acquired now.
Thus, because he is devoid of the six modifications of being, the self is eternal.
Since he is such, he is not slain even when the body is being slain.
And thus, you, fearing ill-repute through the ignorant remark that "this Arjuna is a slayer of his preceptor," ought to engage in the righteous battle prescribed by the scriptures. //20//
But how, O Pārtha, can that person— who knows this Self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable— slay anyone, or cause anyone to be slain? (21)

Śrīdhara: For this very reason, he says "the indestructible" and so forth, to show that the previously mentioned absence of agency as a killer is also well-established. "Eternal" means devoid of growth;
"unchanging" means devoid of decay.
He who knows [the Self] as unborn and undecaying— what person does he kill,
or how could he kill?
Because there is no means for the killing of one who has already become thus;
likewise, having himself become the instigator, how does he cause another to kill,
or in what manner does he cause him to kill?
"Not even anything;
not in any way whatsoever" is the meaning.
By this, it is said: "Do not perceive faults even in me, because I am the instigator. //21//
Madhusūdana:
Having asserted the proposition that "this [Self] neither kills nor is killed," and having established that "it is not killed," he now concludes by establishing that "it does not kill":
*avināśinam*—one whose nature is not to perish, being devoid of the final modification (death).
The reason for this is as follows: "Inexhaustible" (*avyaya*) means that which has no exhaustion (*vyaya*), whether it be the diminution of its parts or the diminution of its qualities;
the meaning is that since destruction is observed through the diminution of parts or the diminution of qualities, destruction is impossible for that which is devoid of both.
[Objection: But we shall infer its perishability by virtue of its being produced (*janyatva*). [Reply: No, he says—“unborn” (*aja*).

It is "unborn" (*aja*) because it is not born, being devoid of primary modification. The reason for this is that it is "eternal" (*nitya*), existing at all times; for birth is observed only for that which was previously non-existent, but never for that which exists in every respect—this is the intended meaning.
Alternatively, "indestructible" means unassailable, that is to say, real; "eternal" means all-pervading. The reason for this is: "unborn and undecaying."
It is devoid of birth and destruction, because for that which is being born or perishing, there is no possibility of omnipresence or reality.
Thus, he who knows—meaning understands through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher and realizes directly—this very embodied being under discussion as his own self, [realizing]:
"I am devoid of all modifications, the illuminator of all, free from all duality, and of the nature of supreme bliss and consciousness."
Thus, such a person who knows this is of a complete nature; whom does he kill?
How does he kill?
The word "what" (kiṃ) is used here in a sense of negation.

The meaning is that it does not kill anyone, nor does it kill in any manner whatsoever. Likewise, the meaning is that it does not cause anyone to be killed, nor does it cause anyone to be killed in any manner whatsoever.
For it is not possible for that which is devoid of all modification and is a non-agent to possess agency in the act of killing.
And so says the Śruti:
"If a person were to know the Self, thinking 'I am this,' desiring what, or for the sake of what desire, would he suffer along with the body? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12).

Thus, for one who knows the Self as pure, it is shown that upon the cessation of superimposition—which is rooted in ignorance—there follows the absence of agency, enjoyership, and so forth, due to the absence of passion, aversion, and the like, which are based on that [ignorance].
This is the Blessed One’s intended meaning here:

in reality, no one at all acts or causes anything to be done, because the nature [of the Self] is devoid of all modification; however, as in a dream, through ignorance one falsely identifies with agency and other such qualities within the Self.
The deluded one;
as it has been said: "Both of them do not understand" (Gītā 2.19).
And the Śruti says: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7), and so forth.
Therefore, all the scriptures have as their intended audience those who are not yet enlightened.

However, the enlightened person—because they have sublated superimposition along with its root—does not falsely identify with agency and other attributes within the Self, just as one who knows a post to be what it is does not mistake it for a thief.
Consequently, because he is free from modification and non-dual, it is said that the enlightened person neither acts nor causes action to be performed.
And thus says the Śruti: "The wise man fears nothing from anywhere" (TaittU 2.9.1).
For Arjuna, having superposed agency upon himself and causality upon the Blessed Lord, suspected the fault arising from violence to reside in both.
The Blessed Lord, knowing his intention, rejected both of those views by stating, "He kills" and "He causes to kill."
The intention is: "Do not entertain the fear of sin by superimposing agency upon the Self and causality upon Me.

Since the Lord intends to include all actions within the prohibition of the Self's agency—established by demonstrating its changelessness—the term "killing" (*han*) is used as a representative example (*upalakṣaṇa*), because it is the most prominent [action] that comes to mind.
Since the reason for the prohibition is the same, it is illogical to assume that another action is permitted;
as he will state later: "For him, there exists no duty" (Gītā 3.17).
Therefore, the prattle of deluded people—that by the mere negation of killing, another action is sanctioned by the Blessed One—is refuted.

Therefore, because the Blessed One has authorized the act of killing by saying "fight," and because the absence of actual agency and so forth is equal in all actions, such is the direction [of the argument]. //21//
Viśvanātha:
Therefore, he says "the Veda" to show that when such knowledge exists, neither you—who are fighting—nor I—who am impelling you to fight—shall incur any fault.
The word "eternally" (*nityam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
By the terms "indestructible," "unborn," and "unchanging," destruction, birth, and decay are negated.
That person characterized by "mal" causes whom to be killed,
and how does he cause him to be killed?
But that person characterized by "tvat" kills whom?
Or how does one kill? //21//

Baladeva: He says "veda" (he knows) to show that there is not even a scent of fault in either one who, possessing knowledge of reality, engages in battle with the thought that it is his duty, or one who causes another to engage.
He who knows—through both scripture and reasoning—this very Self under discussion as indestructible, unborn, immutable, and devoid of decay; [for him there is no fault].
Even though that person is engaged in battle, whom does he kill, or how does he kill?
And therein, even while acting, whom does he cause to be killed, or how does he cause to be killed?
The sense of the rhetorical question (ākṣepa) is: "no one at all, nor in any way whatsoever."
"Endless" is an adverbial modifier of the action of feeling. //21//
Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new; so does the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enter into others that are new.
In the same way, the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new. (22)

Śrīdhara: If it is argued, "Even though the self is indestructible, I grieve upon considering the destruction of its body," he says in response, "As one puts on... clothes" (vāsāṃsi). The meaning is that since new bodies bound by karma are inevitable, there is no occasion for grief at the destruction of that worn-out body. //22//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even if the self is indeed indestructible, since bodies are perishable and battle is the cause of their destruction, why should I bring about the destruction through war of the bodies of Bhīṣma and others, which were achieved by manifold meritorious deeds? To this doubt, the answer is given in the verse beginning with "vāsāṃsi" (clothes).

Just as a person, remaining entirely free from transformation (*vikriyā-śūnya*), discards worn-out clothes and takes up new ones— this much alone is stated in the marriage [verse] for the purpose of proclaiming an excellence of distinction;
by this, it follows by propriety that just as people discard inferior garments and take up superior ones,
so too [the Lord], having discarded the worn-out bodies of Bhīṣma and others— emaciated by age and austerity— assumes other bodies, such as those of gods and so forth.

The meaning is that the embodied soul—one who possesses a body for the performance of eminent dharma—such as Bhīṣma and others, proceeds to and attains the most excellent [bodies] for the enjoyment of the fruits of dharma accumulated over a long time, without the suffering of dwelling in a womb and so forth;
for the Śruti declares: "He assumes another, newer, and more auspicious form—whether that of a Pitṛ, a Gandharva, a Deva, a Prajāpati, or a Brahmā," and so on.

This is what is meant: Bhīṣma and the others, whose bodies have been worn out by the hardships of lifelong religious practice, would otherwise be unable to enjoy the fruits of that practice until their current bodies fall; therefore, if through a righteous war (dharma-yuddha) their worn-out bodies—which obstruct heaven—are cast down and they are rendered fit for the enjoyment of heaven by the acquisition of divine bodies, [then it is for their benefit].
By you, they have indeed been greatly benefited;
for even Duryodhana and the others have received a great favor through the provision of bodies fit for the enjoyment of heaven.
Thus, do not entertain the delusion that this war—which is ultimately so beneficial—is harmful.
Based on the three words "others," "different," and "he goes," the intention of the Blessed One has been inferred in this way.
However, the explanation of the ancient commentators—that by this illustration the unchanging nature of the self is demonstrated—is exceedingly clear. //22//
Viśvanātha:

[Objection: "Surely, after my death in battle, the living soul (jīvātman) will surely abandon the body known as Bhīṣma; therefore, both you and I shall certainly be the cause of that [abandonment]. To this he says: "Vāsāṃsi" (clothes).
The sense is: when one discards old clothes in order to put on new ones, does anyone incur any fault? Such is the meaning.
Likewise, regarding "bodies," the meaning is that Bhīṣma, having cast off his worn-out body, will obtain another divine and new body; therefore, what fault is there on your part or mine? //22//

Baladeva: [Objection: Granted that there may be no destruction of the selves designated as Bhīṣma and others; however, when their bodies—the instruments of their pleasure—are destroyed by battle, there would certainly be the fault of causing the cessation of that pleasure. Otherwise, the scriptures on expiation (prāyaścitta) would become devoid of scope. To this, he says: "Vāsāṃsi... (clothes...).

Just as one puts on new clothes by discarding worn-out, coarse garments, the assumption of a youthful divine body by discarding an aged human body is exceedingly pleasant for those souls. Since both of these occur quickly through battle alone, the sense is: "Do not desist from that which is so beneficial. The term *saṃyāti* means that he attains [the state] swiftly and without the sufferings of dwelling in a womb and so forth.
However, the statements regarding expiation (prāyaścitta) are to be applied to killings other than those occurring in sacrifice or battle. //22//
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it; water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it. (23)
Śrīdhara: By the words "How does he kill? [the Lord] shows the absence of any means for slaying and makes manifest the indestructibility of the self with the verse beginning "Not him," and so forth.
Water does not moisten it by making it soft or supple;
nor does the wind dry it up. //23//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha explains that no injury whatsoever could have occurred to himself from the weapons and missiles employed by you in battle, saying "not him" (nainam).
Weapons refer to swords and the like;
fire refers even to the *āgneya* weapon discharged by you and others;
and water refers even to the *pārjanya* weapon.
Māruta is the Vāyavya weapon. //23//

Baladeva: [Objection: "Surely, when the body is destroyed by the falling of weapons, the Self situated within it must also be destroyed, just as a creature inside a house perishes when the house is burned. To this, he says: "Not him" (nainam). "Weapons" refers to swords and the like.
Pāvaka is the Āgneya weapon;
Āpaḥ is also the Pārjanya weapon;
Māruta is the Vāyavya weapon.
And likewise, by means of the weapons and missiles employed by them, there is no pain whatsoever for himself. //23//
This [Self] is neither to be cut, nor to be burnt, nor to be moistened, nor indeed to be dried up. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. (24)
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this in the verse beginning with "indestructible" (acchedya) and so forth, consisting of one and a half verses.
Because it is without parts, it is indestructible and cannot be moistened;
because it is formless, it cannot be burned.
The sense is that because it lacks fluidity, it is incapable of being dried up;
furthermore, for this reason as well, it is not subject to cutting and so forth,
since it is eternal and indestructible.
All-pervading, immovable, of a stable nature, devoid of the assumption of another form;
unshakable, not abandoning its prior form;
eternal, without beginning. //24//
Madhusūdana:
He states the reason why weapons and the like lack the power to destroy it, and why it is unfit to be destroyed by them produced by them, with the words "indestructible" (acchedya).
Since this is indestructible, therefore weapons do not cut it.
Since this [Self] is not combustible, therefore fire does not burn it;
since it is not moistenable, therefore water does not moisten it;
since it is not desiccable, therefore the wind does not dry it up—this is to be applied in due order.
The particle *eva* is connected with each [term] for the purpose of emphasizing their indivisibility and so forth;
*ca* signifies either conjunction or reason.
The latter half of the verse states the reason for their being unfit for cutting and the like.
This [self] is eternal and devoid of prior and posterior limits; therefore, it is unproduced.

For if it were not all-pervading, it would be impermanent, according to the principle that "as long as there is change, there is division. Furthermore, we do not accept such things as atoms (paramāṇu) and so forth as accepted by other schools.
But this [Self] is all-pervading and omnipresent; therefore, it is indeed eternal.
By this, its being an object to be attained is refuted.
Furthermore, if this were subject to modification, it would not be all-pervading.
But this *sthāṇu* (the Stable One) is changeless;
therefore, it is indeed omnipresent.
By this, its susceptibility to modification is refuted.
If this [self] were mobile and possessed of action, it would then be subject to modification, like a jar or similar objects;
however, since this is immobile, it is not subject to modification. By this, its state of being something to be refined (saṃskāryatva) is refuted.
Transformation (*vikriyā*) is the attainment of another state through the abandonment of a previous state.
Even when the state remains identical, mere motion is "action" (*kriyā*); this is the distinction.
Since this is so, the meaning is that this [Self] is eternal, always uniform in nature, and is not the object of any action whatsoever.
For the status of being an object (*karmatva*) would indeed exist when there is a connection with the fruit of an action consisting in production, attainment, modification, or purification;
however, this [Brahman], because it is eternal, is not something to be produced, since only that which is impermanent can be so produced.
Because it is not something to be produced, unlike a jar or similar objects;
because it is all-pervading, it is not something to be attained, since only delimited things such as water can be attained;
and because it is immovable like a pillar, it is not something to be transformed.
Because that which undergoes modification, such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), is itself the object of modification;
and because it is immovable, it cannot be refined, since only that which possesses activity, such as a mirror, is capable of being refined.
And thus say the scriptures: "Like space, he is all-pervading and eternal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
"He stands alone, firm like a tree in heaven" (ŚvetU 3.9);
"partless, actionless, and tranquil" (ŚvetU 6.19), and so forth; and:
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth; he who dwells in the waters, yet is within the waters; he who dwells in fire..."

Furthermore, the Śruti passage beginning with, "That which is within fire, standing within fire, that which is within air... (BAU 3.7.3ff), shows that although [the Self] is all-pervading, it is not an object of perception because it exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of everything.
For indeed, weapons and the like cut down only that which does not abide within them.
But this [Lord], being the impeller and the inner controller (antaryāmī) of weapons and so forth by bestowing upon them existence and manifestation,
how could weapons and the like ever make him the object of their own operations? This is the intended meaning.
In this regard, scriptural passages such as "by whose splendor the sun shines, kindled with heat" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9) should be reflected upon;
furthermore, the Blessed Lord will clarify this in the seventh chapter—this is the general direction. //24//
Viśvanātha:
Therefore, he says "indestructible" (acchedya) to show that this Self is described in such a manner.

In this context, those of doubtful intellect should understand that the repetition—both verbal and substantial—of the eternality of the individual self (jīvātman) serves the purpose of definitive determination.

It should be understood that in this Kali age, because one employs the expression "Dharma exists, Dharma exists" three or four times, there arises a conviction free from doubt that "Dharma indeed exists.

Being "all-pervading" means that by the power of one's own karma, it resides within all bodies—those of gods, humans, animals, and so forth. The repetition of "immovable" (*sthāṇu*) and "unwavering" (*acala*) is for the purpose of determining its stability.
Because of its extreme subtlety, it is unmanifest; yet, because consciousness pervades the body, it is inconceivable and beyond logical reasoning.
Because it is incapable of the six transformations beginning with birth, it is changeless. //24–25//
Baladeva: He says, "This one is indestructible," meaning that it is precisely because of the absence of cutting and so forth that he is designated by those various names.
The particle *eva* (precisely) is connected with all [the preceding terms].

"All-pervading" means that although he has gone to—that is, reached—all bodies, such as those of gods, humans, animals, birds, and so on, which are caused by their own respective karmas, doing so in succession.
"Sthāṇu" means one whose essential nature is stable;
"acala" means one whose qualities are stable.
The meaning is that this is based on the Vedic scripture: "Verily, this Self is indestructible, for its nature is not subject to annihilation" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14).
Nor should it be explained as "one whose nature is non-cessation," because that meaning is already obtained by the word *avināśī* (imperishable) itself.
Therefore, the meaning is simply: "he whose dharmas are non-ceasing and eternal.
As for the fault of tautology regarding the words *sanātanaḥ* and *śāśvataḥ*, it will be addressed later. //24//
This [Self] is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable; therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve. 25.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the term "unmanifest" (avyakta):
it is unmanifest because it is not an object of the eyes and other [senses];
it is inconceivable because it is also not an object of the mind.
"Unchangeable" means that it is not even within the range of the organs of action.
By the words "it is said," he provides scriptural authority for the statement regarding its eternity and other attributes.
He concludes with the words "therefore, thus," and so forth.
Thus, it has been stated that since the self is devoid of birth and destruction, one should not grieve. //25//

Madhusūdana says that its non-existence [as a manifest entity] follows also from the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend its being divisible and so forth; he states this with the half-verse beginning "This is unmanifest" (*avyakto 'yam*).
For whatever falls within the range of the sense organs is called "manifest" (*vyakta*) because it is perceptible (*pratyakṣatvāt*).
But this [space] is not like that because it is devoid of form and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is that perception does not grasp its being cuttable and so on.
To the objection that there might still be inference even in the absence of perception, he says: "This is inconceivable; that which is conceivable is inferable, but this is distinct from that."

For in some cases, fire and the like are perceived directly through the observation of smoke and so forth for which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped; in other cases, they become objects of inference.
However, the point is that when something is not perceptible, it cannot be an object of inference because the grasping of its pervasion is impossible.
Since even non-perceptible things such as the sense organs are seen to be objects of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), he says: "unchangeable" (*avikārya*).

Whatever possesses modification, such as the eye and so forth, becomes the object of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa-anumāna*), because it is postulated through the impossibility of its own effect otherwise.

But this [Self] is neither an object of transformation nor possessed of modification; therefore, the meaning is that it is not the object of either presumptive testimony or inference based on general observation.
Since even worldly speech is preceded by perception and other means of knowledge, its negation follows from the negation of those very means.

Now, one might object: "But surely, the quality of being indestructible and so forth will be grasped there [in the world] by the Veda itself. To this he says: It is stated that by the Veda, along with its auxiliary sciences (*upakaraṇa*), this [Self] is described in its very nature as indestructible, unmanifest, and so on; it is established through the Veda's primary intention (*tātparya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that even though the Veda is the means of cognizing it, it does not possess the character of establishing qualities such as destructibility.

In this regard, one should observe that there is no redundancy: in the verse "Weapons do not cut this" (Gītā 2.23), the absence of capacity in weapons and other such instruments to destroy it is stated;
in "This is indestructible," etc., its unfitness to be the object of actions such as cutting is stated;
and in "This is unmanifest," the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend its cutting or other such acts is stated. Thus, there is no tautology.

The commentators have resolved the repetition—both in meaning and in wording—found in the verses beginning with "He who knows the indestructible" (*vedāvināśinam*). Because the reality of the Self is difficult to comprehend, Lord Vāsudeva repeatedly introduces the subject and describes that very same reality through different words, thinking: "How indeed might this [Self] come within the range of the intellect of those caught in transmigratory existence?"

By those who say, "The knowledge of reality (tattva) leads to the cessation of saṃsāra" [Śaṅkara-bhāṣya 2.24], and thus having established through the aforementioned arguments that the self is eternal and changeless, he concludes with the half-verse beginning "Therefore," that your grief is not justified.
Since the realization of such a nature of the self removes the cause of grief, when that realization exists, grief is improper; for when the cause is absent, the absence of the effect is necessary.
Therefore, it was entirely appropriate that you grieved because you did not know the Self;
however, having known the Self, you ought not to grieve—this is the intended meaning. //25//
Viśvanātha: None.
Baladeva: The Unmanifest is the inward-looking eye, ungraspable by the senses such as sight;
it is inconceivable, beyond the scope of logic, and accessible through scripture alone.
That the Self is of the nature of knowledge and is the knower, and so forth, is understood from the Śruti itself. It is "unchangeable," meaning incapable of the six kinds of modification.

Here, in order to make easy to understand that reality of the Self which is difficult to grasp—concerning which Hari, while instructing on the essence of the Self through such passages as "But know That to be indestructible," spoke again and again both in words and in their underlying meaning—[the following is said].
Thus, there is no fault;
or rather, it is for the purpose of specification.
Just as when it is said, "This person knows the Dharma," that knowledge is intended to be certain, so it is here.
In this very way, he will state later on with the words "some one sees it as a marvel" and so forth. //25//
Moreover, O mighty-armed one, even if you consider this self to be constantly born or constantly dying, even then you ought not to grieve in this manner. (2.26)

Śrīdhara: Now, even if one accepts that the self is born together with the body and perishes with its destruction, he says "But even so" (*atha cainam*) and so forth, to show that grief should not be felt.
(26) "And yet, O mighty-armed one, even if you consider this self to be constantly born or constantly dead, you still ought not to grieve in this manner. (26)
Madhusūdana:

Thus, the state of the Self being beyond grief has been declared by way of its changelessness; now, the Blessed One establishes the state of being beyond grief even by assuming the presence of change, through two verses.
In this regard, the Buddhists maintain that the Self is of the nature of consciousness and perishes at every moment.

The Lokāyatikas maintain that the body itself is the self, and that although it is stable, it undergoes momentary transformation, being born and perishing; this, they say, is established by direct perception.
Others hold that even though [the self] is distinct from the body, it is born and perishes together with the body.

Still others maintain that it is born at the very time of the beginning of creation like space, persists through the various bodies, remains for the duration of a kalpa, and perishes at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya).
The logicians maintain that the self is indeed eternal, yet it is born and dies;
for they define birth as existence after passing away (pretyabhāva),
which is the connection with a new body, sense organs, and so forth.

In this way, death as well is the severance of the previous body, sense-faculties, and so forth. And both of these [birth and death] belong primarily to that which is eternal, because they have merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) as their cause; for if the substrate were non-eternal, it would follow that there is the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done, and thus its being the substrate of merit and demerit would be untenable.

Some say that birth and death are not primary; others say they occur only in the case of the transmigrating self (*saṃsārin*). In that regard, even under the view of impermanence, [the text] negates the pitiable nature of the self with the words "and yet him" (*atha cainam*).
The word *atha* indicates an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*).
The particle *ca* has the sense of "also.

If, because the reality of the self (*ātma-vastu*) is difficult to comprehend, you lack the capacity for certain determination even after hearing it repeatedly, and thus—without accepting the position stated by me—you resort to another position; [then the following applies].

Even there, relying on the very position of impermanence, if you consider this self to be "always born" or "always dead"—the word *vā* having the sense of "and"—then, according to the position of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), it means "always," that is, at every moment; or, in the alternative case, because it is necessary, it means "constantly" or "inevitably. If you thus postulate, by force of worldly convention, that "this one is born" or "this one is dead," even so—
"O mighty-armed one!
[You are] a leader among men"— this is said either with derision because of his acceptance of a false doctrine,
or with compassion, thinking that such a wrong view is impossible in one like you.

Just as you grieve in this manner, thinking, "Alas, we have resolved to commit a great sin" (Gītā 1.45), and so forth, you yourself— being in exactly such a state— are not fit, that is, you are not worthy,
to engage in such lamentation regarding the body, whether from the perspective of momentariness or the doctrine of the self as being the body.

Furthermore, under the view that birth and destruction are simultaneous, since there would be no existence in another life, the fear of sin would be impossible; yet you indeed grieve out of fear of sin.

Such [fear] is not possible under this [simultaneous] doctrine, because there is an absence of witnessing the destruction of one's kin. The particle *evaṃ* (thus) is used here specifically to grant permission for grief caused by suffering witnessed in the other alternative view.
The meaning of the first verse is that even when sorrow arises from the cause of observed suffering, sorrow caused by the cause of unobserved suffering is in no way appropriate. //26//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, having awakened you from the perspective of scriptural reality (*śāstrīya-tattva*), he says "Now" (*atha*) to awaken you even from the perspective of worldly reality (*vyāvahārika-tattva*); listen!
When the body is born, you consider this [Self] to be eternally and invariably born;
likewise, when the body dies, you consider it to be eternally and invariably dead.
O mighty-armed one—referring to you, a valiant Kshatriya—that battle is also inevitable and your own duty, as it has been said:
"This is the duty of Kṣatriyas ordained by Prajāpati;
there is nothing more terrible than that by which even a brother might slay his own brother"—this is the sense [of the verse]. (26)

Baladeva: Having thus stated the non-lamentability of the individual self (jīvātman) according to his own view, he now states that same [non-lamentability] even regarding the self as propounded by others, for the sake of understanding their position.
Indeed, a disciple who is ignorant of that [other view] might reject it with contempt; therefore, being victorious, [the author] establishes firmness in his own doctrine.

For instance, consciousness arises within the four elements—earth and so forth—which are qualified by human nature and the like, just as the red color of betel arises [in the teeth] or just as the power of intoxication [arises in the body].
The Materialists (Lokāyatikas) maintain that the body itself—consisting of those four elements—is the self;
and they hold that although it is stable, because it undergoes transformation at every moment, it is subject to arising and destruction, as established by worldly perception.
The Vaibhāṣikas and other Buddhists assert that the self, though distinct from the body and consisting of the nature of consciousness, perishes at every moment.
This [verse] refutes the pitiable state of the self according to both views;
"atha" indicates an alternative position, and "ca" has the sense of "also."
If you, being unable to comprehend the true nature of the individual self as described by Me, take recourse in the position of the Lokāyatikas and others,
then, within that doctrine of the body being the self, you consider this self— characterized as the body— to be either eternal or mortal.
The word "vā" has the sense of "and.
Nevertheless, you ought not to grieve for him with such words as, "Alas! What a great sin! and so forth;

for since the nature of transformation is inherent in each thing, the birth and destruction of that [person] and of oneself are unavoidable, and because there is no other birth, the fear of sin is impossible.
"O mighty-armed one"—this address is made with a touch of irony; the sense is that such a wicked view should not be held by you, who are the best of Kṣatriyas and a follower of the Vedas.
(BhG 2.27) For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve over that which is unavoidable. //27//
Śrīdhara: Why is this? To this he says, "of one who is born," and so forth.
For (*hi*), because death is certain (*dhruva*)—that is, fixed—for one who is born upon the exhaustion of the karma that initiated his own [existence].
Moreover, for one who has died, rebirth is indeed certain through the karma performed in that body.
Therefore, since this matter is unavoidable and the reality characterized by birth and death is inevitable, you, being wise, ought not to grieve; you are not fit to do so. //27//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: "But surely, even on the view that the self persists until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūta-saṃplava*), since there is the possibility of both seen and unseen suffering, I grieve out of fear of that. To this, he says with the second verse, beginning with "For of one who is born" (*jātasya hi*): for (*hi*) because of one who is born—who has acquired a connection with a body, senses, and so forth, by virtue of his own performed *dharma*, *adharma*, and so on—...

For a permanent self, death—the inevitable severance of that body and so forth—is certain, being caused by the exhaustion of the karma that initiated it, since conjunction must end in disjunction. Likewise, birth after death is certain for one who possesses residual karma (*sānuśaya*), as this is the subject under discussion for the sake of experiencing the fruits of actions performed in a previous body; thus, there is no deviation from this rule in the case of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
Therefore, since this matter characterized by birth and death is thus unavoidable—meaning it cannot be averted—you, being wise in this way, ought not to grieve.
And so He will say: "Even without you, all shall cease to be" (Gītā 11.32).
For if these men were to continue living without being slain by you in battle, then grief for their sake in the context of war would be appropriate for you.
The sense is this: since these [beings] die of their own accord through the exhaustion of their karma, grief caused by visible suffering is not appropriate for you, who are unable to prevent it.
Thus, even regarding grief caused by invisible suffering, the answer remains the same: "in a matter that cannot be avoided."

For the duty of a Kṣatriya known as battle is as obligatory as the Agnihotra and other rites. That [duty] is derived from the verbal root *yudh* (to fight) in the sense of "striking together," and its form consists of the discharge of weapons conducive to the severing of an enemy's life-force. Because it is prescribed, like the sacrifice to Agni and Soma involving a lion, it does not produce demerit. Thus Gautama records in his Smṛti: "There is no fault in killing in battle, except in the case of those who are without horses, without charioteers, those who are not fighting, those with joined palms, those with disheveled hair, those who have turned their backs, those who are seated, those standing on ground, those mounted on trees, messengers, cows, Brāhmaṇas, and those who proclaim [their status]."
Thus,

it is established that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa who has been excluded [from his duties], because of its inclusion in a list primarily consisting of cows and other such items;
and all of this will be clarified in the verse beginning with "svadharmam api cāvekṣya."

And likewise, since the act of fighting is enjoined as a duty—just like the *agnihotra* sacrifice and other rites—it is unavoidable; and since it is impossible to avoid it, there would be the consequence of sin (*pratyavāya*) from its non-performance. Therefore, as before, you ought not to grieve out of fear of unseen suffering.
However, if the action called "fighting" were merely optional (*kāmya*)—
"Those who fight in battles for the sake of land without turning their backs,
and who do so with non-deceptive weapons, go to heaven like yogis"—
thus says the statement of Yājñavalkya.
Furthermore, from the words of the Blessed One: "Either being slain you will attain heaven, or conquering you will enjoy the earth" (Gītā 2.37).

Even then, because that which has been commenced—even if it is a desire-driven act—must necessarily be brought to completion and is thus equal to a compulsory duty (*nitya*), and because the battle has already been commenced by you, its inevitability is exactly the same.
Alternatively, the two verses concern the position of the self's eternity; for Arjuna, who was a supreme believer, it was impossible to accept a view outside the Vedic tradition.
As for the construction of the words: he is eternal, yet he is born through the power of connection with the body, senses, and so forth; thus, he is "eternally born.

If you consider this very Self—which, though eternal, is "born"—to be so, and likewise consider it, though eternal, to be "dead," even then you ought not to grieve. He states the reason for this with the verse beginning, "For of one who is born... and so on.
The birth and death of the eternal have been explained previously;
the rest is clear.
The commentary should also be applied to this position. //27//
Viśvanātha:
For indeed, because death is certain— that is, inevitable— for him upon the exhaustion of the karma that initiated his own body,
and for one who has died, birth is likewise certainly determined by the karma performed with that body.
"In an unavoidable matter" means that birth and death are indeed impossible to avoid. //27//
Baladeva: Now, the self (*ātman*) is eternal and distinct from the body.

Its birth is its connection with a new body and sense organs; its death, however, is the dissociation from the previous body and sense organs. Since both of these are caused by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), they belong primarily to the eternal self which is their substratum.
The logicians maintain that for a body distinct from that [consciousness], the designation is merely figurative;

for since that [body] is impermanent, it is untenable for it to be the substratum [of consciousness], as this would entail the fallacy of losing what was done and acquiring what was not done. Even in their view, he dispels the notion of the self being an object of grief by the words "of one who is born."
The word *hi* indicates the reason:

for one who is born—meaning one who, by the power of their own karma, has acquired a connection with a body and so forth—even for an eternal self (*ātman*), death, caused by the exhaustion of the karma that initiated that [body], is certain (*dhruva*, i.e., inevitable);
and for one who has died, birth, caused by the karma performed while in that body, would likewise be certain.
Therefore, since this matter consisting of birth and death is thus unavoidable—being impossible to avert—you, being a man of knowledge, ought not to grieve.
Even if you were to desist from battle, these [others] would surely die once their own causal actions are exhausted;
for you, however, there will be a falling away from your own duty (*svadharma*).
Existence. //27//
Beings have the unmanifest as their beginning, the manifest as their middle, O Bhārata, and the unmanifest as their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (2.28)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, having reflected upon the nature of bodies, one should not grieve over the birth and death of the Self as conditioned by them.
Therefore, he says "avyaktādīni" and so forth.
*Avyakta* refers to *pradhāna* (primordial matter).
Those whose beginning— the prior form— is that very [unmanifest state] are "those whose origin is unmanifest" (avyaktādi);
these are the elements, which is to say, the bodies,
because they arise while already existing in the nature of their cause.
Likewise, those whose middle— the manifest, the manifested state between birth and death— is characterized by existence,
and whose dissolution occurs in the unmanifest; for those who are of such a nature,
what cause for lamentation is there?
What lamentation can there be caused by grief?
The meaning is that, for one who has awakened, grief is not appropriate, just as it is not appropriate regarding objects seen in a dream. //28//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, the fact that the self is not to be grieved for has been established in every respect. Now, the Blessed One dispels Arjuna’s apprehension—that even though the self is not to be grieved for, he nevertheless grieves on account of the bodies which consist of an aggregate of elements—by saying, "The unmanifest is their beginning," and so forth.

In the beginning, prior to birth, the elements—bodies composed of the elements such as earth and so forth—are unmanifest and unperceived; in the middle, after birth and before death, they become manifest and perceived; and at the end, they once again become unmanifest.

This is because, according to the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), these bodies exist merely as appearances—like those in dreams, magical illusions, or the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—and do not exist prior to or subsequent to their being known.
