And so, according to the maxim: "That which does not exist in the beginning and in the end, likewise does not exist in the present" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 2.6), these do not exist even in the middle;
furthermore, this follows from what was stated previously: "The coming into being of the non-existent is not found" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.16).
This being the case, what lamentation can there be, or what outburst of grief, regarding those elements which are false and utterly trivial? The meaning is that none whatsoever is appropriate.

For even an ordinary person, having perceived various kinsmen in a dream, does not grieve over their disappearance upon waking; this very point was stated in the Purāṇa: "Having come from non-perception, he has gone again to non-perception"—the remainder of the sense being "the aggregate of beings.
Thus, the implication is that grief directed even toward bodies is not appropriate.
Alternatively, the verse may be interpreted with reference to the great elements (mahābhūtas) such as space:

that which has the unmanifest (avyakta)—namely, consciousness conditioned by ignorance (avidyā)—as its "beginning" or prior state is so described; and that which has become manifest (vyakta) through the two products of ignorance, name and form (nāmarūpa), but not by its own ultimately real nature, is the "middle."

Those elements, such as space and the rest, which possess the state of persistence, have their dissolution in the unmanifest alone; that is, their *nidhana*—their dissolution—is in their own cause, the unmanifest, just as pots and other objects dissolve into clay. Regarding those elements, what cause for lamentation is there? This is as explained previously. And so says the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest (*avyākṛta*); it was manifested by name and form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), and so forth, establishing that the entire phenomenal world has the unmanifest as its material cause.
He demonstrates this:
its status as a locus of dissolution is established by implication, because it is observed that the effect dissolves back into its very cause;
however, there is a detailed exposition in another treatise.

The sense is this: if grief is not appropriate even with respect to the elements such as space, which are insubstantial because they are imagined through ignorance (*ajñāna*), then what need is there to say that it is not appropriate with respect to their effects?
Alternatively, the meaning is that since these [elements] always exist in an unmanifest form, there is no severance [of them]; therefore, lamentation caused by that [severance] is not appropriate.
By addressing him as "O Bhārata," he indicates: "Since you are born of a pure lineage, you are worthy of understanding the scriptural meaning; why then do you not understand it? //28//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, having refuted the object of grief by means of the passage beginning with "it is neither born nor dies" with respect to the Self, and by the statement "for one who is born, death is certain" with respect to the body, he now refutes it with respect to both positions alike by saying "the unmanifest," etc.
"Beings" refers to gods, humans, animals, and so forth.

"Unmanifest" means that in the beginning—prior to birth—there was no manifest appearance (*vyakti*) for them; however, even then, both the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*) and the gross body (*sthūla-deha*) existed in the form of their causes, because the earth and other elements that constitute them were present as causal matter. Thus, the meaning is that they existed in an unmanifest state.
Those whose manifestation is evident in the interim;
those whose [manifestation] does not cease immediately after death.
Even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), because karma and the rest still exist, the elements (*bhūta*) certainly persist in a subtle form.
Therefore, the meaning is that all beings are unmanifest at the beginning and at the end, and manifest in the middle.
As it has been said by the Śrutis: "The classes of stationary and moving beings arise from the Unborn and are joined with causes.
What lamentation is there? What cause for grief is there for wailing?
And so it was said by Nārada:
"Whether you consider the world to be eternal, non-eternal, or both, in every way they are not to be grieved for, except out of affection born of delusion. (BhP 1.13.44) //28//

Baladeva: Now, [the Lord] says "avyaktādīni" (beginning with the unmanifest) to show that grief caused by the destruction of the body is not appropriate, whether one holds the view that the body is the self or the view that the self is distinct from the body, because the subtle elements (*bhūtamātra*) that constitute it are indestructible.

"Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to the subtle *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which is devoid of name and form; those whose beginning is this [unmanifest] are "those whose end is the unmanifest" (*avyaktanidhanāni*).
In that unmanifest *pradhāna* of such a nature, "destruction" refers to those things whose characteristic is the dissolution of name and form.

For instance, when a substance such as clay—which possesses an existent form—enters into a state such as a neck or rim, it is called the "origination" of a jar; however, its entry into a state such as shards, which is opposed to that [prior state], is called its "destruction.
That substance, therefore, remains persisting at all times.
Thus indeed the Blessed Parāśara has said: "The earth becomes a jar; from the jar comes a shard; from that, powder and dust; and from that, an atom" (ViP 2.12.42).
In this way, bodies are unmanifest at their beginning and end due to the non-connection with name and form, but they are manifest in the interim due to the connection with them.

The meaning is this: since the elements that constitute those bodies are always present, when they exist in reality, what cause for lamentation is there? What is the point of wailing on account of grief? However, in the view that the self is distinct from the body and eternal, one must not forget the verse beginning with "clothes" (vāsāṃsi).

As for those who assert the theory of "creation upon perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda), claiming that because the elements are non-existent at the beginning and the end, they are likewise non-existent in the middle and are therefore merely false— like chariots, horses, and so forth in a dream— and thus no grief caused by separation from them is seen by one who has awakened,
their position is weak; for by accepting that, one falls into the Vedic doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda).
Thus, it is established that in both views, there is no sorrow caused by the destruction of the body. //28//
Someone beholds this [Self] as a marvel, and likewise another speaks of it as a marvel.
And another hears of this as something wonderful; yet even having heard it, no one at all truly knows it. //29//
Śrīdhara: Why, then, do even the wise grieve in this world?
With the intention that it is precisely due to the lack of knowledge of the Self, he states the difficulty of knowing the Self in the passage beginning with "as something wonderful" (āścaryavat).
Someone, perceiving this Self through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, perceives it as something wonderful.

Because the Self—which is all-pervading and whose nature is eternal knowledge and bliss—is supramundane, one looks upon it as if seeing something being accomplished by a magician; thus, overcome by a sense of impossibility, one looks on with wonder.
Likewise, another speaks of it as a marvel, and another hears of it.
Furthermore, someone who is overcome by contrary mental cultivation does not know at all even after hearing;
by the word "and" (ca), it should be understood that he also does not know correctly even after speaking or even after seeing. //29//
Madhusūdana:
But surely even many who are learned grieve; why then do you reproach me alone again and again in this way?
Furthermore, according to the maxim that "the dullness belongs to the speaker alone where the listener does not understand," there is a failure to comprehend the meaning of your words.

And since this [Self] belongs to you as well as to others, it is not subject to the two aforementioned defects arising from the fault of one's own mental disposition; with this intention, He speaks of the difficulty of knowing the Self by saying "as a wonder" (*āścaryavat*).

This refers to the embodied being under discussion, who exists as if equal to a wonder—that is, to something marvelous—by virtue of possessing various contradictory attributes that are products of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Though existing, it appears as if non-existent; though its nature is self-luminous consciousness, it appears as if insentient; though a mass of bliss, it appears as if suffering;
though changeless, it appears as if subject to modification; though eternal, it appears as if transient; though manifesting, it appears as if unmanifest;
though non-different from Brahman, it appears as if different from it; though liberated, it appears as if bound; and though non-dual, it appears as if dual.

Someone whose final body is endowed with the means such as tranquility and self-control perceives— through the instructions of the scriptures and teachers— the object of the cognition of various manifold forms as it were; and through the negation of all duality born of ignorance, he directly realizes, by the ripening of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), that [Self] reflected in a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) produced by the great Vedāntic Mahāvākyas, which has the form of the nature of the Supreme Self alone and is the fruit of all meritorious deeds.
Only some, and not everyone;
likewise, "some see this as something wonderful" is an adverbial phrase qualifying the action.

Even the vision of the Self is indeed wonderful, because although it is by its own nature illusory, it is the manifestor of the Real; and although it is born of ignorance (*āvidyaka*), it is the destroyer of ignorance, for by subduing ignorance, it [destroys] that which is its effect.
"He even destroys his own self.
Likewise, "whoever perceives him as a wonder" is an epithet of the agent;
for although he has desisted from ignorance and its effects, due to the power of *prārabdha* karma, he conducts himself as if still possessed of them.
Although he is always established in samādhi, he emerges from it; and even when emerged, he again experiences samādhi.
Thus, due to the variety of his *prārabdha*-karma, his conduct is manifold. Because he has attained knowledge that is difficult to attain, he is desired by the entire world;
therefore, he is truly like a marvel.

The intention [of this] is as follows: these three are all marvelous—the self, the knowledge thereof, and the knower thereof—and since the self is supremely difficult to understand, how could you know it without effort?
Furthermore, the self is difficult to understand due to the absence of an instructor;
for he who knows the self would certainly explain it to another.
Because it is impossible for one who is ignorant to be a teacher,
how could one who knows [the truth] speak [of it] while his mind is generally absorbed in meditation?
Even if his mind were not absorbed, he would be unable to be known by another.
Even if he has understood [the truth] in some way, he speaks only because he is indifferent to purposes such as gain, honor, or fame.
But one who speaks out of mere compassion is as extremely rare as the Supreme Lord; thus it is said: "Another speaks like a marvel, and likewise acts.
He speaks exactly as he knows.
The particle *ca* has the sense of drawing back [the preceding subject] as "this very one.
And he is other, being distinct from all ignorant people;
for it would be a contradiction to say that he is not other than the one who sees.
Here too, the phrase "as if a wonder" (*āścaryavat*) is to be applied to the object (*karman*), the action (*kriyā*), and the agent (*kartṛ*).
Among these, the wonderfulness of the object and the agent has been explained previously; now, however, that of the action is being explained.
It is the speaking of the pure Self (*ātman*), which is not denotable by the word "all."
That is wonderful;
and so says the Śruti: "From whence words return, together with the mind, having failed to reach it.

For the pure Self, which cannot be denoted by any word whatsoever, [it is expressed] by means of a term possessing special power through the *jahad-ajahat-svārtha-lakṣaṇā* (indication where part of the primary meaning is abandoned and part is retained).

The meaning is that even the communication [of reality] by means of an imagined relation, without a delimitor of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), is of the nature of non-conceptual direct intuition (nirvikalpa-sākṣātkāra) and is thus most wonderful.

Alternatively, the communication of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) by such sentences as "That thou art" (tattvam asi)—without denotative power (śakti), without indication (lakṣaṇā), and without any other relation—is like a sentence that awakens one from deep sleep; it is truly marvelous.
This is because the power of words is inconceivable.
Nor does there follow the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of cognition without a relation, for this would be equally true even in the case of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā),
since the relation to the primary meaning is common to many [other things].
If it is argued that there is a restriction based on a specific intention (*tātparya-viśeṣa*), we say no;
for that too is not distinct with respect to all [hearers].
If it is argued that only a certain person perceives a specific intention and not everyone, [we reply:]...
Well then, let it be that there is some specific quality residing in the person, consisting of faultlessness, which acts as the regulator.
Nor is this position free from the same objection [of infinite regress].
Thus, for one whose internal organ is pure, who—preceded by an investigation into the intended meaning (tātparya)—[understands] through indication (lakṣaṇā) [the secondary sense].

Since you yourselves accept that there is a comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, why is it inconsistent to hold that a specific word of that very kind produces an undivided direct realization even without a [conventional] relation? On this view,
because it is not an object of the word's function, the scriptural statement "from which words turn back" is all the more appropriate.
And this intention of the Blessed One has been elaborated upon by the authors of the Vārttika:
"Because ignorance is weak, because the Self consists of the nature of consciousness,
and because the power of words is inconceivable, we know [the Self] through the removal of delusion."
Without even grasping the relationship between the signifier and the signified,
those awakened from deep sleep by others wake up, casting off their slumber.
Since no one perceives sound in deep sleep as they do while awake, when ignorance is destroyed through knowledge, the fruit is the realization: "I am Brahman."
"The cognition 'I am Brahman' arises for one who has destroyed ignorance;
having destroyed it, like a medicine that destroys disease, it perishes along with ignorance," and so on, according to this passage from the *Bṛhad-vārttika*.

Thus, having stated that the Self is difficult to know because the subject matter of the speech, the speaker, and the act of speaking are all of such a wondrous nature, he further states its difficulty due to the rarity of a listener: "And another hears this as something wonderful; even having heard it, one knows it.

Another—distinct from the ordinary observer and the speaker who is not yet liberated—the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), having approached the speaker, the knower of Brahman, in the prescribed manner, [hears this].
He hears—that is, he makes it the object of the inquiry known as "hearing" (śravaṇa), which means he determines it through the ascertainment of the purport of the Vedānta texts.
And having heard it, through the ripening of reflection (manana) and meditative concentration (nididhyāsana), he even perceives it directly, like a marvel.
Thus it has been explained: "Someone perceives this [Self] like a marvel."
Here too, the marvelous nature of the agent arises because he is extremely rare, his mental impurities having been washed away by the merit performed over many lifetimes.
And so it will be said:
"Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection."
"Even among those who strive and have attained perfection, only some know Me in truth" (Gītā 7.3).
"He who is not obtained even for hearing by many;
though many hear Him, they do not know Him."
Wondrous is the speaker; skillful is its attainer.
Wondrous is the knower; skillfully instructed is he.
And because of the Vedic scripture [KaṭhU 1.2.7], the wonderfulness of both the hearing and that which is to be heard should be explained as before.
Now, one might object: "Is it any wonder that he who performs hearing, reflection, and so forth, knows the Self? To this, the author says: "But no one at all... [KaṭhU 1.2.8].
The particle *ca* serves to connect the verbs with their respective objects.
Someone may not know this at all, even while performing such acts as listening [to the teachings];
what then need be said of one who does not perform them?
This is according to the maxim: "That which belongs to this world [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what was previously undertaken, because that is observed" (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.51).
And it has been stated by the authors of the Vārttika:
"If it is asked, 'Whence does that knowledge arise?', it is indeed from the complete destruction of bondage."
"And that [obstruction] exists either in the past, in the future, or in the present" (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika-saṃgraha 294).
Thus, even for those who perform hearing and the other [preliminary practices], knowledge arises only through the complete destruction of obstructions;
otherwise, it does not.
And that destruction of obstructions is, for some, already actual,
as in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha;
for others, it is yet to come.
As in the case of Vāsudeva;
it belongs to someone,
as in the case of Śvetaketu.

And thus, because the destruction of obstacles is extremely difficult to achieve, and because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "knowledge arises for men through the destruction of sinful karma," the essential meaning is that this Self is difficult to comprehend.

However, if the verse were explained as "even having heard this, no one indeed knows it," then there would be no syntactic consistency with the scriptural passage: "A knower who has been instructed by the skillful is a marvel" (KaṭhU 1.2.7).

If there is an objection that this contradicts the Lord’s own words, “Even among those who strive and are perfected, some know Me in truth” (Gītā 7.3), then scholars should forgive this lack of decorum.

Alternatively, the phrase “not even anyone” (*na caiva kaścit*) is connected with every clause; five modes have been stated: no one sees Him, no one speaks of Him, no one hears Him, and even having heard, no one knows Him. Or, someone indeed sees Him but does not speak of Him, while another... [text ends].
Someone sees but does not speak; someone hears that speech and knows its meaning; yet even having heard it, another does not know it; and no one at all remains entirely outside [of this].

However, for those on the side of the ignorant, because they are overwhelmed by doubt and contrary conceptions, the seeing, speaking, and hearing are like a miracle—thus the verse is explained word-for-word.
In the fourth quarter, however, the construction is: "having seen, having spoken, and even having heard. //29//
Viśvanātha:
Now, what is this marvel you speak of? And why is even this a marvel?
Regarding the fact that even for one being awakened, non-discrimination does not depart, he says "as if something wonderful" (āścaryavat) to indicate that this is indeed the truth in that regard;
[he refers to] this Self, the body, both of these forms, and the entire world. //29//

Baladeva: If it be asked, "Even though you, who are omniscient, have instructed me extensively, I do not understand the true nature of the Self which wards off sorrow; what is this?"—to that he says: "As something wonderful" (*āścaryavat*). Although [the Self] is of the nature of both knowledge and bliss, it is not perceived as distinct from them; although it is of the nature of knowledge, it exists as the knower; although its size is like an atom, it has a vast, pervasive body; and although it is connected to various bodies, it is not affected by their respective modifications.

Only someone whose heart has been purified by the performance of their own duties and by truth, austerity, recitation of mantras, and so forth, and who has obtained such knowledge through the grace of the Guru, perceives and experiences according to its true nature this *jīva* taught by me— which stands as something marvelous and extraordinary due to its possession of many contradictory attributes, such as being untouched [by material qualities].

The commentators explain that "as if a marvel" (*āścaryavat*) is either an adverbial modifier of the action or an adjectival modifier of the agent. The meaning is: for whomever one sees this, it is as if a marvel; and whoever sees it, he too is as if a marvel.
The same applies to what follows.
The meaning is that even after hearing this, someone may not have properly polished their heart;
thus, the true nature of the individual self (jīvātman) is difficult to comprehend.
The Śruti also says thus:
"He who is not obtained even for hearing by many;
though many hear Him, they do not know Him."
"Wonderful is the speaker, skilled is its obtainer; wonderful is the knower, well-instructed by the skillful. [KaṭhU 1.2.7] //29//
This embodied soul in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible, O Bharata;
therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings. 30.
Śrīdhara: Thus, teaching the indestructibility of the self in brief, he concludes the section on the absence of grief with the verse beginning "The embodied one" (dehī).
The meaning is clear. //30//
Madhusūdana:
Now, he concludes the teaching on the means for removing the delusion common to all living beings with the words "the embodied one" (*dehī*).
Even when the body of every class of living being is being slain, this embodied one—the Self, whose limiting adjunct is the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*)—is not to be slain.

Since it is certain that [the self] does not cease to exist, therefore you ought not to grieve for any beings— whether gross or subtle— who have entered into states such as those of Bhīṣma and others;
for the gross body is not to be mourned because it is unavoidable.

The meaning is that the subtle body (liṅga-deha) is not to be grieved for because, like the Self (ātman), it is indestructible; thus, it is not proper to grieve for the gross body, the subtle body, or the Self. //30//
Viśvanātha:
Then, having reached a decision, tell me what I should do and what I should not do.
To that, he says "Dehi" (Give) in two verses, saying: "Do not grieve; rather, engage in battle. (30)

Baladeva: Thus, teaching the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is so difficult to comprehend, in brief, He concludes the section on the absence of grief with the words "The embodied one" (*dehī*). Since this embodied soul, the *jīva*, is eternally indestructible even when the bodies of the entire multitude of living beings are being slain, you ought not to grieve for any beings, including those who have taken the form of Bhīṣma and others.
The meaning is that while the souls are eternal and therefore beyond grief, the reality regarding their bodies is that they are necessarily subject to destruction. //30//
Moreover, having regard for your own duty, you ought not to waver; for there exists nothing better for a Kshatriya than a righteous war. (2.31)
Śrīdhara: As for what was said by Arjuna, beginning with "And there is trembling in my body," that too is improper; thus [the Lord] says, "Even your own duty.

Since there is no possibility of the self's destruction, you ought not to waver even in slaying these [men]. Furthermore, the connection is: "Moreover, even considering your own duty, you ought not to waver."
Regarding what was said—"I see no good in slaying my own kin in battle"—he replies with the word "dharmyāt":
[there is] nothing other than fighting, which is not devoid of dharma and is consistent with justice. //31//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, due to the non-discrimination between the two bodies— the gross and the subtle— and their cause, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) called ignorance (avidyā), there arises for Arjuna, as it does for all living beings, a common appearance of the world as being real, consisting of the self, and possessing the attributes of the self, even though that world is illusory.

In order to dispel delusion, he [the Lord] has previously described the true nature of the Self through the discrimination of the three adjuncts (*upādhi*). Now, however, in order to dispel the unique delusion of Arjuna alone— which, caused by defects such as compassion, consists in the perception of unrighteousness due to the abundance of violence and other factors within his own duty called "war"— [the Lord speaks] regarding the fact that war, despite possessing violence and so forth...
The Blessed One makes it known that there is an absence of unrighteousness (adharma) precisely because it is one's own duty (svadharma), by saying "even one's own duty.

This means that not only should one consider the ultimate reality (paramārtha-tattva), but also one's own duty— that is, the duty of a kṣatriya consisting in not turning one's back in battle— having reflected upon it according to the scriptures, one should not waver or deviate from dharma.
You ought not to turn back due to the delusion that [war] is unrighteousness (*adharmatva*).

This being so, as for what you have said regarding war being a cause of sin— from the passage beginning with "Even though these do not see" up to the end with "there will be a certain residence in hell"— [this is countered by the fact that] "How could I slay Bhīṣma in battle," and so forth.

Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the non-commission of acts such as the killing of a preceptor or the killing of a Brahmin—all that has been said precisely through a thorough investigation of the *dharma-śāstras*.

Why? Because for a Kṣatriya, there exists no other means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*) than battle, which is not turned away from its duty (*dharmya*) and does not deviate from righteousness.

For it is battle alone, by way of conquering the earth, that fulfills the duties of a Kṣatriya, such as protecting the subjects and serving the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, the intention is that this alone is most praiseworthy for a Kṣatriya.
And so it has been said by Parāśara:
"For a Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and administering punishment,
should conquer enemy armies and the like, and protect the earth according to Dharma."
Thus [ends Parāśara-smṛti 1.58]. //31//
Manu also says:
"A king protecting his subjects, when challenged by equals, superiors, or inferiors,
must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya."
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to the Brahmins— these are the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
By such passages as these,
and because it has been established in the *Iṣṭy-adhikaraṇa* that the word "king" (*rājan*) denotes merely the Kṣatriya caste,
one should not mistakenly conclude that this duty belongs solely to the protector of the earth (the sovereign).
Even in the cited statement, the phrases "for the Kṣatriya" and "the duty of a Kṣatriya" are clear indicators [of this meaning].

Therefore, it is well said by the Blessed One that war is the praiseworthy duty of a Kṣatriya. There is no fault here, as it is stated through the figurative indication of praise—similar to the expression "others are not cattle; only cows and horses are cattle"—that there exists no other means for attaining the highest good than war.
By this, the argument that it is appropriate to desist from battle because there is something more praiseworthy to perform than it is refuted;
and so too is the statement: "I see no good in slaying my own kin in combat. (31)
Viśvanātha:

Since there is no possibility of the self's destruction, you ought not to tremble—that is, to fear—on account of being slain; the connection is that "having also considered your own duty, you ought not to tremble. //31//

Baladeva: Thus, having first taught the knowledge of the individual self (*jīvātman*) equally to all because of its utility for the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), [the Lord] intends to state that actions performed without desire by those established in yoga produce the steadfastness in the knowledge of the self accompanied by the purification of the heart.
To generate conviction in this regard, [He speaks of] actions performed with desire...
He states that [the duty] bestows desirable fruits through two verses beginning with "svadharmam api.
Indeed, battle is a constant duty for a Kṣatriya, enjoined like the Agnihotra and other rites.
And that [battle], consisting in the destruction of the enemy's life, does not cause sin, just as the killing of animals in the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices does not.
In both cases, this injury is indeed of the nature of a benefit;
for by the renunciation of the inferior body and world, there is the longing for those two which are divine.
And thus says the Smṛti:

In battles, O Brahmin, kings who desire to slay one another and fight with all their might without turning their backs go to heaven. In sacrifices, animals are constantly slaughtered by the twice-born.
"Indeed, even those consecrated by mantras attained heaven," and so forth.
Thus, having considered your own duty, you ought not to waver or deviate from dharma.
By stating "I see no good in what is appropriate" and so on, up to the conclusion that "residence in hell is eternal," you have asserted that war is a cause of sin.
And he says that this [conflict] arises precisely from ignorance, using the words "from the duty" (*dharmyāt*).
For battle itself, by means of conquering the earth, fulfills the duties of a Kṣatriya, such as protecting the subjects and serving one's elders and Brahmins.
Thus spoke the Blessed Parāśara:
For the Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and administering punishment,
should conquer the enemy armies and the like, and protect the earth according to Dharma.
[Parāśara-smṛti 1.58] thus it is said. //31//
"O Pārtha, happy are those Kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle as this, which has come to them by chance and is an open door to heaven. (BhG 2.32)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, since this great spiritual good has come to you of its own accord, why do you waver?
To this he says: "by chance" (yadṛcchayā). They obtain such a battle as this, which has arisen—that is, been attained—even without being sought.
For this is indeed the door to heaven that is free from obstruction;
or rather, the meaning is that only those who obtain such a battle as this are truly happy.
By this, the statement "How indeed, O Mādhava, can we be happy after killing our own kin? is refuted. //32//
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: "Even though war must be undertaken, it is not proper to do so with teachers such as Bhīṣma and Droṇa, because that would be extremely censurable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by chance" (yadṛcchayā), meaning without one's own effort.
The word "ca" is used for emphasis.

Those Kṣatriyas who obtain as their lot such a battle— which presents itself without even being sought, which has Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and other heroic men as its opponents, and which is a means for achieving visible fruits such as fame and the acquisition of a kingdom— they are indeed happy, partakers of happiness alone.
He says, "The door to heaven is open," because in victory one obtains fame and sovereignty through truth and effort alone, and in defeat one obtains heaven very swiftly;

for battle, being an unobstructed means to heaven, produces heaven without any interval, whereas sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma produce it only after a long time, depending on the fall of the body and the absence of obstacles.
This is the meaning.
By the phrase "the door to heaven," any suspicion of transgression (*pratyavāya*)—as in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others—is dispelled;
for although the *śyena* and other such rites are prescribed, they are tainted by the defect of their results.

[The opponents argue: "They are wicked. For the fruit [of war], namely the killing of enemies, is prohibited by such scriptural injunctions as 'one should not harm any living beings' and 'one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa,' because it generates demerit (*pratyavāya*) and because there is no injunction regarding the fruit itself; thus, according to the maxim that 'there is no scope for a prohibition regarding that which is touched by an injunction,' the [prohibition] does not apply here.
[Reply: Indeed, the fruit of war is heaven, and that is not prohibited.
And so Manu says:
"Kings who, desiring to slay one another in battles,
fight with their utmost strength while not turning their backs, go to heaven" (Manu 7.90).

However, because battle is enjoined as a slaughter involving the immolation of animals dedicated to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya) and so forth, it cannot be touched by a prohibition, just like the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.

This is because, as in the case of the taking or non-taking of that cup, there is a possibility of the contraction of a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) due to their equal force, resulting in an option (*vikalpa*).

Thus, according to the maxim that "where there is contact with an injunction, there is no room for a prohibition," battle does not produce demerit (*pratyavāya*), nor does it entail the fault caused by the killing of teachers or Brahmins such as Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
Because they are assassins.
Thus it was said by Manu:
"Whether it be a teacher, or a child or an elder, or a Brahmin of great learning..."
One should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation.
One may slay even an assailant approaching with intent to kill, even if he is a master of the Vedānta; by doing so, one does not become a killer of a Brahmin.
"Killing one who is about to kill (an *atatāyin*) incurs no fault whatsoever for the slayer," and so forth.
Now, an objection:
"In the case of a conflict between two legal codes (*smṛti*), the principle of logic (*nyāya*) is indeed stronger than the literal text."
However, it is an established principle that the treatise on Dharma is more authoritative than the treatise on worldly affairs (Artha-śāstra).
According to this statement of Yājñavalkya (2.21), even in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa who is an *ātatāyin* (one about to commit a mortal sin), there is indeed transgression (*pratyavāya*).
For the injunction "One must not kill a Brāhmaṇa" is a treatise on Dharma (*dharma-śāstra*), since it does not depend upon any visible purpose.

And as for the statement, "One may strike back at one who seeks to kill; by that, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin," this is a treatise on worldly affairs (*artha-śāstra*) because its purpose is the preservation of one's own life.

To this it is replied: even that which prescribes battle is indeed a treatise on dharma (*dharma-śāstra*), just like the injunction, "One should sacrifice a Brahmin for the sake of the Veda. This is because, in the passage "having made pleasure and pain equal," the independence from visible motives will be explained later.

The statement of Yājñavalkya, however, refers to killing committed in deceitful warfare and the like for the sake of visible worldly ends; thus there is no fault. But the author of the Mitākṣarā holds that this very rule applies to one who seizes wealth when dharma and artha coincide, because Āpastamba prescribes this twelve-year penance—referred to by the word "this"—for victory even over an enemy in a fourfold legal dispute according to the *Arthaśāstra* for the purpose of gaining friends and so forth.
He says that this is the supreme teaching: "One must not transgress the dharma-śāstras.
Let it be so; there is no loss for us.
Thus, by speaking of the happiness found in engaging in battle, [the Lord] has refuted what Arjuna said: "For how, O Mādhava, can we be happy after killing our own kin? (32)

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, those who die in a righteous war (nyāya-yuddha) attain even greater happiness than those who are victorious; therefore, by slaying Bhīṣma and the others, you shall instead make them happier than yourself. Thus he says, "by chance" (yadṛcchayā), meaning even without performing the yoga of action (karma-yoga) which is the means for attaining heaven.
"Apāvṛta" means that which has had its obstructions removed. //32//
Baladeva says: "Furthermore, since this great benefit has come to you without effort, trembling on your part is not appropriate. He says this with the word *yadṛcchayā* ("by chance").
The particle *ca* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
Indeed, such a battle with great heroes like Bhīṣma and others, which has presented itself without even exertion, is obtained by fortunate and blessed Kṣatriyas.

The meaning is that through victory one attains fame and sovereignty by means of truthful exertion, and upon death, one very swiftly attains heaven. Clarifying this, he specifies: "the door to heaven is opened," which means that the means for attaining heaven are unobstructed.
Since rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma bring about the attainment of heaven after a much longer period of time, their excellence [consists in this]. //32//
But if you will not engage in this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your own duty and fame, you shall incur sin. (2.33)
Śrīdhara: He states the fault in the opposite case with the words "atha cet" (if, however). //33//
Madhusūdana said:
"But surely I do not desire the fruit of war; O Kṛṣṇa, I do not long for victory."

Since it has been said, "Even for the sovereignty of the three worlds," one might wonder how that [war] is to be performed by me. Anticipating this doubt, he states the fault in not performing it with the words "But if" (*atha cet*).
"But if" (*atha*) indicates an alternative position.

This [war] is characterized by heroic men such as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others; it is *dharmya*, meaning not corrupted by defects such as violence, or rather, not departed from the dharma of the virtuous.
And that has been shown by Manu:
"While fighting his enemies in battle, one should not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with those having hollow tips, nor with those smeared with poison, nor with those whose points are set ablaze with fire."
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."

One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

"One who, recollecting the dharma of the virtuous, does not strike one who has met with the calamity of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away—[for such a person is righteous]. (Manu 7.91–94).
Indeed, one who fights while transgressing the dharma of the virtuous would be a sinner.

But if you, though challenged by enemies, do not engage in battle— even a righteous war— out of fear of violating dharma or worldly convention, and instead turn back in retreat, then you will abandon your own duty (*svadharma*), which consists of the performance of battle as ordained by such scriptures as: "Having conquered the enemy armies, one should protect the earth according to dharma" (Parāśara-smṛti 1.58).

The intention is this: by abandoning and failing to carry out [your duty], and by abandoning fame resulting from encounters with Mahādeva and others, you will incur only the sin born of battle— due to withdrawing from battle which is forbidden by such scriptures as "one should not retreat from the fray"— and you will not obtain either merit or fame.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "Having abandoned the merit accumulated over many lifetimes, you will incur only the sin committed by the king.

Since these wicked men will certainly kill you if you turn back, the intention is: "Do not become one who, having turned back and been killed, abandons his own long-earned good deeds and becomes a mere partaker of the evil deeds earned by others."
And so Manu says:
"But he who, being afraid, turns back in battle and is slain by his enemies,
takes upon himself whatever evil deed his master has committed."

"And whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter, the master takes all that from one who is turned back and slain" (Manu 7.95–96). Yājñavalkya also says: "The king takes away the merit of those who flee after being struck."

Therefore, what was said—"Even if I were to slay these aggressors, sin alone would take hold of us" (Gītā 1.36), and "I do not wish to kill them, even though they are killing me, O Madhusūdana" (Gītā 1.35)—is refuted. //33//
Viśvanātha:
He states the fault in the contrary case with the four verses beginning with "atha" (33).
Baladeva: With the words beginning with "atha," he shows the defects in the opposing view.

Having abandoned your own duty characterized by battle, as well as your fame obtained through the slaying of Rudra, Santoshana, Nivatakavacha, and others, you will incur sin; that is, you will attain what is forbidden by the Smritis, namely the abandonment of one's own duty (svadharma), such as [the injunction] "one should not turn back from battle. //33//
And people will also speak of your undying infamy; for one who has been highly esteemed, infamy is worse than death. (2.34)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "infamy" (akīrti):
"imperishable" means eternal;
"of one who is esteemed" means of one who is highly regarded.
It exceeds; it becomes greater. //34//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, it has been shown that by abandoning battle, there is the non-attainment of the two desired goals—fame and dharma—and the attainment of the undesired, namely sin.
Among these, the undesired thing called "sin" yields the fruit of suffering through an intermediate process, because its consequences pertain to the next world.
He says "infamy" (akīrtim) to indicate that which is characterized by the censure of the cultured, which yields undesirable results in the near future, and is utterly unbearable.

Living beings—such as gods, sages, and humans—will speak of your imperishable, long-lasting infamy among one another in the course of conversation, saying, "This man is not righteous," or "This man is not a hero.
The two particles [ca and vā] have the sense of a conjunction between the destruction of fame and the loss of dharma.
Not only will you abandon fame and merit, but you will also incur sin;
moreover, not only will you yourself incur infamy, but living beings will also speak of it—such is the meaning of the two particles (*ca* and *api*).
[Objection: But surely, since there is doubt of one's own death in battle, even infamy must be endured for the sake of avoiding that, because the protection of oneself is of paramount importance.
And so it is said in the Śāntiparvan:
"One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, gifts, and sowing dissension— either all together or individually— and never by means of war."
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two combatants,
and defeat likewise occurs in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
"When even the three previously mentioned expedients are impossible,
he should fight in such a way that, being well-equipped, he conquers his enemies. Thus it has been stated by Manu as well.

And thus, he dispels the doubt of one who fears death as to what the suffering of ill-repute might be: for a person of esteemed character who is highly regarded by others for qualities such as being righteous-souled or heroic—qualities not obtainable through any other means—the ill-repute exceeds even death; that is, it becomes more grievous than death itself.
What is the reason? Because of this, death itself is better than infamy due to its inferiority;
for you too have been highly esteemed through your association with Mahādeva and others.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that you will not be able to endure the suffering of ill-repute.

However, the cited statement—because it belongs to the *Arthaśāstra* (treatise on statecraft)—is weaker than the *Dharmaśāstra* (treatise on law), such as [Manu 7.88]: "He shall not turn back from battle," and so forth; this is the sense. //34//
Viśvanātha:
"Imperishable" means undecaying.
Of one who is honored—that is, one who is highly established. //34//
Baladeva said: "It is not merely a matter of the loss of your own duty and reputation;
rather, when war has commenced, all beings and all the worlds will speak of your imperishable and eternal infamy, saying that Arjuna fled.
If you should object, 'Surely I must endure this infamy because I am afraid of death,' he says in response: 'Of one who is highly esteemed'—that is, one who is exceedingly well-established."
It exceeds, that is, it becomes superior;
and thus, for such a reputation, death itself is better. //34//
The great chariot-warriors will think that you have desisted from the battle out of fear; and having been highly esteemed by them, you will now fall into contempt. (35)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "out of fear":
those very people by whom you were previously esteemed for your many virtues might, out of fear, think that you have retreated from the battle;
consequently, having been highly regarded before, you will fall into contempt and insignificance. (35)
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha:
You, who hold him in high esteem—thinking that our enemy Arjuna is a great hero—have become the object of his great respect.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Now, when you cease from battle, you will incur insignificance; Duryodhana and those other great chariot-warriors (mahārathas) will think that you have withdrawn from the fight out of fear alone.
The underlying intention is that for Kṣatriyas, a cause for ceasing battle other than fear—such as affection for kinsmen—is not logically tenable. //35//

Baladeva: If you should object, "How can there be infamy for me, who have desisted from battle out of concern for the sin of destroying my lineage and out of compassion?"—to that he says, "Out of fear.
Great chariot-warriors such as Duryodhana and others will consider you to have withdrawn from the fight out of fear of Karṇa and the rest, and not out of compassion for your kinsmen.
For it is not possible for a hero to cease from battle through affection for his kin without fear of the enemy; this is the meaning.

Previously, you were highly esteemed by them as a hero and an enemy, and were regarded as possessing many virtues; now that the battle has arrived, you will suffer the unbearable humiliation caused by them when they say, "This man is a coward; he has retreated. (35)
And your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, censuring your capability; what indeed could be more painful than that? (2.36)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "unspeakable words" (avācya-vādān):
your enemies, those who wish you ill, will utter unspeakable words—terms that are unworthy of being spoken. //36//
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: "Granted that great chariot-warriors such as Bhīṣma might not hold me in high regard, yet Duryodhana and the other enemies will surely honor me for withdrawing from battle, as it would be a service to them. To this he says: "Not to be spoken of...
Your enemies, Duryodhana and the rest, who revile your extraordinary prowess which is world-renowned—[they do so because they are incapable of facing it].

The intended meaning is that they will utter many various kinds of improper words— speech that is unfit for utterance, such as terms like "eunuch" or "sesame seeds"— but they will not hold you in high regard.
Alternatively, the syntactical connection is that those enemies, disparaging your capability and your worthiness of praise, will utter words that ought not to be spoken.

Now, one might object: "Unable to endure the more grievous suffering caused by the slaughter of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others, I desisted from battle; will I not then be able to endure the suffering of being censured for my lack of prowess by the enemy? To this he says: *tataḥ*—from that, meaning from the suffering of receiving such censure—there is no suffering whatsoever that is *duḥkhataram*, i.e., more painful or greater than that. This is the meaning. //36//
Viśvanātha:
"Inexpressible words" refers to harsh utterances such as "eunuch," and so forth. //36//
Baladeva said: "And what is unspeakable?

Your enemies, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who are intent on your harm, will speak many unspeakable words—terms such as 'eunuch' or 'barren sesame'—while censuring your already established capability and prowess.
What greater suffering could there be than hearing such unspeakable insults?"
And thus, by these six [verses], it has been shown that war leads to the absence of heaven and causes ill repute for one who is dispassionate toward it. //36//
Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle. (37)
Śrīdhara: Regarding what was said in "Nor do we know this" (Gītā 2.6), he says "Whether slain... and so forth.
The meaning is that in either case, there is only gain for you. //37//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might object that in battle there is the censure of neutral parties due to the killing of teachers and others, whereas upon withdrawal there is the censure of enemies; thus, it is like a rope with snares on both sides. Anticipating this, [the Lord says] that for the sake of battle, there is certainty of gain in both victory and defeat.
Thus, he states that rising up is necessary with the words "or slain" (*hato vā*).
The first half-verse is clear.
Since you will gain [merit] in either case, rise for battle having made the firm resolve: "I shall either conquer my enemies or die."
Even though there was doubt regarding the outcome of the battle, the duty to fight was certain;
by this, the objection beginning with "Nor do we know which is better for us" (Gītā 2.6) and so forth is refuted. //37//
Viśvanātha:
Now, there is indeed no certainty that victory will belong to me alone in battle;
therefore, one might ask how one should proceed to fight. To this, he says: "He is slain" (hataḥ). //37//
Baladeva: If you say, "I desisted from that [battle] because I lacked the certainty that victory would surely be mine," to that he says, "Or slain" (hato vā).
The sense is that in either case, there is gain for you. //37//
Having made pleasure and pain equal, as well as gain and loss, victory and defeat, then engage in battle; thus you shall not incur sin. (2.38)

Śrīdhara: Regarding what was said, "Sin alone shall cling to us" (Gītā 1.36), he says "having made pleasure and pain equal," and so forth; likewise, one should regard gain and loss as well, which are the causes of those two.
Having also made victory and defeat equal, as they are both caused by those two [factors];
the reason for their equality is the absence of joy and dejection. "Be disciplined" means be prepared.
The meaning is that by abandoning the desire for pleasure and the like, and fighting with the awareness that it is your own duty, you shall not incur sin. //38//
Madhusūdana:
But in that case, if one engages in battle with heaven as the objective, there would be a contradiction of its being an obligatory duty (*nitya*).

However, if one engages in battle with sovereignty as the objective, then because it belongs to the science of polity (*artha-śāstra*), it would be weaker than the science of dharma (*dharma-śāstra*).

If it is argued that, consequently, how could there be sin from the non-performance of a desired [act], and how could there be righteousness in the killing of a teacher, a Brahmin, or others for a visible purpose—thus contradicting the meaning of the verse beginning with "atha cet" (if, however)—to this he replies: "sukha-duḥkhe" (pleasure and pain). "Making them equal" means being free from attachment and aversion.

Without developing attachment toward pleasure, its cause, gain, its cause, or victory, and likewise without developing aversion toward pain, its cause, loss, its cause, or defeat, engage in battle; that is, be ready for action.

Thus, having abandoned the desire for pleasure or the desire for the cessation of pain, if you fight with the understanding that it is your own duty (*svadharma*), [you will incur no sin] even on account of the killing of teachers, Brahmins, and others, nor on account of the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*).
And you shall not incur sin.

For he who performs [the rite] out of a desire for its fruit incurs the sin caused by the killing of a guru, a brāhmaṇa, or others; or he who does not perform it incurs the sin caused by the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*).
Therefore, the intention already explained previously is that one who performs it without a desire for the fruit incurs neither of these two kinds of sin.
"There is no fault in stating the incidental fruits of one's own actions, as in: 'Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth' (Gītā 2.37).

Likewise, Āpastamba records in his Smṛti: 'Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as well; so too, while practicing dharma, worldly benefits arise as a consequence, but even if they do not arise, there is no loss of dharma.'"

Therefore, because the science of war (yuddha-śāstra) does not constitute the science of worldly gain (artha-śāstra), such statements as "it would result only in sin for us" (Gītā 1.36) and so forth are refuted. //38//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, for you, fighting is in every way your duty. Even so, regarding that which you fear will be a cause of sin, he says, "having made pleasure and pain equal," meaning: fight after learning from me the method by which no sin arises.
The cause of that [suffering] is gain and loss, as well as the acquisition of a kingdom and the fall from royalty;

the cause of that too is victory and defeat. Having made these equal through discernment—that is, having contemplated them as being the same—then, for you who possess such knowledge characterized by equanimity, no sin whatsoever shall exist.
As it will be said: "He is not tainted by evil, like a lotus leaf by water" (Gītā 5.10). //38//
Baladeva: [Objection: But surely the meaning of the verse beginning with "atha cet tvam" has already been explained;

since a war undertaken for the sake of kingdom and such things produces sin by being the cause of the destruction of gurus, brahmins, and others. [Reply: To the one fighting according to the path of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there would be no sin caused by that destruction; thus He says, "sukha... (in the following verse).
In this context, "establishing equanimity" (sāmya-karaṇam) should be understood as remaining free from modification (nirvikāratvam) in various circumstances.

Without developing attachment toward pleasure, its cause, or victory; and without developing aversion toward pain, its cause, failure to gain, or defeat—remaining with a mind undisturbed in each of these situations—you should therefore prepare yourself for battle.
The meaning is: "Be prepared to fight with the thought that this is merely your own duty.
Thus, as a warrior following the path of one seeking liberation, you shall not incur sin, which is the cause of its destruction;
for he who fights while desiring the fruits of action incurs that sin.
The meaning is that one who seeks consciousness (vijñāna) dispels ancient, infinite demerit.

If it is asked, "How can there be engagement in difficult acts such as battle or giving without attachment to the fruit? consider that in this case, the attachment to the bliss of the infinite Self is the motivator, just as attachment to kingship and the like is the motivator for falling from a cliff, as stated in BhG 2.39.
This wisdom has been declared to you from the perspective of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, by which wisdom joined, you shall cast off the bond of action. (39)
Śrīdhara: Concluding the instruction on the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), he introduces the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) as its means, beginning with the words "This," and so forth.
That by which the reality of things (*vastu-tattva*) is correctly discerned (*saṃkhyāyate*) or revealed is *saṃkhyā*, meaning perfect knowledge.
The reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva*) shining forth within that [knowledge] is *sāṅkhya*.
This wisdom has been declared to you as that which is to be practiced therein.

Even though this has been thus declared, if the reality of the Self (ātma-tattva) does not become directly perceived by you, then, for the sake of the direct perception of the reality of the Self through the gateway of the purification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), listen to this wisdom regarding Karma-yoga.

Endowed with that intellect, having purified your inner organ through the yoga of action dedicated to the Supreme Lord, you shall—by means of the direct knowledge obtained through His grace—thoroughly cast off and abandon the bondage consisting of karma. //39//
Madhusūdana:

Now, even if it be granted that there is no sin for one who fights with the understanding that it is his own duty (*svadharma*), nevertheless, your instruction to me regarding the necessity of engaging in battle is not appropriate.

From the passage beginning with "He who knows him as the slayer" (Gītā 2.19) up to the end with "How, O Pārtha, does that person cause anyone to be slain or slay anyone? (Gītā 2.21), all ritual action is rejected for the man of knowledge;

for it is impossible for such a one to have the cognition, "I am of a pure nature, neither agent nor enjoyer, yet having fought in battle, I shall enjoy its fruit," because of the contradiction between knowledge and action, which cannot coexist like light and darkness. Thus, there is no possibility of the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action.
And this intention of Arjuna will become clear in the verse beginning with "If the higher [path]...
Therefore, if it is argued that it is not appropriate to give instruction on both knowledge and action directed toward a single person,
the Blessed One says, "This [is so]," because the instruction on knowledge and action is appropriate due to the distinction between the states of the knower and the non-knower.

These twenty-one verses beginning with "This [is she], but not I" have been declared to you; in the *Sāṅkhya*—so called because the supreme reality (*paramātma-tattva*) is correctly explained (*samyak khyāyate*) and established therein as being devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*sarvopādhi-śūnyatayā*)—that which is established by means of that very [text] through the completion of its intended meaning is the person who is both *Sāṅkhya* and *Aupaniṣada*. This is the sense.

In that regard, I have spoken to you of that intellect (*buddhi*)—the knowledge whose object is the "That-Only" (*tan-mātra*), which is the cause for the cessation of all misfortunes. For one possessing such knowledge, no action whatsoever is prescribed, because it will be stated later: "For him, there is no duty to be performed.
If, however, despite my having spoken thus, this understanding does not arise in you due to a defect of the mind (*citta-doṣa*), [then...]
Therefore, for the sake of the direct realization of the reality of the Self through the removal of that [ignorance], you must practice *karma-yoga* alone.

Regarding that *yoga*, namely *karma-yoga*, listen to this intelligence characterized by the renunciation of attachment to results— which was mentioned here as "having made pleasure and pain equal"— which I shall explain to you in detail.
The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate the exclusion of the previous cognition from being the object of yoga.

Thus, since the instruction on knowledge is for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is pure, whereas the instruction on action is for one whose internal organ is impure, what room is there for a contradiction based on a suspicion of their combination? This is the underlying intention.
He praises the cognition whose object is yoga by describing its result: as [one acts] in actions with a resolute cognition...

Being disciplined, you will thoroughly cast off—that is, abandon—the cause of karma, which is characterized by impurity and constitutes an obstruction to knowledge; you will do so in such a way that future obstructions do not arise.

This is the sense: the obstruction to knowledge caused by karma can be removed only by karma itself known as *dharma*, according to the Vedic scripture: "Dharma removes evil" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 13.6).

However, inquiry characterized by hearing and so forth removes obstacles such as the impossibility [of realization] through the medium of direct perception for one who is already free from the obstacle consisting of ritual action; therefore, it cannot be taught for the purpose of dispelling the bondage of ritual action. Consequently, because your internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is extremely defiled, you must perform only ritual action, which is an external auxiliary means (*bahir-aṅga-sādhana*).
"Even the fitness for hearing [the scriptures] has not yet arisen in you, let alone the fitness for knowledge. And so he will say: "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47).

By this, the objection that the Blessed One has taught Arjuna only external means such as ritual action (*karma*), while neglecting internal means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth— which are the proper instruments for Sāṅkhya-based discernment—

is refuted. Furthermore, in the interpretation of the ancient commentators that "you shall abandon the bondage of action, which is transmigratory existence, through the attainment of knowledge caused by the grace of the Lord," one must avoid the fault of textual interpolation (*adhyāhāra*) and the redundancy of the word "action" (*karma*).
Viśvanātha:
He concludes the teaching on the yoga of knowledge with the words "This" (eṣa).
Sāṅkhya is that by which the reality of things (vastu-tattva) is correctly perceived or revealed; it is perfect knowledge.
Regarding that, the wisdom to be practiced has been described.

Now, listen to this wisdom which is to be practiced in yoga—namely, in bhakti-yoga—which is about to be declared; endowed with and possessed of which wisdom concerning devotion [one attains the goal].
The bondage of karma is saṃsāra. //39//

Baladeva: Concluding the exposition on the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), he begins to describe its means—the yoga of action free from desire (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*)—with the verse beginning "This...
According to etymology (*nirukti*), *sāṅkhyopaniṣad* refers to that by which reality (*tattva*) is correctly known (*saṅkhyāyate*) or determined;
that which is propounded by it, the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*), is *sāṅkhya*.

This understanding regarding that [Self], which is derived from secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*), has been set forth for you by the passage beginning with "But I am not... and ending with "therefore all beings...";
if this does not arise in your mind due to its defects, then, in yoga, the Brahmins [should seek it] through the recitation of the Vedas.

Listen to this intellect (buddhi) which is to be practiced in the yoga of selfless action (niṣkāma-karma-yoga) regarding the knowledge mentioned in such Vedic passages as, "They desire to know [Brahman] by means of sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting.
He praises that intellect by stating its fruit with the words beginning with "yayā" (by which).

"Performing actions by the command of the Blessed One, while undertaking tasks of great exertion, you shall cross over saṃsāra through the steadfastness of self-knowledge that has arisen within you by virtue of the greatness of each respective purpose.
[This refers to] that which has cattle, sons, kingdom, and so forth as its fruits.
In this scripture, it is defined that action performed with desire bears the fruit of knowledge, whereas that which is free from desire does not. //39//
In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist; even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear. 40.

Śrīdhara: Now, since actions such as agriculture sometimes deviate from their results due to a preponderance of obstacles, and since the possibility of sin (pratyavāya) exists due to defects in the auxiliary factors such as mantras, how can there be the destruction of the bondage of action through the yoga of action?
To this, he says: "Not here," and so forth.
In this yoga of action performed without desire, there is no destruction— that is, no fruitlessness— of the forward step, which is the undertaking;
nor does any adverse result exist,
because, since the action is directed solely toward the Lord, obstacles, defects, and the like are impossible.

Furthermore, even a very small undertaking, merely the beginning of this dharma—the yoga of action performed for the sake of propitiating the Lord—protects one from great fear, that is, from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
The meaning is that, unlike optional rites (kāmya-karma), it does not suffer fruitlessness through defects in its constituent parts or other such flaws. //40//
Madhusūdana:
But surely, according to the Śruti passage, "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know that very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity,

and by fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), all ritual actions are directed toward the desire for knowledge and knowledge itself, by means of the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*).
Because of its application there, and because purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*) serves as the means, the performance of ritual action is enjoined for me.

In that regard, since the destruction of results is established by scripture— namely, "Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so there the world won by merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6)— knowledge is enjoined with reference to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

Since sacrifices and the like being performed are motivated by desire (*kāmya*), they must be executed with the inclusion of all their constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*); thus, even if a single part is incomplete, a defect (*vaiguṇya*) arises. Furthermore, since it is impossible for a single person—even within the span of a lifetime—to perform all the actions prescribed in such scriptural injunctions as "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*), how can there be any hope for the result expressed in the words "whence shall you cast off the bond of action"? To this, the Blessed One says: "Not so. (2.40)

That which is advanced toward—that is, the fruit which is commenced by action—is "progress" (*abhikrama*); its destruction has been demonstrated in the passage beginning with "As here... and so forth. However, such destruction does not exist in this yoga of desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*).
This is because this fruit, being purity in the form of the destruction of sin, lacks the quality of being an object of experience denoted by the word "world," and thus its destruction is impossible.

Furthermore, since the fruit of action is the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) culminating in realization (*vedana*), and since realization immediately produces the fruit that is the cessation of ignorance, [there is no intermediate result to perish].

Since destruction is impossible without having produced a fruit, it is rightly said that here there is no destruction of the fruit. As it has been stated: "In this regard, whatever censure there is applies to the fruit and not to the action;
for an action performed after relinquishing the desire for its fruit brings about purification."

Likewise, no deficiency exists here—that is, no deficiency caused by the omission of auxiliary members (*aṅga*)—because of the statement "there is no [deficiency]" (*na... vidyate tam*). This is because obligatory rites (*nitya*) alone are enjoined for the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by way of destroying previously acquired evil, and in that context there is no rule requiring the performance of all auxiliary members.

Even in the view that optional rites (*kāmya*) are also enjoined according to the principle of "separate connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*), they are equivalent to the obligatory rites when they are devoid of any expectation of results.

For there is no inherent difference between the optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) Agnihotra; rather, the designations "optional" and "obligatory" arise solely from the presence or absence of the desire for a fruit. And these two positions have been stated in the Vārttika:

The injunction for the obligatory rites, such as the recitation of the Vedas, will be stated by the sentence "This very [person]" (tam etam) for the purpose of generating the knowledge of the unity of the Self.
"Or rather, even for optional rites (*kāmya-karma*), there is the purpose of seeking knowledge (*vividiṣā*),
because of the distinctness of their connection [to different ends] as expressed in the passage 'Him, this very one' (*tam etam*).

And thus, since there is a rule regarding the performance of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅga-upasaṃhāra*) only when a rite is performed with an intention toward its specific fruit, [the obligatory rite] is of a different character from that.

The meaning is that since the completion of a rite for the sake of purification can be achieved through a substitute and so forth, there is no sin resulting from a deficiency in its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Thus, within this dharma for the sake of purification—which is enjoined by such scriptural passages as "This very [dharma]"—if even a small portion is performed according to one's ability, whether in terms of number or procedure, for the purpose of worshipping the Lord; |||
He protects the practitioner from the great fear of saṃsāra by bringing about the grace of the Blessed One;
even if one is addicted to all kinds of sins, by meditating for even a moment upon the Imperishable,
he becomes once more an ascetic, the purifier of those who purify the assembly.
This is because of such traditional texts (smṛti).

Furthermore, in the statement "this very [knowledge]," since there is no injunction for a combination [of knowledge and action], and since the gradation of practice is logically established solely through the gradation of impurity, it is rightly said: "you shall cast off the bondage of karma. //40//
Viśvanātha:
Here, yoga is of two kinds: that consisting of devotion (bhakti) such as hearing and chanting, and that consisting of selfless action (niṣkāma-karma) dedicated to the Blessed Lord.

In this context, since the qualification for action alone has been established, the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) is first described. This is because of the statement, "Be free from the three modes of nature, O Arjuna" (Gītā 2.45), and because it is well known in the Eleventh Skandha that a person becomes free from the three modes through devotion alone, as devotion itself transcends the three modes.

Furthermore, since knowledge and action—being characterized by the qualities of goodness (*sattva*) and passion (*rajas*)—cannot logically result in freedom from the three modes, devotion, defined as the dedication of actions to the Lord, establishes merely the absence of fruitlessness in action.
But it does not receive the designation of "devotion" (bhakti) for itself precisely because it lacks primacy.
Furthermore, if it were held that even action offered to the Lord is indeed devotion,
then what would action be?
If it is argued that only that action which is not offered to the Blessed One is truly "action," we say no;
for even the state of non-action (naiṣkarmya) is devoid of value if it is bereft of devotion to the Imperishable (Acyuta).
Even stainless knowledge is not truly beautiful; how much less so that which is eternally inauspicious, nor that action which, though performed without motive, has not been offered to the Lord.
Since its futility has been demonstrated by these words of Nārada,
it follows that here devotion— characterized solely by hearing, chanting, and so forth, which serves as the means for attaining the sweetness of the Lord’s feet— is being defined;
just as selfless karma-yoga must also be defined [in its own context].

Both of these should be understood as being denoted by the term *buddhi-yoga*, because of the statements: "I give that *buddhi-yoga* by which they come unto Me" (10.10), and "For action is far inferior to *buddhi-yoga*, O Dhanañjaya" (2.49).
Now, He declares the majesty of *bhakti-yoga*—consisting of hearing, chanting, and so forth regarding the Nirguṇa—with the words "Not here," etc.
In this yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga), even if only a slight progress is made— that is, if merely the beginning is undertaken— there is no destruction of this bhakti-yoga,
nor does any adverse result (pratyavāya) arise.

The implication is that in the yoga of action (karma-yoga), for one who has begun the practice and then failed to carry it out, both the loss of the fruit of the action and the occurrence of adverse results would follow.
[Objection: "In that case, for one who desires to practice devotion but fails to perform the appropriate devotion, there would surely be no fruit of devotion.
To this, he says: "Even a little" (*svalpam*). This refers to whatever measure of devotion existed at the time of the commencement of this dharma, even if it were very slight.
The meaning is "she too.
She indeed protects one from the great fear of *saṃsāra*, because of such scriptural statements as: "By merely hearing her name once, even a *pukkaśa* is liberated from *saṃsāra*" (BhP 6.16.44).
And because it is seen to be so in the case of Ajāmila and others;
for, O Uddhava, there is not even an atom of destruction of My dharma when its constituent parts are first undertaken.
"By me, this has been rightly resolved because of my being devoid of qualities and free from desire for rewards"—
by these words of the Blessed One, it is seen that there is indeed a single meaning with this present statement.
However, in that context, the reason was put forward that because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), an entity transcending the qualities (*guṇātīta*) can never be destroyed;
that same reason should be understood here as well.

Nor should it be said that even action performed without desire becomes "devoid of qualities" solely through the power of offering it to the Lord—for it has been stated: "Offering one's own action to Me, whether fruitless or of a sattvic nature, is one's duty" (BhP 11.25.23).
Baladeva: With the following understanding, he praises Karma-yoga: "Not so" (na iha).

Because of the statement in the passage beginning with "This very one" (tam etam), there is no destruction of the fruit-producing nature of the *abhikrama*—that is, the commencement—in the Karma-yoga performed without desire;
the meaning is that there is no futility for a commencement that has not been brought to completion.
Furthermore, even if there is a deficiency in the mantras or other auxiliary components, no transgression occurs;
for by the greatness of its dedication to the Self, and by the name of the Blessed Lord—namely "Oṃ Tat Sat"—that [transgression] is destroyed.
In this world, even a small portion of the dharma characterized by obligatory rites that has been performed and offered to the Blessed Lord protects the practitioner from the great fear of saṃsāra.
And he will say thus: "O Pārtha, neither here nor in the hereafter... (Gītā 6.40) and so forth.
Ritual actions performed for the sake of desire, when carried out with the inclusion of all their constituent parts (*aṅga*), lead to the aforementioned results;
however, if there is a deficiency in the mantras or other constituent parts, they produce adverse consequences (*pratyavāya*).

However, actions performed without desire, when carried out according to one's ability, certainly produce the fruit characterized by steadfastness in knowledge for the reasons already stated; they do not give rise to any transgression. //40//
O joy of the Kurus, in this world the intellect characterized by resolute determination is single; for the intellect of those lacking such determination is indeed many-branched and infinite. 41.
Śrīdhara: In response to the question "Why?", he states the difference between the two with the words "of the nature of resolve" (*vyavasāyātmikā*).

Here, in the yoga of action characterized by the worship of the Lord, there arises but one single-minded intellect—of the nature of resolve, meaning a certainty that "I shall surely cross over [saṃsāra] through devotion to the Supreme Lord alone.
But for those who lack resolve—those seekers of sense-objects who are turned away from the worship of the Lord—their intellects are infinite, because their desires are infinite.
For even there, many branches of cognition arise due to various distinctions such as the fruit being the result of action or the fruit being the result of a quality.
Indeed, certain obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites performed for the sake of propitiating the Lord do not perish even if some auxiliary factor is deficient;
for they are prescribed with the injunction: "One should perform them in whatever manner one is able."
Nor is there any deficiency [in this case],
because even a deficiency is pacified by being dedicated solely to the Lord;
however, desirable action (kāmya-karma) is not like that.
Therefore, the sense is that there is indeed a great disparity. //41//
Madhusūdana:
To establish this, [the author] states that those [qualities] enjoined by the phrase "this very" (tam etam) have a single referent in the words "of the nature of resolve" (vyavasāyātmikā).

O descendant of Kuru, on this path to the highest good, whether in the context of the phrase "this very" or in the statement itself, [it refers to] that which consists of resolve—that is, that which consists of the ascertainment of the true nature of the Self.

The single *buddhi* (realization) intended as the goal for all four stages of life (*āśrama*) is understood through the instrumental case in the passage beginning with "by the recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacanena*),
which indicates that each [means] is an independent means [to that end].
For if they had different goals, there would be a requirement for their combination (*samuccaya*).
