The meaning is that although they have a single purpose, there is no such authority here as there is in the case of the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—where the dual compound (*dvandva-samāsa*) is used—or as in the phrase "to Agni and to Prajāpati," where the word "and" (*ca*) is employed; [therefore, the two are not to be taken together].

Because they share a single fruit, the intellect whose objects are Sāṅkhya and whose objects are Yoga is one, characterized by resolute determination, and is opposed to all contrary forms of cognition.

The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that the meaning is this: the [Vedic] cognition is subverting because it arises from faultless Vedic statements, whereas other cognitions belonging to those lacking firm resolve are themselves subverted.
Others, however, [hold that one thinks]: "I shall cross over saṃsāra solely through the propitiation of the Supreme Lord."
They say that in this yoga of action, the intellect becomes single-pointed and fixed solely on certainty;
for even in every respect, according to the section on knowledge (*jñāna-kāṇḍa*), even a small portion of this dharma protects one from great fear—this is logical.
In the section on action (*karma-kāṇḍa*), however, there are many branches and numerous divisions, because desires themselves are manifold.

Furthermore, due to the distinctions among the branches of various types— such as the fruits of action and the fruits of qualities— the intellects of those lacking resolve, who desire this or that particular fruit, become infinite.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of illustrating the well-known infinity of these intellects.
Therefore, the intention is that there is a great distinction between these actions for the sake of purification and those optional (kāmya) actions. //41//
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, he says "vyavasāya... because among all forms of intellect, the intellect concerning the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) alone is declared to be superior.
Here, in this yoga of devotion, there is but one single intellect characterized by resolute determination (vyavasāyātmikā).

This very chanting, remembering, and service to the feet of the Lord as instructed by my glorious guru is my means of practice (*sādhana*), this alone is my goal (*sādhya*), and this alone is my life-breath; it cannot be abandoned in either the state of practice or the state of attainment. This alone is my desire, this alone is my duty, and nothing else is my duty, nor is there anything else.
"May there be happiness or may there be suffering; may saṃsāra perish or may it not perish—even in a dream, let that which is desirable remain.
A mind characterized by such a firm resolve can arise only in one whose devotion is sincere.
As it has been said: "Therefore, one who is full of faith and possesses firm resolve should worship Me with devotion" (BhP 11.20.28).
He says "many" to show that the intellect is not indeed one in other cases.
Those [intellects] which have many branches are "many. For instance, in the yoga of action, because desires are infinite, the intellects are infinite.

In the same way, regarding the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), first there is the intellect directed toward desireless action (*niṣkāma-karman*) for the sake of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); then, once that is purified, there is the intellect directed toward the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*).
At that time, there is the intellect directed toward knowledge.

Furthermore, for the sake of ensuring that knowledge does not prove fruitless, there is the intellect directed toward devotion (*bhakti*), as stated by the Lord: "And one should surrender knowledge unto Me. Thus, there is the intellect directed toward the renunciation of knowledge and the intellect directed toward devotion; therefore, the types of intellect are infinite.
Because action, knowledge, and devotion must necessarily be practiced, their respective branches are likewise infinite. //41//
Baladeva: He states the superiority of the intellect regarding desireless action over the intellect regarding optional (kāmya) action with the words "vyavasāya" and so forth.

O descendant of Kuru, here among all Vedic actions, one whose mind is purified by desireless actions consisting of the worship of the Lord—through the knowledge inherent within them like the fibers of a lotus stalk—realizes the true nature of the Self.

The intellect of those who lack resolve—namely, those performers of ritual acts motivated by desire—is indeed manifold. This is because their intellect takes the form of the certainty "I shall experience [the results]," which has a single object; that is to say, it is directed toward a single experience for all of them. However, the intellects of those lacking resolve are infinite.
Because its objects of desire are infinite— such as cattle, food, sons, heaven, and so forth—
and because even within those, there are many branches;
for even in rites such as the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, which have a single primary fruit, we hear of the expectation of numerous intermediate fruits, such as long life and excellent progeny.

For in this case, only the knowledge of a self distinct from the body is required, and not the true nature of the self as previously described; for if that [true nature] were ascertained, engagement in optional rites (kāmya-karma) would be impossible. //41//
O Pārtha, those who are unwise, who delight in the ritualistic declarations of the Vedas and who assert that there is nothing else, utter this flowery speech. (2.42)

Those whose nature is desire, who look toward heaven, [follow] that path which yields birth and the fruits of action, which abounds in various ritual acts, and which leads toward enjoyment and power. //43//

For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [attachment], the intellect characterized by resolute determination is not established in meditative concentration. //44//
Śrīdhara: Now, why do even those possessed by desire not abandon their painful desires and instead adopt a resolute intellect? To this he says, "This speech," and so forth.

This speech—which is like a flowering poisonous creeper, appearing beautiful only at first sight—is that which they proclaim as "excellent" and as being solely intent upon the fruit of the ultimate truth, namely, the scriptural revelation of fruits such as heaven.

The connection with the third verse is as follows: for those whose minds have been carried away by that speech, an intellect characterized by resolve is not established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Why do they speak thus?
Because they are unwise and deluded.
In this context, the reason is "those who delight in Vedic discourse. By "Vedic discourse" are meant those explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) found in the Veda, such as:
"Indeed, for one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, their merit becomes inexhaustible."
Likewise, there are those who delight in such [mantras] as "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal" (RV 8.48.3) and so forth;
they are devoted to and find pleasure in these very [formulas].
For this reason, they are habitually inclined to declare that there is no other reality of the Lord (īśvara-tattva) to be attained beyond this. //42//
Therefore, it says "those whose souls are possessed by desire. "Those whose souls are possessed by desire" means those whose minds are agitated by desire;
therefore, they are those for whom heaven alone is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

It is so called because it bestows birth, actions, and their fruits therein. The ellipsis [of the verb] is "they proclaim that [Veda]," which possesses many specific rites that serve as the means for attaining—that is, reaching—that state of enjoyment and sovereignty. //43//
And thus [it is said]: "For those who are attached to enjoyments and power," and so forth.
This refers to those whose minds have been carried away—that is, attracted—by that flowery speech, being deeply engrossed in enjoyments and power.
*Samādhi* is one-pointedness of mind.
That is to say, it is the state of being oriented toward the Supreme Lord.
However, an intellect characterized by certainty regarding that [state] is not enjoined;
this is a construction where the object and the agent are identical.
The meaning is that it does not arise. //44//
Madhusūdana:

Anticipating the objection— “Why does a resolute intellect not arise even for those who lack resolve, since the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) are the same?”— he states with the three verses beginning with “yām imām” that it does not arise due to the presence of obstacles.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Abounding in specific ritual acts directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and sovereignty. Enjoyment (*bhoga*) refers to that which consists of drinking nectar, sporting with Urvaśī, the fragrance of the *pārijāta* tree, and so forth; and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the lordship over the gods and others. The "attainment" (*gati*) is the reaching of these two.
That which is "abounding" (*bahulām*) refers to those specific ritual acts (*kriyā-viśeṣa*) that serve as the means for them, such as the *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifices.
"Extensive" means that which expounds, to an extreme degree, the entire collection of rituals and means for attaining enjoyments and power;
for it is well known that the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section) is everywhere far more extensive than the *jñānakāṇḍa* (the knowledge section).
They "proclaim" such speech characterized as the *karmakāṇḍa*, meaning they accept it as preeminent, having as its fruit the ultimate [worldly] goals such as heaven and the like.
Who are these "unwise" ones? They are those devoid of the understanding of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) produced by critical inquiry.

Therefore, they are "devoted to the Vedic doctrines"—that is, devoted only to those *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) found in the Veda such as, "For one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, their merit becomes inexhaustible," and so forth, [accepting] them as the very truth of the Veda's meaning, thinking, "It is exactly thus."
Satisfied by false conviction,
O Pārtha,

they say, "There is nothing else," because, in their view, there is no section on knowledge (jñāna-kāṇḍa) other than the section on ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa), since the entire Veda is devoted solely to action.

The meaning is that they are habitually disposed to speak at great length—claiming that there is no other unsurpassed fruit of knowledge than the expectation of the fruits of karma—and thus they propound matters contrary to the section on knowledge (*jñāna-kāṇḍa*).
Why are they haters of liberation?
Because they are "desire-natured" (*kāma-ātmānaḥ*), being composed of desire due to their minds being agitated by hundreds of objects of desire.

This being so, why do they not desire even liberation? Because they are "intent on heaven" (*svarga-parāḥ*), meaning those for whom heaven alone is the supreme and most excellent goal due to its being devoid of [the presence of] Urvaśī and others; [anything] beyond heaven is not so.
Wandering under the delusion that there is no human goal (puruṣārtha) to be attained, they lack discernment and dispassion; that is to say, they are unable even to endure talk of liberation.

Furthermore, for those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are deeply attached to the previously mentioned enjoyments and power because they fail to perceive defects such as their perishability, and whose minds—meaning their discriminative knowledge (viveka-jñāna)—have been "snatched away" or obscured by that speech which delights in specific ritual actions, such is their state.

Explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) serve the purpose of praise; it is well known that the authority of the Veda applies to its intended subject matter when that is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition.

However, for those who are unable to understand this, the intellect—which consists of resolute determination—is not established, nor does it arise, within the internal organ during meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is the meaning.

Or rather, it means that for them there is no intellect characterized by resolve regarding the object of concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya*). This is because the locative case is identical whether it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or the object (*viṣaya*). The verbal suffix *la* in the form "is ordained" (*vidhīyate*) is used in the sense of the reflexive passive (*karma-kartari*).

Furthermore, based on the etymology "that in which everything is concentrated" (*samādhīyate*), *samādhi* refers either to the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); thus, there is no assumption of an unestablished meaning.

In the interpretation that "abiding in the thought 'I am Brahman' is samādhi, but the intellect characterized by resolve directed toward that [Brahman] does not arise," conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone is respected.

The underlying meaning is this: although optional rites such as the *agnihotra* are not distinguished from those performed for the sake of purification, they nevertheless fail to produce the purity of the inner organ (*āśaya-śuddhi*) due to the defect of attachment to results.
However, purification that conforms to worldly enjoyments is not conducive to knowledge.
To demonstrate this very point, the phrase "those who are attached to enjoyments and power" is taken up once again.

But actions performed without any expectation of fruit bring about the purification conducive to knowledge; thus, it is established that there is a difference in the results for the wise and the unwise.
And this will be explained in detail further on. //42-44//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, he says "this speech which... to show that those who perform actions with desire are even more dull-witted than the undetermined ones. "Flower-like speech" means speech that is merely pleasing on the surface, like a flower that is ultimately fruitless.

The connection with the third [verse] is as follows: for those who "proclaim"—that is, who declare from every side that "this alone is the most excellent Vedic word"—and whose minds are carried away by that speech, a resolute intellect is not established. The meaning is that because such an intellect is impossible among them, it is not taught to them.
Why do they speak thus?
Because they are unwise and foolish.
The reason for this is that among the Vedic texts there are *arthavādas* (eulogistic statements), such as: "For one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, their merit becomes indeed inexhaustible."
"Having drunk the Soma, we have become immortal"—such are their opening words.
What kind of speech do those who prattle that there is no other reality than the Lord (Īśvara) actually utter?

It is that which "takes" or bestows—that is, presents—abundantly those specific ritual acts which grant birth, karma, and its fruits, leading toward the attainment of enjoyments and lordship. //42-43//
And consequently, for those whose minds have been carried away— that is, attracted— by that flowery speech to which they are attached to enjoyments and power,
no intellect characterized by certainty regarding *samādhi*— which is one-pointedness of mind and exclusive orientation toward the Supreme Lord— is established.
This is an impersonal construction (*bhāve prayoga*).
The meaning is that it does not arise; such is the statement of the Master (Svāmin). //44//

Baladeva: If it be argued that these [people] might indeed possess a resolute intellect because the Vedic texts are equal [in authority], [the Lord] says "yām" (which) in three verses to show that it does not arise due to defects of the mind:
"The ignorant ones, those of little knowledge, proclaim this speech—such as 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma'—and they imagine, 'This alone is the preeminent Vedic word.
For those whose minds are carried away by that speech, a resolute intellect is not established in their concentrated minds; it does not dawn upon them—this is the connection."
To the question "What kind of speech? he says: "Flowering."
The meaning is that they are fruitless, like a flowering poisonous creeper which is pleasing to the mind only at first sight.
To the question "Why do they speak thus?", he says: "In the Vedas, those doctrines such as 'We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal'..."

"Indeed, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes inexhaustible"—such are the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages). Devoted to these alone, they possess the conviction that "this is exactly so," precisely because the Veda speaks the truth.

For this very reason, they hold that there is nothing else; that is, other than the fruit of ritual action such as heaven, there exists no other attainable goal characterized by liberation—an unsurpassed, eternal bliss consisting in the knowledge of the supreme reality of the individual soul.

The meaning is that they are characterized by the habit of asserting that the Vedāntic statements which expound that [Brahman] are subordinate to ritual action because of the oneness of the agent and the deity who are auxiliary parts of that action. //42//
He speaks of the defect of the mind: those whose souls are possessed by desire (*kāmātmānaḥ*) are those whose minds are seized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sensual pleasure.
To the question, "If that is so, why do they not desire such liberation?", he replies with the word *svarga*:
those for whom heaven itself is the supreme nectar (*sudhā*), because it is endowed with celestial nymphs and other delights.
The meaning is that, because they are seized by such latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they do not speak anything else.
"Birth and action" (*janma-karma*) refers to birth, characterized by the connection with a body and sense organs,
and therein, action (*karma*) refers to that which is prescribed for each respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
And the fruit consists of perishable things such as cattle, food, heaven, and so forth.

That speech—which speaks of those specific rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which are abundant and manifold, and which grant those fruits pre-eminently and without interruption, leading to the attainment of the state of enjoyment and sovereignty—is what they say; this is how it connects with the preceding [sentence].

The meaning is: "the attainment of those two," namely, enjoyment (bhoga)—consisting of drinking nectar, celestial maidens, and so forth—and sovereignty (aiśvarya), which is lordship over the gods and other beings. //43//

Baladeva: Regarding the word "bhoge" (in enjoyment), for those who are attached to the previously mentioned enjoyment and power (*bhoga-aiśvarya*), whose minds— their discriminative knowledge— have been carried away or lost by that flowery speech because they fail to perceive the defect of perishability inherent in those two, [the Lord speaks] regarding this very state of *samādhi*.

According to its etymological derivation (*nirukti*), "samādhi" means that the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the self's reality is correctly placed (*sam-ā-dhīyate*) within this; thus, the meaning is that the mind is concentrated upon that [object]. //44//
The Vedas deal with the realm of the three qualities; be free from these three qualities, O Arjuna.
Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, beyond the pursuit of acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self. 2.45.

Śrīdhara: Now, if heaven and the like are not the supreme fruit, then why does the Veda enjoin ritual actions as the means to achieve them? To this he says: "The domain of the three gunas... and so forth.
Those who possess the three *guṇas* and have desires are the qualified persons; for them, the Vedas are intended to establish the connection between action and its fruit.
But you, become free from the three *guṇas* and free from desire.
Regarding that, He states the means: "Be free from the pairs of opposites (*nirdvandvaḥ*)."
Pleasure and pain, cold and heat, and so forth are the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). Be free from them; the meaning is: endure them.
How so?
To this he says: "being established in constant existence"; the meaning is, "having relied upon steadfastness."

Likewise, one should be free from acquisition and preservation; acquisition (*yoga*) is the taking possession of what has not been obtained, while preservation (*kṣema*) is the protection of what has been obtained.
One who is free from that [distraction],
self-possessed and vigilant—
for it is not possible for one who is agitated by the pairs of opposites, preoccupied with acquisition and preservation, and negligent, to transcend the three qualities. //45//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: Granted that for those with desires, let there be no such thing due to the defect of their underlying intention; however, for those who are desireless and perform action with a resolute intellect, since the nature of action leads to the attainment of results such as heaven, the obstruction to knowledge remains the same. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the three qualities... (traiguṇya).

The activity of the three *guṇas* is "the state of the three *guṇas*" (*traiguṇya*); *saṃsāra* has desire as its root. Those *Vedas* whose subject matter consists of that very [state]—namely, those consisting of the *karmakāṇḍa*—inform only that person who desires a particular fruit of what they perform; this is the meaning.

For even though there is an injunction such as "the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* [sacrifices] are for all desires," the attainment of all fruits does not occur from a single performance, because of the absence of the respective specific desires.
It is established in the *Yogasiddhi* section that whatever fruit one performs an action with the desire for, that very fruit results from that performance.
Since there is an absence of fruit when there is an absence of desire, therefore, O Arjuna, become free from the three qualities and devoid of desire.
By this, transmigration is refuted on account of the inherent nature of action (*karma-svābhāvya*).

Now, one might object: since clothing and other things are required for the sake of counteracting the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, how can there be freedom from desire? To this he says: "free from the pairs of opposites" (*nirdvandvaḥ*).
The word "be" (*bhava*) is connected to every [clause].
According to the principle stated in the verse beginning with "But the contacts of the senses," be patient toward the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat;
likewise, remain established in that [state].
For one whose *sattva* is overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, thinking "I shall die from the affliction of cold, heat, and so forth," becomes averse to *dharma*.
You, however, should overcome *rajas* and *tamas* and take hold of *sattva* alone.
[Objection: Even while enduring cold, heat, and the like, must one not adopt some means for the sake of counteracting hunger, thirst, and so forth?

Since that which has been acquired must be protected, when effort is made for that purpose, how can there be "abiding in being" (sattvasthatva)? To this he says: "free from acquisition and preservation" (niryogakṣema).
Acquisition (yoga) is the gaining of what has not yet been obtained; [preservation (kṣema) is the guarding of what has been obtained].
"Security" means the preservation of what has been attained;
"be devoid of that" means be free from attachments that cause distraction of the mind. This is the meaning.
One should not entertain such thoughts as, "How shall I live if this is so?
For the Supreme Lord, who is the inner controller of all, will Himself provide for your acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) and so forth; thus it is said: "the self-possessed" (ātmavān).
He is "self-possessed" whose self—the Supreme Self—abides as both the object of meditation and the provider of acquisition, preservation, and so on.

The meaning is: "Having resolved that 'for me, who am propitiating the Supreme Lord by renouncing all desires, He Himself will provide whatever is required for the mere maintenance of the body,' you should remain free from anxiety";
or alternatively, "be self-possessed," which means "be vigilant. //45//
Viśvanātha:
But you, having become detached from the means for achieving the four aims of human life, should take refuge in the yoga of devotion alone; thus he says, "traiguṇya-...

The Vedas have as their objects those things consisting of the three guṇas—namely action, knowledge, and so forth—which are to be illuminated. The suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own primary sense (*svārthe*).
And this has been stated according to the maxim that "designations are made on the basis of abundance";
however, it is devotion alone that leads one [to the goal], as in such scriptural passages as:
"He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as he does for the Divine," and so forth.

Furthermore, the *Smṛtis* such as the *Pañcarātra*, as well as the *Upaniṣads* such as the *Gītā*, the *Upadeśa-sāhasrī*, and the *Gopāla-tāpanī*, indeed take even qualityless (*nirguṇa*) devotion as their subject matter; for if devotion were not declared in the Vedas, it would simply lack authority.
Therefore, depart from those injunctions of knowledge and action consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) which are declared in the Vedas, and do not perform them.
However, you must by all means perform those injunctions for devotion prescribed in the Vedas;
in their performance,
do so without recourse to the rules of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Pañcarātra.
Exclusive devotion to Hari leads only to the emergence of extraordinary signs.
Thus, this fault is indeed unavoidable.
Therefore, for those with qualities as well as those who have transcended the qualities,
the Vedas are not their domain, whether they possess the three qualities or are free from the three qualities.

In this regard, however, you should become free from the three qualities (niṣtraiguṇya). Through devotion to Me alone—which is itself beyond the qualities—become one who has emerged from those things consisting of the three qualities.
Consequently, be free from the pairs of opposites (nirdvandva), devoid of honor and dishonor and the like, which are composed of the qualities.
Therefore, he is "such" (tathā) because he dwells only with eternal beings—living entities who are My devotees.

If one were to explain [the verse] as "be eternally established in the quality of goodness" (nityaṃ sattva-guṇastho bhava), there would be a contradiction with the explanation "be free from the three qualities" (nistraiguṇyo bhava).
Yoga is the attainment of what has not yet been attained.

"Security" (*kṣema*) is the preservation of what has been acquired; [the devotee] is devoid of that [effort], because, solely through the power of tasting the flavor of devotion to Me, he does not pursue those two [acquisition and preservation]. "I carry their acquisition and security" (*yoga-kṣemam vāhayāmy aham*): this is because I alone, out of affection for My devotees, bear that burden.
The self-possessed one is endowed with the intelligence granted by Me.
Herein lies the discernment between being beyond the three qualities (niṣtraiguṇya) and being within the three qualities (traiguṇya),
as it was stated in the eleventh [chapter]:
"One's own duty (nija-karma) is *sāttvika* when it is offered to Me or performed without desire for fruit;
it is *rājasa* when it is performed with a desire for results; and it is *tāmasa* when it consists primarily of violence and the like.
Regarding the phrase "or without fruit" (*niṣphalaṃ vā*), the meaning is that occasional duty (*naimittika*) is performed without any longing for its result.
Knowledge pertaining to liberation is characterized by sattva; that which is characterized by rajas is dualistic;
knowledge pertaining to material nature is characterized by tamas; and that which is established in Me is remembered as being beyond the gunas.
Dwelling in the forest is said to be sattvic; dwelling in the village is rajasic;
dwelling in a gambling hall is tamasic; but my abode is beyond the gunas.
The agent who is free from attachment is considered *sāttvika*; the one blinded by passion is *rājasa*;
the one whose memory is lost is *tāmasa*; and the one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) takes refuge in me.

Faith directed toward the self is characterized by *sattva*; faith in ritual action is characterized by *rajas*; that which is in unrighteousness is characteristic of *tamas*; but faith in service to Me is beyond the *guṇas*.
Food that is wholesome, pure, unlabored, easily obtainable, and conducive to the quality of goodness (sattva) is prescribed;
that which is most dear to the senses is of the nature of passion (rajas); and that which causes pain, is impure, and is not conducive to health is of the nature of darkness (tamas).

"Sattvic happiness arises from the Self; rajasic happiness arises from sense objects; tamasic happiness arises from delusion and dejection; but that which is beyond the gunas (nirguṇa) takes refuge in Me. By this passage ending thus, the conquest of the three gunas—even for one who somehow abides within them through devotion—is also described immediately thereafter, as follows:
Indeed, substance, place, time, knowledge, action, the agent,
faith, state, effort, completion, and the three qualities— all these are indeed [the causes].
O bull among men, all entities consisting of qualities are presided over by the Puruṣa and the Unmanifest; whether seen, heard, or meditated upon, or even conceived by the intellect.
These transmigrations of the person are bound by the qualities and their activities;
O gentle one, he by whom these— born of the mind— are conquered through the life-force of the qualities,
being established in me by the yoga of devotion, attains my own state of being.
Therefore, the conquest of the three qualities occurs through devotion alone that is itself devoid of qualities, and not otherwise.
Regarding this, later on, in response to the question "How does one transcend these three qualities?", it will be said:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion..."
"Having transcended these qualities, he is fit for becoming Brahman" (Gītā 14.26).
And the commentary of Śrī Svāmī Carana is as follows: the word "ca" here has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārtha*).
This refers to one who serves Me alone, the Supreme Lord, with unswerving *bhakti-yoga*.
Be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna; be beyond the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, devoid of the concern for acquisition and preservation, and self-possessed. 45.

Baladeva: [Objection: But surely, even for those performing actions without regard for results, those actions would still join them with their own fruits due to their inherent nature; therefore, how can that understanding arise? To this, he says: "By the three qualities" (traiguṇya). Traiguṇya is the action of the three qualities (guṇas).

According to the rule *guṇa-vacana-brāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.124), the suffix *ṣyañ* signifies "the state of desiring that. The Vedas pertaining to that are the ritual sections (*karma-kāṇḍa*). You, however, being established in the Vedānta which is the head of those [Vedas], become free from the three qualities (*niṣtraiguṇya*) and desireless (*niṣkāma*).
This is the meaning: the Veda, out of affection for millions of ancestors, [speaks of] those who have been turned away from the beginningless Lord and bound by the qualities of *māyā*.

To those who are attached to the happiness created by His qualities—such as the *sāttvika* and others—and who desire them, He reveals the fruits [of their actions] and inspires confidence in them toward Himself.

Through that confidence, those who cultivate Him reach that intellect (*buddhi*) by means of the certainty regarding His true nature as it is known from the Upaniṣads, which stand at the summit of all knowledge; thus, even those fruits not desired by them do not fail to accrue.
For it is heard that only those things which are desired constitute their fruits.
Nor can it be said that all the Vedas have as their object the three *guṇas*, for that would result in the state of being free from the three *guṇas* lacking any authoritative basis.

[Objection: But is it not said, "But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, arise from cold and heat... and so on, through such reflection, that one should become a bearer of dualities?
In this context, the reason is "eternal.
The meaning is that which is eternally existent, unchanging, residing in the individual soul (jīva), and situated therein—that is what is to be contemplated.
For that very reason, one is free from acquisition and preservation (niryogakṣema).
The meaning is: yoga is the acquisition of what has not been acquired, and *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been acquired; one should be devoid of that [distraction].
If it is argued that hunger and thirst are likewise obstructive, he says "possessing the Self" (*ātmavān*).
The meaning is: one should be such a person for whom the Self—the Supreme Self, the sustainer of the universe—is the object of meditation.
The meaning is that he shall provide for the maintenance of your body. //45//
As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir when there is a flood of water everywhere,
so much purpose is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who possesses true knowledge.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that a resolute intellect whose object is the worship of the Lord for the sake of liberation—by abandoning the various fruits prescribed in the Vedas—is indeed a "bad intellect. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As much as... (yāvān). A "well" (*udapāna*) is that in which water is drunk, such as a large pond, a well, a lake, and so forth.
Since it is impossible to obtain all one's needs from a single small amount of water in such a place, one must go here and there to obtain them individually.
Just as every purpose or utility, such as bathing, drinking, and so forth, becomes available all at once in a great lake filled with water overflowing from every side;

even so, whatever purpose exists in all the Vedas in the form of the fruits of various rituals— all that is attained by the Brahmin who possesses a resolute intellect, who understands [this], and who is established in Brahman.
It is indeed so;
for all joys of hunger are included within the bliss of Brahman, according to the Vedic scripture: "Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very bliss."
Therefore, the meaning is that this alone is right understanding. //46//
Madhusūdana:

Nor should it be suspected that by performing action with the renunciation of all desires, I might be deprived of those various joys produced by such actions; for [it is said], "as much as... (yāvān).
"In a well" (*udapāne*) means in a small reservoir;
the singular number is used because it refers to the class [of such reservoirs].
Whatever purpose there may be—whatever utility consisting of bathing, drinking, and so forth—that same purpose is indeed fulfilled in a large reservoir where water overflows from all sides.

For just as mountain torrents flowing from all directions meet together in a single valley, where the purpose served by the water produced by each individually becomes even greater when combined— since all those torrents are contained within that very same pool— so it is here.

Thus, whatever benefit exists in all the Vedas and in the ritual acts for specific desires (*kāmya-karma*) taught therein— extending up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha— that same benefit accrues to the Brāhmaṇa who has realized the reality of Brahman (*brahma-tattva*), who desires to become Brahman;
for the minor pleasures are portions of the bliss of Brahman, and thus those minor pleasures are inherently included within it.
For the Śruti declares: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss.

Although bliss is one, it is designated as having parts—like a whole and its portions—by taking into account the various limitations imposed by adjuncts (*upādhi*) constructed through ignorance (*avidyā*), just as space is conceptually divided by the delimitation of jars and other objects.

Thus, when self-knowledge arises for you whose internal organ has been purified by desireless actions (*niṣkāma-karma*), there will be the attainment of the bliss of the Supreme Brahman; and when all bliss is attained in that manner, there is no room for the distraction caused by the pursuit of petty pleasures.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "Perform actions free from desire for the sake of attaining knowledge of reality, which brings about supreme bliss.

In this regard, one should observe that in the case of the illustrative application (dārṣṭāntika), the three words "yathā," "tathā," and "bhavati" are to be supplied, and the two words "yāvān" and "tāvān" are to be connected. //46//
Viśvanātha:

Ah! What more need be said regarding the majesty of the yoga of devotion, which is free from desire and devoid of qualities, wherein neither destruction nor transgression exist even at its mere commencement?
That one achieves the goal of life by even a very small amount will also be declared to Uddhava in the Eleventh Canto:
O Uddhava, not even an atom of my dharma shall perish at the commencement of its constituent parts;
this has been firmly resolved by me with perfect correctness.
"Because it is devoid of qualities, it is free from desire.

However, even *bhakti-yoga* performed with desire is expressed by the term "resolute intellect" (*vyavasāyātmikā buddhi*). He establishes this through the analogy beginning with the words "as much as" (*yāvān*).

"Udapāna" is a singular term used for the class [of water sources]; it refers to wells (*kūpa*). "As much purpose as there may be" means that one well serves the purpose of purification rites, while another serves the purpose of cleaning the teeth.
One is for the purpose of washing clothes and so forth; another is for the purpose of cleansing the hair and so forth; and another is for the purpose of bathing.

The meaning is that for someone whose sole purpose is drinking, whatever the need or whatever the requirements may be in all those various wells and water sources, since the performance of tasks such as purification can be accomplished in just one of them;
furthermore, while there is the fatigue of wandering from one well to another individually, in the lake this is done without such exertion.
Likewise, a distinction should be observed: that while wells contain water of a foul taste, a lake contains only very pleasant water.

Similarly, whatever purposes are served by the propitiation of various respective deities across all the Vedas, those same purposes are achieved for a learned Brāhmaṇa who understands through the propitiation of the Lord alone—specifically for one who knows the *brahman*, meaning the Veda, and who, despite being a knower of the Veda, understands the purport of the Veda and possesses especially profound devotion (*bhakti*).
As it is stated in the Second Canto:
"One who desires spiritual luster should worship Brahmā;
one who desires sensory power should worship Indra; and one who desires progeny should worship Prajāpati. [BhP 2.3.2]
According to the statement beginning with "But one desiring prosperity [should worship] divine illusion," [it is said]:
"Whether free from desire, possessing all desires, or desiring liberation, one of noble intellect should worship the Supreme Person through intense yoga of devotion" (BhP 2.3.10).

Thus, just as the rays of the sun are intense when unmixed with clouds and the like, so too the intensity of the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) should be understood as its being unmixed with knowledge, ritual action, and so forth.
In this regard, "the accomplishment of many desires from many [sources]" refers entirely to the state of having a manifold intellect (bahu-buddhitva).

"The accomplishment of all desires from the Blessed Lord alone" should be understood as the state of having a single-pointed intellect (eka-buddhitva), due to the singleness of focus on that one part, arising from the excellence of the object. //46//

Baladeva: To the question, "How can there be the arising of that [supreme] knowledge for me, who am studying all the Vedas, given the great expenditure of time and the resulting manifold distractions? he says: "Yāvān" (as much as), etc., and "sarvataḥ samplutodake" (in a pool overflowing with water from all sides).

In a vast reservoir of water, whatever purpose—such as bathing, drinking, and so forth—is sought by those desiring such things, just that much is obtained from it. Thus, the purpose is fulfilled by that [reservoir].

Thus, in all the Vedas along with their Upaniṣads, whatever purpose there may be— characterized by the attainment of that knowledge— for a Brāhmaṇa who studies the Veda and desires to obtain the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, that very purpose is accomplished by him through them; such is the meaning.
And thus, since that [knowledge] would be established without delay by one's own Vedic branch together with its Upaniṣads, the cognition of it would surely arise;
here, in the case of the illustrandum as well, the two words "as much as" (yāvān tāvān) are to be supplied. //46//
Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits;
let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. 47.

Śrīdhara: In that case, one might act with the intention that all fruits of action will arise solely from the propitiation of the Supreme Lord; anticipating the objection, "What is the use of ritual action?", he says "In action alone" (karmaṇy eva) to prevent that. For you, who seek the knowledge of reality, your authority lies in action alone.
"Let there be no desire for authority over its fruits.
Anticipating the objection— "But surely, when an action is performed, its fruit must necessarily follow, just as satiety follows from eating"— he says "no."
"Do not be one for whom the fruit of action is the motive.
This means: do not be such a person for whom the fruit of action is the cause of engagement.

The sense is that since only that which is desired, such as heaven and the like, constitutes a "fruit" by virtue of being a qualification of the person enjoined (*niyojya*), there would be no fruit that is undesired.
Therefore, out of fear that the fruit will become a cause of bondage, let there be no attachment—that is, no persistence—in *akarma*, which is the non-performance of action. //47//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might object: "If the attainment of supreme bliss is achieved by acquiring self-knowledge through desireless actions, then self-knowledge alone should be acquired; what is the use of these laborious actions which serve as only external means? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In action alone... (karmaṇy eva).

Since your internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is impure and thus unfit for the arising of true knowledge (*tāttvika-jñāna*), let there be for you an inclination toward action alone— which purifies the internal organ— in the form of the realization, "This must be done by me," but not toward steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*),

such as the investigation of Vedānta texts and the like. Furthermore, while you are performing action, let there never be at any stage— whether before, after, or during the performance— an inclination toward its fruits, such as heaven and so forth, in the form of the thought, "This must be enjoyed by me."
Let there be no such thought.

[Objection: Even in the absence of the cognition "this must be enjoyed by me," the action will produce its fruit through its own inherent power. [Reply: No; he says, "Do not become the cause of the fruit of action.
For one who performs an action out of a desire for its fruit becomes the cause—the producer—of that fruit.
But you, being free from desire, let not karma be the cause for the fruit [of action].
For it has been stated that action performed by one free from desire, with the intention of offering it to the Blessed One, does not lead to a result.
To the question, "If there is no fruit, what is the purpose of action? he says: "Let there be no attachment of yours to inaction."
If you do not desire a result, what is the use of action which is of the nature of suffering? Therefore, let there be no pleasure in your non-performance [of action]. //47//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, having taken as His object Arjuna alone—His own dear friend—the Blessed Lord, desiring to explain the paths of knowledge, devotion, and action, spoke of the yoga of knowledge and devotion; then, considering Arjuna’s lack of qualification for those two, He taught the yoga of selfless action with the words, "In action... (2.47).
"Regarding the words *mā phaleṣu* (do not [be attached] to fruits): even those who desire fruits can possess extremely pure minds;
however, the sense is that I have spoken to you after knowing that you are, for the most part, one of pure mind.
[Objection: But surely, once an action is performed, its fruit will necessarily come to pass."

Regarding this, he says: "Do not become the cause of the fruit of action. For one who performs action out of a desire for its fruit becomes the cause—that is, the producer—of that fruit. The meaning is that I offer this blessing: "May you not be such a person. Let there be no attachment of yours to *akarma* (inaction), which is the non-performance of one's own duty (*svadharma*), nor to *vikarma* (mis-action), which is sin.

However, it should be understood that by granting the blessing once more, "But let there be hatred alone," [the Lord] intends that no great consistency is desired between the preceding and following statements in this chapter, as evidenced by Arjuna’s remark in the subsequent chapter, "You are, as it were, confusing my mind with these mixed words."

However, this should be understood here as the internal dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna: "Just as I abide by your command in the role of charioteer and so forth, so you too should abide by my command. //47//

Baladeva: Now, if it is held that the perfection of knowledge is achieved through ritual actions (*karma*), then since tranquility (*śama*) and the like are its internal means, they alone should be practiced; what is the use of those [actions] involving such great effort?
To this, he says: "In action alone" (*karmaṇy eva*). The singular number is used for the genus.
Even though fighting is your own duty (*svadharma*), since you possess an unrighteous mindset and an impure heart,

let there be for you only the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the actions themselves, such as battle— thinking, "I must experience these"— but let there be no entitlement for you to their binding fruits, thinking, "I must experience these."

If it is argued that even in the absence of a desire for results, those actions might still connect one with their own fruits, he says in response: "Do not let [action] be the cause. You must not be the cause—the producer—of the fruits of action. Actions performed with desire connect one with their own fruits, because it is taught that only those fruits which were desired serve as the "fruit" by way of being a qualification of the person to whom the result is assigned (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*).

Therefore, out of fear that binding fruits will accrue, let there be no attachment—that is, no pleasure—in *akarma*, the non-performance of action; rather, let there be only aversion toward it. This is the meaning.

Actions performed without desire will, like grains of grain on a staff, bring about the culmination of steadfastness in knowledge within oneself; the meaning is that tranquility and the other virtues must simply follow upon that. //47//
Established in yoga, perform actions while abandoning attachment, O Dhanañjaya;
becoming the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga. 2.48
Śrīdhara: What then?
"Established in yoga. Yoga is the state of being solely intent upon the Supreme Lord.
Remaining therein, perform actions;
likewise, having abandoned attachment and the insistence on being the agent, perform them solely by taking refuge in the Lord.
Becoming equanimous toward the success or failure of even the fruit of that knowledge, perform them solely by taking refuge in the Lord.
Since such equanimity itself is called "yoga" by the wise, because its nature consists in the concentration of the mind. //48//
Madhusūdana explains what was previously stated in the words "established in yoga" (yoga-stha):
O Dhanañjaya, being established in yoga, perform actions while abandoning attachment— that is, the desire for results— and the insistence on agency.

Here, because of the plural number, the word *te* (they) refers specifically to those who possess the qualification for action; whereas in the phrase "in the genus" (*jātau*), the singular number is used.

He states the means for abandoning attachment: "Having become the same in success and failure, having abandoned joy at the attainment of a result and dejection at its non-attainment, perform actions solely with the intention of worshipping the Lord."
[Objection: But was it not previously stated that "yoga" refers to action?
Yet here it is said, "established in yoga, perform actions. How, then, can this be understood? To this he says: "Equanimity is called yoga."

The meaning is that this very equanimity toward success and failure is what is expressed by the word "yoga" in the phrase "one who is established in yoga," and not "action"; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Here, the commentary follows the path of the Bhāṣyakāra (Śaṅkara), according to which the latter half of the verse provides an explanation of the former half, thereby avoiding tautology.
In the phrase "having made pleasure and pain equal," the necessity of performing battle alone was stated because of the context of equanimity regarding victory and defeat.
In this case, however, the distinction is that all actions are to be performed by renouncing all fruits, whether seen or unseen. //48//
Viśvanātha:
[The Lord] teaches the manner of desireless action in the verse beginning with "yoga-sthaḥ.
The sense is that, maintaining an equanimous mind toward victory and defeat, one should perform battle itself as one's own duty (svadharma).
This very yoga of action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma-yoga) transforms into the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga);
thus, the yoga of knowledge should also be understood according to the intended meaning of the preceding and following passages. //48//
Baladeva: He clarifies what was stated previously with the words "established in yoga" (*yoga-stha*).
Having abandoned attachment—that is, the desire for results and the insistence on agency—you, being established in yoga, perform actions such as battle;
by the first [verse], there is indeed an immersion into *māyā*.
By the second [verse], however, there is the theft of the attributes of the Supreme Lord, whose characteristic is sovereignty;
by that, there is the subversion of His māyā.
Therefore, the sense is that both of these must be abandoned.
He explains the term "established in yoga" with the words "in success and failure.

Having become equanimous toward the attainment or non-attainment of the results associated with those [practices], such as victory and so forth, perform your duty while free from attachment and aversion.
This very equanimity is what was designated by the word "yoga" in the verse beginning with "established in yoga," because its nature is the concentration of the mind (citta-samādhi). //48//
For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya. Seek refuge in wisdom; those motivated by fruits are pitiable. (2.49)

Śrīdhara: But optional (kāmya) action is extremely inferior; thus he says, "by far. Karma-yoga performed with a resolute intellect—being either the yoga of wisdom or having wisdom as its means—is superior. Compared to that, other optional action which serves as a means is "far inferior," meaning it is exceedingly base.
Since this is so, therefore seek—meaning practice—the yoga of action as a refuge or support for the intellect, that is, for knowledge;
or rather, take refuge in the Lord as the protector within the intellect.

Let the wretched and miserable men who possess desires be the cause for the fruits of action, for the Śruti says: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is wretched" (BAU 3.8.10). //49//
Madhusūdana:

Now, is the performance of ritual action itself the human goal (puruṣārtha), such that it must always be performed even if it is fruitless, according to the maxim that "even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose"? If you argue that it is better to perform ritual action precisely out of a desire for its fruit, [the Lord] says "no," with the words beginning with "dūreṇa" (from afar).

O Dhanañjaya, since action performed with a desire for results— which is the cause of birth and death— is far inferior by a great distance to the yoga of self-knowledge, which consists of the yoga of action performed without desire as a means to attaining self-realization; or rather, since all action whatsoever is far inferior to the yoga of the intellect directed toward the Supreme Self.

Therefore, seek refuge—that is, desire to perform—the yoga of action free from desire (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*), which is the protector that removes all misfortunes by destroying the sins that act as obstacles to the realization of the Supreme Self.

But those who have results as their motive—those who desire fruits and perform inferior action—are miserable; the meaning is that they are always dependent on others and extremely wretched due to the rotation of the water-wheel of birth, death, and so forth. As the Śruti says: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10).

Likewise, you too should not be a miser; rather, the intention is that you should practice the yoga of action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma-yoga), which generates self-knowledge that turns back all misfortunes.

For just as miserly people, acquiring wealth with extreme pain, are unable to experience the great happiness born of giving and other virtues due to their greed for mere visible pleasure, and thus deceive themselves—so it is here.

Performing actions with great suffering, yet cheated of the experience of supreme bliss by greed for mere trifling fruits—oh, what misfortune and delusion they possess! This is what is implied by the word "miserable" (kṛpaṇa). //49//
Viśvanātha:
He censures action performed with desire with the words "far indeed.
"Inferior" means extremely base; it refers to action motivated by desire.
Through the yoga of the intellect—that is, through the yoga of action performed as a dedication to the Supreme Lord consisting of desireless action—[one attains the goal].
"The yoga of the intellect" refers precisely to the yoga of desireless action within the intellect. //49//
Baladeva: Now, with the words "far indeed," He declares the inferiority of action performed for the sake of desire;
O Dhanañjaya, action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom.

The meaning is that *kāmya* (desire-driven) action— which is the cause of the evils of birth, death, and so forth— is far inferior, by way of being extremely remote, to *niṣkāma-karma-yoga* (the yoga of desireless action), which serves as the means for attaining the realization of the true nature of the Self.
Since this is so, therefore you should seek refuge— that is, take recourse— in *buddhi*, the knowledge of the true nature of that [Self], and practice *niṣkāma-karma-yoga*.

But those who regard cause and effect, who desire fruits, and who perform inferior actions—they are miserable; the meaning is that they are wretched, being subject to the continuous flow of karma and its resulting births. Thus, you should not be miserable. For in this world, the miserable are indeed those who, greedy for mere fragments of unseen happiness gained through wealth acquired with great hardship, are unable to give away their riches and are thus deprived of the great bliss of giving; likewise, they are those whose actions are performed with great toil.
It is implied that those who are greedy for such trivial fruits become deceived by their own great happiness. //49//
One endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds here in this world;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in actions. (2.50)
Śrīdhara: He says "one endowed with wisdom" (buddhi-yukta) because such a person is superior due to being joined with the yoga of wisdom.
Good deeds lead to the attainment of heaven and the like, while evil deeds lead to the attainment of hell and the like;
both of these he abandons right here in this very birth through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, apply yourself—that is, exert yourself—to yoga for that purpose, namely to the yoga of action;
for yoga is indeed skill in actions.

That skill, or state of proficiency, belongs to one who abides in actions known as their own duty (svadharma) and possesses an even-mindedness toward success and failure through a mind surrendered to the Lord.
For that indeed is skillfulness: that even those actions which have the nature of bondage cease their inherent nature through the intellect of equanimity.
Therefore, become one who is endowed with the intellect of equanimity. 50.
Madhusūdana:
Having thus stated the defect in the absence of the yoga of intellect (*buddhi-yoga*), he speaks of its merit in its presence with the words "intellect" (*buddhi*).

Here, one who is joined with intellect—meaning joined with the intellect of equanimity (*samatva-buddhi*)—in these actions abandons and relinquishes both good and evil deeds, that is, merit and sin, by means of the attainment of knowledge through the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*).
Since this is so, therefore you should apply yourself— that is, strive and exert yourself— to the yoga of the intellect of equanimity;

for such a yoga of the intellect of equanimity is the skill (kauśalam), the state of being fit (kuśala-bhāva), of one whose mind is offered to the Lord as he engages in actions— namely, that even those actions which are causes of bondage become non-existent and result in liberation.
That is great skill:
the yoga of action, when joined with the intellect of equanimity, effects the destruction of even wicked actions despite being of the nature of action; thus it is highly skillful.
But you are not skillful, since, although you possess consciousness, you do not effect the destruction of the wicked that is of your own kind; this contrast (vyatireka) is implied here.

Alternatively, when action is performed here with a mind endowed with equanimity, one who is "endowed with wisdom"—meaning one who has attained direct realization of the Supreme Self—through the gateway of the purification of the *sattva* quality, abandons both good and evil deeds.
Therefore, apply yourself to the yoga of action characterized by the intellect of equanimity;
for among all actions, the yoga of action characterized by the intellect of equanimity is "skill," meaning it is clever (*kuśala*) and adept at warding off wicked deeds. //50//
Viśvanātha: Apply yourself—that is, strive—for Yoga, which has the characteristics already described;
for among actions, whether with desire or free from desire, Yoga itself consists precisely in performing action with equanimity.
Skillfulness means proficiency. //50//
Baladeva: He states the power of the aforementioned yoga of wisdom with the words "buddhi... etc.

Here, he who performs actions joined with wisdom—meaning joined with that wisdom which consists in the renunciation of primary fruits and equanimity toward the attainment or non-attainment of secondary results—he abandons, that is, destroys, both merit and demerit accumulated since beginningless time, which are obstacles to knowledge; this is the meaning.

Therefore, apply yourself—that is, strive—for the aforementioned yoga of the intellect (buddhi-yoga), because the yoga of action (karma-yoga) is connected with such an intellect. And there is skill—cleverness—in that very which binds, for through contact with the intellect, it is transformed into a liberator by the analogy of mercury whose poison has been purified. //50//
For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action,
are liberated from the bondage of birth and go to the state that is free from all suffering. (2.51)
Śrīdhara: He explains the manner in which actions serve as a means to liberation with the words "born of action" (*karmajam*).

Having abandoned the fruit born of action and performing action solely for the sake of worshipping the Lord, the wise—having become knowers—being liberated from the bondage consisting of birth, attain the state of Viṣṇu, which is free from ailment and devoid of all calamities.
They go to the state known as liberation. //51//
Madhusūdana:

Anticipating the objection that "the destruction of evil deeds is required, but not the destruction of good deeds, because that would result in the loss of human purpose," he states the word "born of action" (*karma-ja*) to show that the fruit [of renunciation] is the attainment of the supreme human purpose through the abandonment of insignificant results.

For, being endowed with the intellect of equanimity (*samatva-buddhi*), and having abandoned the fruit born of action, those wise ones perform actions solely for the sake of propitiating the Lord; through the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*), they become possessed of the wisdom regarding the Self arising from such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
Being such, they are liberated from the bondage consisting of birth, and are completely—without remainder—released by means of that which is characterized as absolute and specific.

The meaning is that the liberated ones go to— that is, they attain non-differently— the state to be reached, which is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpa*), the stainless Brahman, free from the disease consisting of ignorance and its effects, and the fearless goal of human endeavor known as liberation (*mokṣa*).
For this reason, those who perform actions with an attitude of equanimity, having abandoned the desire for fruits, achieve purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) through them.

Having attained the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva*) produced by such authoritative means as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), and having realized its effects, they proceed to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu— known as liberation (*mokṣa*)— which consists in the cessation of all misfortunes and the attainment of supreme bliss. Therefore, in response to the statement, "Tell me decisively what would be for my welfare" (*Gītā* 2.7), it is said that one who desires the highest good (*śreyas*) should practice this kind of *karma-yoga*.
This is the intention of the Blessed One. //51//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Regarding the phrase "born of action":
those who are possessed of such intelligence—wise men endowed with that kind of understanding—perform actions having abandoned the fruit born of action.

Having attained wisdom regarding the true nature of the Self as it exists within action, and being thus liberated from the bondage of birth, they go to the stainless, affliction-free state of Vaikuṇṭha.
Therefore, the intention is that you too, desiring the highest good, should perform such actions.
Since knowledge of one's own self is the cause of knowledge of the supreme self, it is logical that the former is also the cause for attaining that state. //51//
When your intellect has crossed beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard. (2.52)
Śrīdhara: In response to the expectation, "When shall I attain that state?", he says in two verses beginning with "yadā" (when).
Delusion (*moha*) is the notion of self (*ātma-buddhi*) regarding the body and so forth;
that itself is the thicket (*kalila*), the dense forest.
According to the traditional lexicographical authority (abhidhāna-koṣa) which states that "kalila" means "gahana" (thicket or dense forest),
the meaning is as follows:
when you are thus engaged in the worship of the Supreme Lord, by His grace, your intellect [will abandon] that which is characterized by the identification with the body.

Then you will cross over with particular ease the dense and difficult forest consisting of delusion; you will reach, that is, attain, detachment (*nirveda*)—meaning dispassion (*vairāgya*)—regarding both what is to be heard and the meaning of what has been heard.
The sense is that, because those two are not to be grasped, you will no longer engage in the desire to know them. //52//
Madhusūdana:
To the question, "When will the purification of my being (*sattva-śuddhi*) occur for one who performs actions in this manner?", he says: "When...
For there is no fixed rule regarding time, such that the purification of the being occurs after only this much time.

But when— at which time— your intellect, your inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), shall transcend the thicket of delusion— that is to say, it shall pass beyond the profound turbidity consisting of non-discrimination, such as the play of ignorance in the form of "I am this" and "this is mine," and having cast off the impurity of *rajas* and *tamas*, shall attain a state of purity.
Then, at that time, you will attain—that is, reach—dispassion (*nirveda*), which is freedom from craving, regarding both what is to be heard and the fruits of what has been heard.
This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Having examined the worlds built by karma, a Brahmin attains dispassion" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
The intention is that through the fruit of dispassion, you will know the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). //52//
Viśvanātha:
He says "When" (yadā) to indicate that through the practice of desireless action dedicated to the Supreme Lord, your yoga will come to pass.
Your intellect—meaning your internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—will cross over the dense thicket of delusion, which is a profound abyss consisting of ignorance, specifically and with great intensity.

Then, regarding things that ought to be heard among those things to be heard, and even regarding what has already been heard among those things heard, you will attain detachment (*nirveda*). This is because both non-conviction (*asambhāvanā*) and contrary conviction (*viparīta-bhāvanā*) have been destroyed. The sense is that you will think: "What is the use now of hearing the words of scriptural instruction?
For me at this time, it is entirely appropriate to practice only in the means of realization (*sādhana*) at every moment. //52//
Baladeva: If it be asked, "When will the wisdom directed toward the Self arise in me who am performing actions free from desire? he says "When" (yadā) in response.

When your intellect—the internal organ—will cross beyond the thicket of delusion, which is a dense forest of ignorance caused by the longing for trifling fruits; that is to say, when it will abandon it, then you will attain—that is, you will reach—dispassion (*nirveda*) regarding those trifling fruits, both those previously heard and those yet to be heard.

Because of the scriptural statement, "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brahmin should attain detachment," the meaning is that since one will examine those [worlds] as the object of that [detachment] by means of detachment as the result, there is no fixed rule regarding the time for this. //52//
When your intellect, which has been perplexed by the various Vedic injunctions, shall stand unshakable and immovable in meditative concentration, then you will attain Yoga. 53.

Śrīdhara: And then, "by the scriptures" (śrutibhiḥ) means by the hearing of various worldly and Vedic matters; when your intellect, which was previously distracted and thus conflicted, shall become established in meditative absorption (samādhi).
Samādhi is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), in whom the mind is concentrated (*samādhīyate*).
In Him [the mind] is motionless, not drawn away by internal objects;
for this very reason, it is immovable (*acalā*).
Through proficiency in practice, once it has become firmly established in that very state, you shall attain yoga—the fruit of yoga, which is the knowledge of reality. //53//
Madhusūdana:

In response to the inquiry as to when the attainment of knowledge occurs for one who has thus developed detachment (*nirveda*) through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he says "śruti" and so forth.

Previously, your intellect was distracted—being possessed of various doubts and misconceptions—having been led astray by the various scriptural statements (*śruti*) concerning diverse fruits, whose true purport had not been investigated.

When—at which time—having abandoned that distraction through the perception of defects born from purity and discernment, she shall remain motionless in the Supreme Self within samādhi; being free from the distractions characterized by waking and dreaming, she shall be immovable and devoid of the fluctuations characterized by dissolution (laya) such as deep sleep, fainting, and stupor;
that is to say, having abandoned the two defects characterized by dissolution and distraction, she will become fully composed (samāhitā).

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: being "unwavering"—meaning free from the doubts of impossibility and the contrary notions [of doubt]—and "steady" through service characterized by long duration, uninterruptedness, and reverence, and being untainted by heterogeneous cognitions, it will remain established in the Self like a lamp in a windless place.
At that time, one attains *yoga*, which is characterized by the unity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

You shall attain the fruit of all yoga—the indivisible direct realization (*akhaṇḍa-sākṣātkāra*) produced by such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Then, because there will be no further goal to be accomplished, you will have fulfilled your duty and become one whose wisdom is established; this is the intended meaning. //53//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, "contradicted" (*vipratipannā*) means being in disagreement or not in accord with the various worldly and Vedic meanings heard in the scriptures—that is to say, being opposed to them. The reason for this is that she is "unwavering" (*niścalā*), meaning she has turned away from moving toward those various [contradictory] meanings.

However, when [the mind] is steady—that is, stable—in the concentration whose characteristics will be described in the sixth chapter, then through the attainment of direct experience (aparokṣānubhava), one is "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta); this is the meaning. //53//

Baladeva: If you should object, "Since I have attained purity of heart through the performance of ritual action out of detachment from the fruits of action, and since self-knowledge has arisen within me, when will there be the direct realization of the Self?"—to that he says:
"By the Śruti," etc.
By the Śruti, such as the passage beginning with "That very one" (*tam etam*), which awakens one to the fact that rituals are pregnant with knowledge, [the notion of] contradiction is removed.

In particular, when your intellect has become fully perfected—immovable and free from both the notions of impossibility and erroneous conceptions—it will remain as steady in the mind during meditative absorption (samādhi) as the flame of a lamp in a windless place; at that time, you shall attain Yoga, which is characterized by self-realization.
This is the meaning: actions performed without desire for fruits lead to the culmination of knowledge in the form of the state of one whose wisdom is established (sthita-prajña).
But the state of one whose wisdom is steady, which consists in the culmination of knowledge, is the experience of the Self. //53//
Arjuna said:
O Keśava, what is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi?
What would one of steady wisdom speak? How would he sit? How would he move? 54.
Śrīdhara: Desiring to know the characteristics of one who knows the reality of the Self as described in the preceding verse, Arjuna said: "Of one whose wisdom is steady" (*sthita-prajñasya*).
What is the description of one who is established in natural *samādhi*, and for whom, therefore, wisdom—the intellect—is steady and unwavering?
"Speech" (*bhāṣā*) means that by which one speaks; that is to say, it refers to the characteristic.
The meaning is: by what characteristic is one said to be "steadfast in wisdom"? Likewise, the meaning is: how should one who is steadfast in intellect speak, sit, and walk? //54//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus obtained the opportunity, Arjuna spoke in order to understand the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established (sthita-prajña),
thinking that the very characteristics of those liberated while living (jīvan-mukta) are themselves the means to liberation for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu).
He whose wisdom is established as "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi) is one of steady wisdom; such a person possesses two states: being established in samādhi and having an emergent mind.
Therefore, he specifies: "What is the description of the one of steady wisdom who is established in samādhi?
Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*).
"Bhāṣā" (speech) is that by which one speaks; it is the characteristic.
The meaning is: by what characteristic is one established in samādhi and possessed of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña) designated by others?
And what would that person of steady intellect—the one whose mind has emerged from [meditation]—himself say?
Regarding praise, blame, and the like, what [expression] characterized by rejoicing, aversion, and so forth would he utter, and how?

In all these cases, the potential suffix (*liṅ*) denotes possibility. Likewise, thinking "What was it?"—in order to restrain the mind that has strayed outward—how does he exercise restraint over the external sense organs?
At the time when there is an absence of such suppression, what would he go toward, and how would he encounter sense objects?
The meaning is: what are his acts of speaking, sitting, and walking like—being distinct from those of foolish people?
Thus, there are four questions; the one who stands firm in the state of meditative absorption (samādhi) is the one of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña).
Regarding the three [qualities] in one who has risen [from meditation] and whose wisdom is established:
by addressing him as "O Keśava," he indicates that because You are the inner controller of all, You alone are capable of speaking such a secret. //54//
Viśvanātha:
Having heard that "the intellect of one in samādhi is immovable," he asks for the true characteristic of the yogin by means of the words "of the one whose wisdom is established" (sthita-prajñasya).
This refers to one whose *prajñā*—that is, the intellect (*buddhi*)—is established, meaning steady and immovable.
What is "speech" (bhāṣā)? It is called speech because one speaks by means of it; what is its definition? This is the meaning.
Of what kind of person who is established in concentration? That is, one who will remain in concentration. Its meaning is: "and thus is the one whose wisdom is steady."
"Established in samādhi" refers to the two designations for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
"What would he say? means: when pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor, praise and blame, or affection and aversion arise, what would he say?
The meaning is: what would he speak, whether clearly or to himself?
What is meant by "should remain"? What kind of absence of movement of the senses toward external objects is that?
And what is meant by "should go"?
Or what kind of movement toward those [objects] is it? //54//

Baladeva: Having been addressed thus, Arjuna asks with the verse beginning "sthitaprajña" (the one of steady wisdom) in order to understand the characteristics of the one of steady wisdom mentioned in the preceding verse.
Regarding the one of steady wisdom here, there are four questions: one concerns the one established in samādhi, while three concern the one who has emerged from it.

For instance: what is the speech, what is the characteristic, of one who stands firm, whose wisdom and intellect are steady, and who is established in samādhi? Based on the etymology "that by which one speaks," the meaning is: by what characteristic is one called "steadfast in wisdom" (sthita-prajña)?
Likewise, how should one whose wisdom is established (sthita-prajña), having emerged from meditation, engage in speaking and other such activities?
The meaning is: what are those activities of his like, which are distinct from those of ordinary people?
In that regard, what should he speak?
When praise or blame, or affection or aversion toward himself or others, arise— whether expressed aloud or occurring within his own mind— what should he say?
How should he sit amidst external objects, how should he restrain his senses,
and what path should he follow?
What is that? And in the absence of restraint, how could one attain the objects? This is the meaning. The word "triṣu" (in three) expresses possibility. //54//
The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, when one abandons all desires that have entered the mind,
But when one is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be established in wisdom. //55//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, those very means of knowledge belonging to the seeker (*sādhaka*) are themselves the natural characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the perfected one (*siddha*).
Therefore, while describing the characteristics of the perfected one, [the Lord] states the internal means of knowledge until the end of the chapter.
In that regard, He provides the answer to the first question with two verses beginning with "He abandons" (*prajahāti*).
When one completely abandons the desires residing in the mind, he states the cause for such renunciation with the word "ātmani.

Being "ātmarāmaḥ"—delighting in the Self alone, in his own very self which is of the nature of supreme bliss, and being satisfied by himself—he abandons the cravings for trivial objects; at that time, by that characteristic—
The sage is said to be one whose wisdom is firmly established. //55//
Madhusūdana:
To these four questions, the Blessed One gave the answer in sequence, beginning with "He abandons" and continuing until the end of the chapter.

He [abandons] desires—specific modifications of the mind such as desire, volition, and so forth—which are divided into the categories of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), misconception (*viparyaya*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), sleep (*nidrā*), and memory (*smṛti*).
