When one thoroughly abandons—that is, completely relinquishes by means of subverting the cause—all those [objects] that have been elaborated in five ways in other tantras without exception, and when one becomes entirely devoid of all mental fluctuations (*sarva-vṛtti-śūnya*), then one is called "established in wisdom" (*sthita-prajña*); the remainder of the sentence is that such a person is said to be "established in samādhi.
He states that desires are fit for abandonment because they are of the nature of non-self (*anātma-dharmatva*) by saying "situated in the mind" (*manogatān*).
For if these were the attributes of the self (*ātman*), they could not be abandoned, because—like the heat of fire—they would be inherent by nature.
However, these are the attributes of the mind (*manas*);
therefore, the meaning is that they can indeed be abandoned through the abandonment of that [mind].

One might object: "How can there be that particular state of contentment, which is perceived through signs such as a serene countenance, for one whose wisdom is established, if all desires have been renounced? To this he says: [The wise man] is satisfied—that is, fully satiated—by the Self alone, which is of the nature of supreme bliss, and not by the non-Self, which is insubstantial; he is satisfied by the Self manifesting in its own form as self-luminous consciousness, and not by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), because of the attainment of the supreme human goal.
And so says the Śruti:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman" (KaṭhU 2.3.14).

And thus, one who is established in samādhi is indeed the one of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña) who is described by such words expressing these characteristics; this is the answer to the first question. //55//
Viśvanātha:
He provides the answer to the four questions in sequence, beginning with "he abandons" and continuing until the end of the chapter.
"All" means that in respect to any object whatsoever, he has not even the slightest desire.
The phrase "those gone to the mind" indicates the fitness for renunciation regarding desires as being of the nature of the self (*ātma-dharmatva*).

The underlying sense is that if they were indeed properties of the self, then they could not be abandoned, just as heat cannot be abandoned from fire. The reason for this is: "satisfied by that which is the bliss of the Self attained when the mind has been withdrawn into the Self."
And thus says the Śruti:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman" (KaṭhU 2.3.14). //55//

Baladeva: Thus questioned, the Blessed One gave the answer to the four questions in sequence until the completion of the chapter. Therein, he spoke the answer to the first question with the single verse beginning "He abandons" (prajahāti), O Pārtha.
When one completely abandons and renounces all desires that have entered the mind and reside within it, then one is said to be "steadfast in wisdom.
Since desires are of the nature of the mind, their abandonment is logical;
the sense is that if they were of the nature of the Self, they would be as difficult to relinquish as heat is to fire.
If it is asked, "How can he remain like dry wood? the text replies: "In the Self alone.

This means that when the mind has been withdrawn into the Self, he is satisfied and fully contented by the Self—which manifests as his own nature in the form of self-luminous bliss—and having abandoned all desire for trivial objects, he dwells in the garden of the bliss of the Self;
this is the meaning of being established in samādhi and possessing steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*).

The word *ātman* is used for the person (*pums*), for essential nature (*svabhāva*), for the mind at the point of death (*prayantamanas*), for fortitude (*dhṛti*), for wisdom (*manīṣā*), and also for the body (*śarīra*) and Brahman.
Thus says the author of the Medinīkośa;
and here, "Brahman" should be understood as either the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśvara). //55//
One whose mind is unperturbed in sorrows, who is free from longing for pleasures, and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed— he is called a sage of steady wisdom. (2.56)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even amidst sorrows" (*duḥkheṣv api*):
he is one whose mind is undisturbed (*anudvigna*) and unagitated even when sorrows have arrived;
he is one from whom longing (*spṛhā*) has departed even amidst pleasures (*sukheṣu*).
The reason for this is as follows: it is because [the mind] is *vīta*—that is, free from (*apagata*) passion (*rāga*), fear (*bhaya*), and anger (*krodha*).
In this context, *rāga* means attachment (*prīti*).
That sage is said to be one whose intellect is firmly established (*sthita-dhī*). //56//
Madhusūdana:
Now, the speech, sitting, and walking of one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajña*) when emerged from meditation must be explained as distinct from those of foolish people.
Regarding that, he provides the answer to the question "What would he speak? with the two verses beginning with "In sorrows" (*duḥkheṣu*).

Sufferings are of three kinds: those caused by grief, delusion, fever, headache, and so forth, which are internal (*ādhyātmika*); those inflicted by tigers, snakes, and the like, which are external (*ādhibhautika*);

and those caused by excessive wind, excessive rain, and so forth, which are celestial (*ādhidaivika*). Regarding these sufferings—specific modifications of the mental faculty consisting of the torment resulting from the transformation of *rajas*, brought about by the fruition of previously commenced sinful karma—one does not become agitated, meaning one does not become distressed due to an inability to avoid suffering.
One whose mind is such is "one of undisturbed mind.

For when suffering befalls one who lacks discernment, there arises a specific modification of the mind—characterized by darkness (tāmasa), consisting of delusion, and known as "distress" (udvega)—which takes the form of remorse, such as: "Alas, I am a sinner! Shame on me, a wicked soul, who shares in such suffering! Who could dispel such misery for me?"
If this [ignorance] were present at the time of committing a sinful act, it would be effective as an obstacle to its engagement.

However, occurring at the time of experiencing the result, it is useless because—given that the cause exists—the effect cannot be eliminated. Furthermore, since it consists of a delusion born of non-discrimination, such as thinking "why does suffering arise for me even though the cause of suffering is present," it cannot exist in one who possesses steady wisdom, the discriminating person.
For only suffering is obtained through *prārabdha* karma, but not even the delusion that follows thereafter.
If it is argued that because it is a cause for further suffering, that delusion too must be obtained through another *prārabdha* karma, we say no;

because for one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajña*), delusion is impossible due to the destruction of the ignorance that is the material cause of delusion, and thus there is an absence of *prārabdha* karma capable of bringing about the suffering produced by that delusion.

In whatever manner the mere maintenance of the body may be accomplished through the fruits of *prārabdha* karma, its occurrence—even in the absence of delusion—is possible by way of the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*); this will be explained in detail later.

Likewise, regarding the three kinds of pleasures—specific mental modifications (*citta-vṛtti*) consisting of joy that are transformations of *sattva* brought about by the *prārabdha* merit of past actions—one is "free from longing," meaning devoid of desire for future pleasures of that same nature.

For that which is called "longing" (spṛhā) is indeed a delusion— a tamasic mental modification consisting merely of a vain desire for a pleasure of a similar kind at the time of experiencing a pleasure—
arising only in one who lacks discrimination.
Indeed, an effect cannot come into being in the absence of its cause.

Therefore, just as anxiety in the form of a vain longing— that the effect should not arise when the cause is present— is impossible for one possessed of discernment, likewise, craving in the form of a vain longing— that the effect should arise when the cause is absent— is also untenable,
because karma that has already begun (prārabdha-karman) yields only pleasure [in this context].
Alternatively, the mental state consisting of joy is expressed by the word "longing" (*spṛhā*);
that too is indeed a delusion.

It takes the form of an exultation such as: "Oh, how fortunate I am, for such happiness has come upon me! Who in the three worlds could be my equal, or by what means might such happiness of mine not be interrupted? It is of this nature.
This is a *tāmasī* (darkness-born) mental modification.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "He who does not increase his pleasures upon obtaining fuel and the like, like a fire, is one whose craving has departed.
And the Lord will say: "One should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant" (*Gītā* 5.20).
That [ignorance] also cannot belong to one who possesses discrimination, because it is an error.
Likewise, one is free from passion, fear, and anger.
Passion (*rāga*) is a particular modification of the mind consisting of attachment toward sense objects, rooted in the superimposition of attractiveness, and taking the form of extreme clinging.

Fear (*bhaya*) is a particular modification of the mind characterized by dejection, occurring when that which destroys an object of attachment has appeared, and one perceives oneself as lacking the capacity to ward it off.

Similarly, anger (*krodha*) is a particular modification of the mind characterized by a blazing intensity, occurring when that which destroys an object of attachment has appeared, and one perceives oneself as possessing the capacity to ward it off.
Since all these have departed from him because they are of the nature of error (*viparyaya*), he is described as such.
Such a sage, whose nature is contemplation—a renunciant—is called one of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*).

A person of such characteristics, being firm-minded (*sthita-dhī*), should speak words such as those concerning freedom from agitation and desirelessness in order to manifest his own realization for the sake of instructing disciples; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) stated.
And likewise, another seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should not be agitated by suffering nor exult in pleasure.
And the intention is that he should be free from passion, fear, and anger. //56//
Viśvanātha:

To answer the question "What should he say?", he says: "With a mind undisturbed amidst sufferings—whether internal such as hunger, thirst, fever, or diseases of the head, or external arising from snakes, tigers, and so forth—he thinks, 'This suffering, which has begun, must necessarily be experienced by me.'"

The meaning is that even when questioned by someone in this way, he speaks clearly while remaining inwardly composed; thus, he does not tremble amidst sufferings. For a wise person, the very absence of such facial contortions is the discernible sign of his lack of agitation.
The meaning is that a hypocrite, who displays signs of artificial non-agitation, is recognized by the wise as one who has simply fallen from his state.

Likewise, even when pleasures are present, for one who says to himself and clearly to others, "I am free from longing" and "this [karmic] momentum (prārabdha) must necessarily be experienced," the sign of his lack of desire for pleasure is evident.
The sense is that this is to be understood by the wise alone.
He clarifies and demonstrates those very marks: he is one whose passion—that is, attachment—to pleasures and to kinsmen has departed (vīta).
Just as in the case of the queen of the primordial Bharata.
When he was brought to his side and desired to cut off his own head, O base king, there was no fear in him, nor did anger arise within him. //56//
Baladeva: Now, with the two verses beginning with "In sorrows," he provides the answer to the question, "What would one whose wisdom is steady say when aroused [from samādhi]?

The meaning is that when the three kinds of sorrows—internal and so forth—have arisen, his mind is unperturbed; whether questioned by someone or speaking to himself, he says, "These are the fruits of past actions (prārabdha) that must necessarily be experienced by me," and thus he does not tremble before them.

The meaning is that even when pleasures such as excellent food and honors are presented, he is free from longing and devoid of craving; whether questioned by someone or speaking to himself, thinking "these things drawn by my past karma must necessarily be experienced," he does not have a joyful face when approached by them.
"Vīta" means: *vīta-rāgaḥ* is one who is devoid of affection for desirable things;

*vīta-bhayaḥ* is one who is devoid of dejection when those who seize his objects are encountered, thinking, "These [objects] of mine, which are difficult to obtain, are being taken away by you who are righteous"; and *vīta-krodhaḥ* is one who is devoid of anger toward those very same people, thinking, "How can these [objects] of mine, belonging to a powerful man, be seized by you wretches?"
And he is free from anger.
Such a sage, whose nature is self-contemplation, is one of steady wisdom—this is the meaning.
Thus, speaking of his own experience either to others or within himself, he does not utter words of agitation or longing; this is the reply. //56//
He who is without attachment everywhere, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various good or evil fortune— his wisdom is firmly established. (2.57)
Śrīdhara: He states the answer to the question "How should he speak? with the word *yaḥ* ("he who").

He who is everywhere devoid of attachment—even toward sons, friends, and so forth—is free from affection. Therefore, even when encountering various auspicious and favorable things through the persistence of past impressions (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), he does not rejoice; and encountering what is inauspicious and adverse, he neither hates nor censures it.
But he speaks only as one who is indifferent;
the meaning is that his wisdom is firmly established. //57//
Madhusūdana: Furthermore,

that sage who is free from attachment even toward the vital functions and so forth in all bodies— being devoid in every way of that particular state of mind called *sneha* (affection), which is synonymous with love directed toward others and by whose presence the loss or gain of another is projected upon oneself— is [the one described].

It should be understood that while there is no attachment [to anything else], one must indeed be possessed of supreme attachment toward the Blessed One, the Supreme Self; for the absence of attachment to what is not the Self has that [Supreme Self] as its purpose.
Having encountered a pleasant object that serves as a cause for happiness—brought about by various *prārabdha* karmas—he does not rejoice, meaning he does not praise it with an excess of elation.
Having encountered an unpleasant object that serves as a cause for suffering, he does not feel aversion, meaning he does not criticize it preceded by inner malice.

For an ignorant person, one's own wife and so forth, which are causes of pleasure, are "pleasant objects"; the mental modification (*dhī-vṛtti*) that proceeds toward praising their qualities is a form of delusion called "rejoicing."
And that [envy] is of the nature of *tamas*, because it is useless since the description of another's qualities and so forth lacks the purpose of inspiring interest in them.

Thus, the excellence of another's knowledge and the like—which, by generating envy, becomes a cause of suffering—is an inauspicious object for this person; it is a specific modification of the mental faculty (*dhī-vṛtti*) consisting of delusion that prompts such censure and the like.
That [state] is also characterized by *tamas*,
because it would be futile as it lacks the purpose of preventing such censure.
Since those two— delight and aversion— are forms of delusion and are *tāmasa*, how could they possibly exist in one established in wisdom, who is non-deluded and composed of pure *sattva*?

Therefore, because there is no cause for wavering, the wisdom of that sage—who is free from attachment and devoid of joy and sorrow—is established in the reality of the Supreme Self and culminates in its fruit; this is the meaning of "one whose wisdom is steady.
In this way, any other seeker of liberation should likewise be free from attachment toward everything.
The intended meaning is that one should not praise upon encountering the auspicious, nor should one revile upon encountering the inauspicious.
In this context, the statement "one should not utter speech in the form of blame, praise, and so forth" expresses the negative correlative (vyatireka). //57//
Viśvanātha:

"Free from attachment" means being devoid of attachment based on a specific motive (*sopādhi*); because of his compassionate nature, he possesses only a slight, motiveless (*nirupādhi*) degree of affection. Having received various well-known honors, food, and so forth, as well as his own service which is auspicious, or having received inauspicious treatment such as disrespect or blows with the fist, he does not rejoice in them respectively.

He does not praise you by saying, "You are righteous; serve the Paramahaṃsas and be happy," nor does he speak with hatred, cursing you, "You are a sinful soul; fall into hell. His wisdom is established and fixed in meditative concentration; this is the meaning of what is called "well-established wisdom. //57//
Baladeva: He who is "ya" (he) is one who possesses no attachment toward any living beings—that is, he is devoid of attachment based on limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

Due to his compassion, however, there is indeed a slight natural affection that is free from such conditions. Having obtained various well-known auspicious things—such as excellent food, garlands, and sandalwood paste—he does not rejoice; nor, being most virtuous, does he say to the giver, "May you live long."
Having encountered the unpleasant, such as contempt or blows from a staff, he does not feel hatred; nor does he curse, saying, "You are a wicked man, perish!
He possesses wisdom—this is the meaning of being "one whose wisdom is established."
In this context, the definition of that [speech] is established by way of contrast: it is speech that does not consist of praise or blame. //57//
And when he completely withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, his wisdom is firmly established. (2.58)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "when":

when this yogi withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth—from all sides—thus, being established in knowledge, he withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses, that is, from all sense-objects.
"His wisdom is firmly established"—this sentence has already had its meaning explained. //58//
Madhusūdana:
The Blessed One now begins to provide the answer to the question "What was [the state] then? with six verses.

Therein, he says this to show that the seated posture of one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajña*) consists in withdrawing the senses—which had become distracted through emergence due to the force of *prārabdha*-karma—and remaining solely for the sake of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Regarding the word *yadā*: this one who has emerged (*vyutthita*) is [emerged] from all things, that is, from all objects of the senses (*indriyārtha*), such as sound and so forth;
the particle *ca* has the sense of "furthermore" (*punar-arthe*).
When he withdraws them again and draws them back together, contracting them—
therein the simile is like the limbs of a tortoise;
then it is clear that his wisdom is firmly established.
In the two preceding verses, the absence of all tamasic modifications was stated even during the state of emergence (vyutthāna);
now, however, the distinction is that there is the absence of all modifications during the state of meditative absorption (samādhi). //58//
Viśvanātha: He provides the answer to the question "What was it? with the words "When...
[He] withdraws the senses—the ears and so forth—from the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.

The meaning is that for one whose wisdom is steady, "sitting" consists of restraining the movement of the self-controlled senses toward external objects and establishing them in stillness within the interior.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a tortoise, by its own will, withdraws its limbs—the mouth, eyes, and so forth—into its own interior. //58//
Baladeva: Now, with the six verses beginning with "When," he provides the answer to the question "What was it like?

The grammatical construction is as follows: when this yogi effortlessly withdraws—meaning draws back—the senses, such as hearing and the rest, which are under his own control, from their objects, such as sound and the rest, then his wisdom is established.
Here is an illustration: "like a tortoise its limbs.

Just as a tortoise effortlessly withdraws its face, hands, and feet, so too the withdrawal of the senses from their objects and their establishment within is the posture of one whose wisdom is steady. //58//
The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food, with the exception of the taste for them; even that taste turns away from him upon seeing the Supreme. 59.

Śrīdhara: Now, it might be argued that the non-engagement of the senses with their objects cannot be the defining characteristic of one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajña*), because there is no distinction between such a person and the dull-witted, the diseased, or those intent on fasting, all of whom likewise refrain from engaging with sense-objects. To this, he says: "The objects... (*viṣayā*).
The "taking" (*āhāra*) of objects by means of the senses is their grasping.
For one who is without such taking—that is, for the ignorant embodied being who identifies with the body and does not grasp objects through the senses—passion, meaning desire, does not cease;
the sense is that longing does not turn back.
Alternatively, for one who abstains from food and is devoted to fasting, sense objects generally cease because one who is tormented by hunger lacks interest in sound, touch, and so forth;
however, with the exception of taste, the desire for taste does not cease—this is the meaning.
The rest is the same. //59//
Madhusūdana:
[Objection: Even for a fool, the withdrawal of the senses from sense-objects occurs due to the influence of disease and the like; how then can it be said that his wisdom is established?
To this, he says: "The objects... [and so forth].

For one who abstains from food, who does not take in sense objects through the senses—whether he be a fool possessing bodily pride and a physical body, a sick man, or even a wooden ascetic—the sense objects such as sound and the rest do indeed cease; however, "except for taste," meaning that apart from the thirst for taste, the objects may cease for the ignorant man, but the passion directed toward them does not cease. This is the meaning.

But for this person of steady wisdom—who, having seen the supreme goal of man and having realized "I am that very [Self]," remains established therein—his "taste" (rasa), which is even attachment to petty pleasures, ceases;
by the force of the word "api" (even), sense objects also cease.
This has been explained previously in the passage beginning with "To whatever extent there is purpose," and so forth.

And thus, the meaning is that the cessation of objects associated with passion is the characteristic of one whose wisdom is established; therefore, there is no deviation [from this definition] in the case of a fool.

Since the eradication of objects associated with passion does not occur without the correct vision of the Supreme Self, the intention is that one should achieve stability in that wisdom—which consists of correct vision and effects the eradication of objects associated with passion—through great effort. //59//
Viśvanātha:

Even for a fool, it may happen that the senses do not waver toward their objects due to fasting or the influence of disease and so forth; regarding this, he says: "Objects," etc. *Rasa-varjam*—*rasa* here means passion or desire; excluding that.
The meaning is that desire for sense objects does not cease;
however, for this person of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*), having seen the Supreme, the Self (*paramātman*), desire for sense objects ceases—thus there is no deviation from the definition.
Furthermore, for one capable of the direct realization of the Self, this is indeed the means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*).
The intended meaning is that it is not, however, established [as such]. //59//

Baladeva: [Objection: Indeed, it is observed that the non-functioning of the senses toward sense-objects occurs in a fool who is afflicted by disease; how then can this be a characteristic of one whose wisdom is established? To this, he says: "The objects... Even in the case of a foolish embodied being who does not take food or perform other activities due to the fear of illness—though he is without nourishment—the objects and the experiences thereof cease;
however, the meaning is that *rasa*—meaning attachment or thirst—that is, the thirst for sense-objects, does not cease.

But for this one of steady wisdom, even "taste"—that is, attachment to sense objects—ceases and perishes upon seeing and experiencing the Self, which is self-luminous bliss beyond all objects; thus, the cessation of attachment to objects is his defining characteristic, and there is no deviation from this rule. //59//
For, O son of Kuntī, even the mind of a wise man who strives is forcibly carried away by the turbulent senses. (2.60)
Śrīdhara: Without the restraint of the senses, the state of one whose wisdom is established does not occur;
therefore, he says "even for one who strives" in two verses to show that great effort must be exerted in that regard during the stage of practice.
"For one who strives" means for one making an effort for the sake of liberation.
Even for the wise and discerning, the senses forcibly carry away the mind;
for they are "distracting," meaning they have the nature of crushing or agitating it. //60//
Madhusūdana:

Regarding that, the restraint of the external senses and the restraint of the mind are the uncommon causes for the stability of wisdom, because it is observed that in their absence, wisdom perishes. To state this, he first describes the fault arising from the lack of restraint of the external senses with the words "yatataḥ" (of one who strives).
O Kaunteya,
even for one who exerts effort again and again, consisting in the perception of the defects of sense-objects,

the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is not contradictory; for, since the root *cakṣiṅ* is marked with the *ṅit* sign, it is made known that the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) is not mandatory when the root is *anudāttet*.
Even the mind of a wise man—one who possesses ultimate discernment—though rendered free from modification for even a moment, the senses carry it away, bringing it back to a state of transformation.

[Objection: Surely, when discernment is present as its opposite, how can there be the occurrence of transformation? To this he replies: they are "disturbing," meaning they have the nature of agitating; because of their extreme power, they are capable of crushing discernment.
Therefore, even while the wise man—the master—is looking on, and while discernment—the protector—is present, they act by force, violently and by compulsion.

The meaning is that, because they are all-pervasive destroyers, when the mind has entered into the wisdom born of discrimination (*vivekaja-prajñā*), the senses draw it away from there by causing it to enter their own respective objects.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates well-known fact.

For this matter is well known in the world: just as violent robbers, having forcibly overcome both a wealthy man and his wealth-guardian, seize the wealth even while the two of them are looking on, so too do the senses carry away the mind when objects are present. //60//
Viśvanātha:
However, in the state of the practitioner (sādhaka), there is indeed great effort, yet there is no power at all to completely reverse the senses; thus he says, "he strives."
"Pramāthīni" means those that have the nature of crushing; the sense is that they are agitating. //60//
Baladeva: Now, he speaks of the difficulty of her steadfastness in knowledge with the words "for even of one striving" (*yatato hi*).

Even for a wise man (*vipaścitaḥ*)—one who possesses the discriminative knowledge of the nature of the self as distinct from sense-objects—and who is therefore exerting himself to conquer the senses, the senses, such as hearing and the rest, acting as agents, forcibly carry away the mind, as if by force.
The meaning is that they carry away [the mind] and cause it to incline toward sense objects.

Now, one might ask: since the opposing knowledge of discrimination (*viveka-jñāna*) is present, how can they carry it away? To this he says, "disturbing" (*pramāthinī*); the meaning is that because they are exceedingly powerful, they are capable of crushing that knowledge.

Therefore, just as a great treasure is guarded from thieves, the protection of steadfastness in knowledge from the senses constitutes the "sitting" (*āsana*) of one whose wisdom is established. //60//
Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. (2.61)

Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore [the Lord says] "those. The disciplined yogin, having restrained those senses, should sit intent on Me (mat-para), he under whose control the senses remain obedient.
And by this, the answer to the question "How was he? is: "He remained with his senses brought under control. //61//
Madhusūdana:
If that is so, then what is the remedy for that? To this he says: "tāni" (those).

Having restrained—that is, brought under control—all those senses which serve as the means for knowledge and action, being disciplined, concentrated, and having the mind subdued, one should sit—that is, remain—free from worldly activity.
If it is asked how those who cause agitation may be brought under one's own control, he says in response: "one for whom I am the Supreme" (*mat-para*).
This means one for whom I, Vāsudeva, the Self of all, am the Supreme—the most excellent and that which is to be accepted; such a person is a single-minded devotee of mine (*ekānta-mad-bhakta*).
Thus it has been said: "No inauspiciousness exists anywhere for the devotees of Vāsudeva."

For just as in the world, bandits are subdued by taking refuge with a powerful king, and knowing "this man is under the king's protection," they themselves become submissive to him; in the very same way, by taking refuge with the Blessed One, the inner controller of all, the wicked senses are to be restrained through His power alone, and further, thinking "this person is under the Blessed One's protection," they become submissive to Him.
Such is the meaning of "becoming thus.
And how devotion to the Blessed One possesses great power,
we shall explain in detail further on.
He states the result of the mastery of the senses with the words "for [when they are] under control.
This is clear.
Thus, by saying "being one whose senses are mastered, he sat," the answer to the question "what did he do? has been stated. //61//
Viśvanātha:
"Devoted to Me" means "My devotee.
That there is no conquest of the senses without devotion to Me should be understood everywhere, even in the subsequent text.
As it was said by Uddhava: "O Lotus-eyed One, for the most part, yogis who strive to fix their minds fail due to a lack of concentration, being exhausted by the effort of restraining the mind."
"Then, therefore, the swans should take refuge in the lotus feet that yield bliss. (BhP 11.29.1–2).
By the words "for they are under control," it is stated that the senses of one whose wisdom is established become subdued; thus, a distinction from the practitioner is expressed. //61//

Baladeva: Now, if it be asked, "Even for those who have conquered their senses, self-realization is not perceived; what then is the means to that?", he says: "Having restrained all these... Restraining all these [senses], being intent on Me (*mat-para*) and established in Me (*man-niṣṭha*), one should sit—that is, remain—steadfast, having achieved the concentration of yoga.
The sense is that by the power of devotion to Me, the vision of one's own Self, preceded by the conquest of all the senses, becomes easily attainable.
Thus they remember:
"Just as fire with its upraised flames burns the dry grass when fanned by the wind,
so Viṣṇu, abiding in the mind, [burns] all the impurities of the yogins," and so forth.
The word "vaśe" (under control) is clear.
Thus, the answer has been given to the question: "What was his state of abiding through having brought the senses under control? //61//
For a person dwelling on sense objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment, desire is born; and from desire, anger is produced. (2.62)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion comes the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory comes the destruction of discernment; and from the destruction of discernment, one perishes. //63//

Śrīdhara: Having stated the fault in the absence of restraint of the external senses, he states the fault in the absence of restraint of the mind with two verses beginning with "dhyāyataḥ" (meditating).
For a person who meditates upon sense-objects with the notion that they possess inherent qualities, attachment—that is, clinging—arises toward them.
And from that attachment, an excessive desire for them arises.
Furthermore, from desire, when it is obstructed by something, anger arises.
Moreover, "from anger" means that from anger comes delusion, which is the absence of discrimination between what should and should not be done.

Then, from that, there is the confusion, the wavering, and the falling away from the mindfulness taught by the scriptures and the teacher; from that, there is the destruction of the intellect— that is, of consciousness—
just like the suppression [of vitality] in trees and the like.
Then he perishes and becomes like one who is dead. //62-63//
Madhusūdana:

Even for a person who has restrained the external senses, if they mentally contemplate—repeatedly thinking about—objects such as sound and the like, there arises an attachment (*saṅga*), a clinging (*āsaṅga*) to those objects, characterized by a false attribution of excellence (*śobhanādhyāsa*), in the form: "These are the causes of my supreme happiness."

A specific kind of affection arises from attachment, characterized by the cognition that [the object] is a cause of pleasure; from that arises desire, which is a specific form of craving, in the form "May these things belong to me.
From that desire, when it is obstructed by something, anger—which has that obstruction as its object and consists of a burning nature—is produced.
From anger arises delusion (*saṃmoha*), which consists in the absence of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

From delusion comes the confusion of memory (*smṛti-vibhrama*); "confusion" refers to the wandering away from, the deviation, or the failure of memory—that is, the failure to reflect upon the meaning taught by the scriptures and the teacher.

And from that failure of memory comes the destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the mental function whose form is the unity of the Self; this occurs because of an obstruction caused by the accumulation of the defect of contrary cultivation (*viparīta-bhāvanā*), resulting in the non-arising of the intellect or the incapacity of that which has arisen to produce its fruit.

Through the destruction of the intellect, one perishes; and through the disappearance of that intellect, which is the fruit [of action], one perishes and becomes unfit for any human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
For in the world, it is conventionally said that "one who has become unfit for human purposes is as good as dead";
therefore, it is said that "one perishes."

Since, in this way, even for one who has restrained the external senses, the attainment of supreme misfortune occurs in the absence of restraint over the mind, the intention is that one should restrain the mind with great effort.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "Having restrained all these, let him sit disciplined. (62–63)
Viśvanātha:

The mastery of the mind alone is the cause for the mastery of the external senses for one whose wisdom is established. However, he says "dhyāyantaḥ" (meditating) to explain what would happen in the total absence of such mastery of the mind;
*saṅga* means attachment.
Through attachment to them, there arises an excessive desire or longing; from that desire, when it is obstructed by something, anger arises;
and from anger comes delusion, which is the absence of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
And from that comes the loss of memory regarding one's own goal as taught by the scripture;
and from that comes the destruction of the intellect’s correct discernment.
Thereupon, one perishes and falls into the pit of saṃsāra. //62-63//
Baladeva: Even for one who has conquered the senses, misfortune remains difficult to ward off if the mind is not fixed upon Me; thus He says with two verses beginning with "dhyāyataḥ.
For the yogin who meditates—that is, repeatedly contemplates—objects such as sound and so forth, perceiving them as causes of happiness, attachment (*saṅga*) arises toward them.
From that attachment as a cause, desire and thirst (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) for those objects are born.
And from desire, when it is obstructed by something, anger arises as a flame of the mind; that [anger] becomes the adversary of its [desire's] obstruction.
From anger comes delusion (*saṃmoha*), which is the destruction of the discerning knowledge that distinguishes between what should and should not be done.
From delusion comes the confusion or ruin of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and the continuity of effort toward the conquest of the senses and so forth.
Due to the loss of mindfulness, there is the destruction of the intellect’s resolve, which is intended for self-knowledge.
From the destruction of the intellect, one perishes; that is to say, one becomes immersed again in the enjoyment of sense objects and wanders in saṃsāra.
The underlying meaning is that, because of taking refuge in passion, the weakened mind joins those [objects] with their respective domains.
And thus, one who desires to conquer the mind should practice my worship. //62-63//
But he who, with his self under control, moves among sense objects with the senses free from attachment and aversion, being disciplined in soul, attains serenity. (2.64)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But since the senses, by their very nature, are inclined toward their objects, they cannot be restrained; thus this defect is difficult to avoid. How, then, can one possess steady wisdom (sthita-prajña)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says in two verses beginning with "attachment and aversion":
"Even while moving among and enjoying sense-objects with senses that are free from attachment and aversion and devoid of pride, one attains serenity—that is, peace."
He states that freedom from passion and hatred is indeed "the self" (ātman).
One whose self—that is, the mind—is governed by senses under its own control is one for whom the self and mind are subject to his will.
By this very [statement], the answer to the fourth question—"How should he proceed?"—is given: he moves toward sense-objects with senses that are under his own command. //64//
Madhusūdana:
Stating that there is no fault even in the absence of restraint over the external senses provided the mind is restrained, he gives the answer to the question "What would happen? in eight verses.
One whose mind is not composed, even if he restrains his external senses, falls from the goal of human life by contemplating sense objects with a mind corrupted by passion and hatred.
The word "tu," however, signifies a distinction from what precedes.

One whose internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) has been brought under control, moving through—that is, perceiving—permissible objects such as sound and so forth by means of the senses, such as hearing, which are either under his own control or dependent on the mind, and which are thus free from or devoid of attachment and aversion; such a person is one whose self is disciplined.
One attains clarity, serenity, and lucidity of mind—the fitness for the direct realization of the Supreme Self.
The senses, when impelled by passion and aversion, become causes of defect;
however, when the mind is under one's own control, there is neither passion nor aversion.
And in the absence of those two, there is no activity of the sense faculties dependent upon them;
since the apprehension of objects occurs unavoidably,
it does not bring about any fault, and thus there is no contradiction to purity— this is the intended meaning.

By this, the doubt is dispelled: "If even the mere remembrance of sense objects is a cause of misfortune, then how much more so their enjoyment? One who enjoys sense objects for the sake of living—how could he not incur misfortune? Furthermore, the answer to the question "How does one go [to the goal]? has been stated: namely, that one attains the sense objects by means of the senses under one's own control. //64//
Viśvanātha:

Stating that there is no fault even in the perception of objects by the senses under one's own control when there is an absence of grasping at mental objects, he provides the answer to the question "How does one who is steady-in-wisdom move? with the verse beginning with *rāga*.
One whose self—that is, the mind—is submissive and established in his word is [the one described].
"One who is obedient, receptive to discipline, abiding by one's word, and attentive; one who is submissive, devoted, modest, humble, and respectful"—thus says Amara.
For such a qualified person, who attains favor, what need is there to mention that even the grasping of sense-objects is not a fault?
On the contrary, it is indeed a virtue.
The meaning is that for one whose wisdom is established, both the renunciation and the acceptance of sense objects—namely, sitting and wandering—are auspicious for him. //64//

Baladeva: Stating that there is no fault even in the failure to conquer the ears and other senses once the mind has been conquered, he provides the answer to the question "How should one proceed? with these eight verses beginning with "rāga" (verse 10).

It was said that even one who has conquered the external senses is fallen from the ultimate goal if his mind is not offered to Me. One whose self is disciplined (*vidheyātman*)—meaning one whose mind is under his own control and offered to Me—is for that very reason one whose mental impurities, such as passion and the like, have been burnt away.

But he, even while moving among or experiencing forbidden objects such as sound through the sense organs— the ears and so forth— which are under his own control, dependent on the mind, and for that very reason free from attachment and aversion, attains *prasāda*, meaning he reaches a state of stainless mind due to the removal of impurities such as attachment to sense objects. //64//
In clarity, the destruction of all sufferings arises for him; for the intellect of one whose mind is clear quickly becomes firmly established. (65)
Śrīdhara: Regarding what would happen when grace (*prasāda*) is attained, he says "grace" (*prasāde*). When grace is attained, there is the destruction of all suffering;
consequently, the meaning is that the intellect of one whose mind is serene becomes firmly established. //65//
It was stated that one attains serenity (*prasāda*); regarding that, it is now explained what occurs when serenity exists, in the verse beginning with "In serenity.

When there is serenity of the mind, which consists of its own natural clarity (*svacchatva*), the abandonment—that is, the destruction—of all sufferings, such as those internal and so forth, which are the manifestations of ignorance, arises for this ascetic.

For indeed, because the intellect of a yogi whose mind is serene quickly—that is, very swiftly—becomes established in the form of the identity of Brahman and the Self; it becomes "pari-avasthitā," meaning it remains firm on all sides due to the absence of obstacles such as contrary conceptions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*). Consequently, when serenity exists, there is the stabilization of the intellect; from that, the cessation of ignorance which is opposed to it; and from that, the abandonment of all suffering which is its effect. Thus, although this occurs in a sequence, there is no contradiction in stating that serenity causes the abandonment of all suffering, as this is said for the sake of emphasizing its excellence. //65//
Viśvanātha:

The intellect comes to rest—that is, it becomes fixed upon its own desired object in every respect. Thus, even due to the absence of grasping external objects, the grasping of the appropriate object is his happiness; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "of one with a serene mind," it should be understood that the serenity of the mind arises through devotion alone.
That without devotion there is no serenity of mind has been explained in detail in the First Canto itself;
for even Vyāsa, despite having completed his study of the Vedānta scriptures, attained serenity of mind only through the devotion instructed by Śrī Nārada. (65)
Baladeva: To explain what occurs when there is serenity, he says: when the mind of this yogin is serene, the cessation of all sufferings produced by contact with material nature arises.
For one whose consciousness is serene, the intellect—having as its object the true nature of the Self—becomes established; that is, it becomes steady. //65//
For one who is undisciplined, there is no discernment; for the undisciplined, there is no contemplation.
For one who does not contemplate, there is no peace; and for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness? (66)

Śrīdhara: He establishes, by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), that the restraint of the senses is the means for attaining the state of one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajñatā*), stating "there is not.
For the undisciplined person—whose senses are not brought under control—wisdom does not exist;
that is, through the instructions of the scriptures and the teacher, the wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding the Self simply does not arise.
Whence can there be any talk of its establishment?
To the question "whence," he says: "and not.
Nor is there cultivation—that is, meditative absorption—for that which is illogical.
For through cultivation, the mind becomes established in the Self;

and that [cultivation] does not exist for one who is undisciplined. Furthermore, for one who does not cultivate—that is, for one who does not practice meditation on the Self—there is no peace, which is the stilling of the mind within the Self.
For one who is not tranquil, whence can there be happiness? The meaning is: from liberation-bliss. //66//
Madhusūdana:
He confirms this very point by way of its opposite with the words "it does not exist.

For one who is undisciplined—that is, one whose mind is unconquered—the intellect directed toward the Self, which is produced by the investigation of Vedānta known as hearing and reflection, does not exist; it does not arise.

In the absence of that cognition, there can be no contemplation (*bhāvanā*)—consisting of profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*)—which takes the form of a continuous flow of homogeneous cognitions uninterrupted by heterogeneous ones.

The negative particle (*na*) is to be construed with "exists" (*asti*) in every instance. Furthermore, for one who does not contemplate the Self, there is no peace consisting in the cessation of ignorance along with its effects; nor is there the direct realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self produced by the Vedāntic statements.
For one who is not tranquil and devoid of the direct realization of the Self, how can there be happiness? The meaning is that there can be no bliss of liberation. //66//
Viśvanātha:
He confirms the stated point by means of a negative formulation with the words "there is not.
For one who is unyoked—that is, one whose mind is not mastered—there is no intellect (*buddhi*), meaning no wisdom (*prajñā*) directed toward the Self.

For one who is undisciplined and devoid of such wisdom, there is no cultivation—that is, no meditation upon the Supreme Lord. For one who does not cultivate and has not performed meditation, there is no peace, which is the cessation of sense objects.
For one who lacks peace, there is no happiness, which is the bliss of the Self. //66//

Baladeva: He states the previously mentioned point by way of its contrapositive: for one who is unyoked—that is, a non-yogi whose mind is not fixed upon Me—there is no *buddhi* as previously defined; it does not exist.
For that very reason, he possesses no such *bhāvanā*, nor even the contemplation of such a Self.
For one who does not contemplate such a Self, there is no *śānti*, which is the cessation of craving for sense objects.
For one who is not tranquil and is agitated by craving for those [objects], how could there be happiness characterized by the experience of the self as the nature of self-luminous bliss? //66//
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters. (67)
Śrīdhara: Regarding the statement, "There is no wisdom for one who is undisciplined" (Gītā 2.66), he states the reason here with the words "of the senses" (*indriyāṇām*).

When even a single sense among those that are unsubdued and wandering at will among objects follows the mind—that is, when it goes along with the mind because it has been brought under control—[then there is no peace].
At that very moment, it carries away the wisdom or intellect of even a single sense organ, the mind, or the person, making it distracted by sense objects;
what need is there to mention that it carries away the wisdom of many?
It is just as when the wind causes the boat of a negligent helmsman to whirl about in every direction. //67//
Madhusūdana:
To the question, "Why does one who is undisciplined lack wisdom? he says, "Of the senses," and so forth.
Among the senses that are moving—that is, operating—within their respective objects, if even a single sense is made the target and the mind is directed toward it, being impelled [by that sense].
It functions; this is the sense. The *lakāra* suffix is used here in the sense of the agent being the object (*karma-kartari*).

That sense-faculty, even though it is one, when followed by the mind, carries away—that is, removes—the practitioner’s wisdom regarding the self, which is scriptural and has the self as its object, because the mind is then occupied with that [external] object.
The meaning is: when even a single sense faculty carries away one's wisdom, what need is there to mention that they all carry it away?
The illustration is clear. The word "in water" (*ambhasi*) was used to indicate that the wind possesses the power to carry away a boat on the water, but not on the ground.

Thus, Viśvanātha indicates that even in the case of the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*), it is only when there is flicker of the mind—which corresponds to water—that the sense organ possesses the capacity to carry away wisdom, but not when there is steadiness of the mind—which corresponds to earth.

He establishes that for one who is undisciplined, there is no true intellect, by stating: "Among the senses wandering among their respective objects, whichever single sense of mine follows [the lead]..."
When it acts as a follower of all the senses of men,
that very mind carries away his wisdom and intellect,
just as a contrary wind carries away a boat being carried along on the water. //67//
Baladeva: He states the fault that arises from the lack of restraint of the senses when the mind is not fixed upon Me, beginning with the words "indriyāṇām.

Among the senses wandering among objects and remaining unsubdued, if the mind is directed toward or engages with even one—whether it be the ear or the eye—that single sense, accompanied by the mind, carries away or removes the wisdom of the one who impels it, which has the discerned Self as its object; this occurs because the mind is drawn toward that [sensory] object.
What more need be said? All of them [are like this].
Just as a headwind [hinders] a boat being carried along on the water, so it is with these. //67//
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are completely withdrawn from the objects of the senses— his wisdom is firmly established. (2.68)
Śrīdhara: He concludes that the restraint of the senses is the means for the state of one whose wisdom is established by saying "therefore.
The meaning of this conclusion regarding its being a means is that it should be understood that his wisdom is firmly established.
O Mahābāho!
Thus, by addressing him in this way, he indicates that since you are capable of subduing enemies, you must likewise possess the capacity for this task as well. //68//
Madhusūdana says: "For because it is so, therefore...
[means] "in every way," that is, all [the senses] together with the mind.
By addressing him as "O mighty-armed one" (*mahābāho*), it indicates that because he is capable of warding off all enemies, he is likewise capable of warding off the enemies that are the senses.
The rest is clear.
The word "his" (*tasya*) refers to both the perfected one (*siddha*) and the seeker (*sādhaka*).

This is because the fact that restraint of the senses is a characteristic of one whose wisdom is established must be concluded as being a means for attaining wisdom for one who seeks liberation. //68//
Viśvanātha:
[This refers to] one whose mind is restrained;
O mighty-armed one!
Thus, the meaning is: just as you subdue your enemies, so too should you subdue the mind. //68//
Baladeva says: "Therefore" means:
for one whose mind is fixed on Me, there arises a firm foundation in the Self.
"O mighty-armed one" means: just as you restrain your enemies, so too should you restrain your senses.

By these verses, O Blessed One, it should be understood that for one who has attained steadfast wisdom (*sthita-prajña*), the conquest of the senses is natural and inherent; however, for one who is still practicing, it constitutes the means of accomplishment. //68//
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. (2.69)

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that no one is seen in the world who, like one fast asleep, is entirely devoid of activities such as seeing and has completely restrained the senses; therefore, this definition [of yoga] is unattainable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which is night for all beings. That which is night for all beings—
The night is like a night; it is the state of being established in the Self (*ātma-niṣṭhā*).
For those whose minds are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, there is an absence of activities such as seeing and so forth during that [state].
In that state of being established in the Self, the self-controlled one—whose senses are restrained—awakens while others are awake.
For the sage who perceives the reality of the self, there is night;
the meaning is that during that [night], he has no such activities as seeing and so forth.
This is what is being said: just as for nocturnal animals such as owls, vision occurs only at night and not by day.
Thus, even for one who knows Brahman and has opened his eyes, the vision is fixed on Brahman alone and not upon sense objects; therefore, this definition is not impossible. //69//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, it has been stated that one who desires liberation must practice restraint of the senses through deliberate effort for the sake of stabilizing wisdom; however, for one whose wisdom is established, the restraint of all the senses is self-evident.
To this effect, he says: "That which is night," etc.
That wisdom in the form of the direct realization "I am Brahman," born from the sentences of the Vedanta, is night, as it were, for all ignorant beings, because it is non-manifest to them.

In that "night of all beings," which is characterized by the knowledge of Brahman, he who remains awake—having awakened from the sleep of ignorance, being vigilant, and possessing restraint of the senses—is called one of steady wisdom;
this is the meaning.

But that sleep of ignorance, characterized by the perception of duality, in which all beings are fast asleep and yet remain awake, acting as if in a dream—that night does not shine for the sage of steady wisdom who perceives the reality of the Self through direct intuition.
For as long as one has not awakened, there is indeed the vision of a dream; however, because delusion terminates upon awakening, such vision ceases at the time of the knowledge of reality.
However, no conventional usage whatsoever is caused by delusion.
As it has been stated by the authors of the Vārttika:
"In the conventional usage regarding causal factors (kāraka), one does not perceive a pure reality."
And when the object is established as pure, the activity of the agent likewise [ceases].
"This cycle of existence is night for the crow and the owl who do not know the Self," so said Hari himself: "That which is night for all beings...
Thus, for one whose vision is perverted, there is no vision of reality, because perverted vision is produced by the non-perception of reality.

And for one who has the vision of reality (*vastu-darśana*), there is no distorted vision (*viparīta-darśana*), because the non-vision of reality—which is the cause of distorted vision—is sublated by the vision of reality.
Thus says the Śruti: "Where there is, as it were, something else, there one might see another;
but where for [the knower] everything has become the Self alone, whom could he see and by what?"
Thus he states the distinction between knowledge and ignorance:

just as day is night for the crow who is blind at night, and night is day for the owl who is blind by day; and for the owl seeing at night, that which is day is indeed night for the crow—this is a great wonder.

Therefore, how could there be for those who perceive reality any conventional usage of ignorance-based factors such as action and its agents? The meaning is that the restraint of the senses is established for him quite naturally. //69//
Viśvanātha:
However, for one whose wisdom is established, the restraint of all the senses is indeed self-evident; thus he says, "When...
For the intellect is of two kinds: that which is directed toward the Self and that which is directed toward sense objects.
In this regard, that intellect which is inclined toward the self is night for all beings.
Just as people sleeping during the night do not know what may happen at any moment,
so too all beings do not know the reality being attained by the intellect inclined toward the self.
But in that state, the self-controlled one who possesses steady wisdom remains awake;
he does not sleep.
Therefore, he directly experiences the bliss that culminates in the realization of the Self.
In that intellect which is inclined toward sense objects, the elements are awake;
those who are intent upon it directly experience the pleasure, grief, delusion, and so forth arising from sense objects, but they do not sleep therein.
For the sage whose wisdom is established, that [intellect] is night; the meaning is that he does not experience anything whatsoever that is intent upon it.

But it means one who observes the objects of the world which bestow pleasure and pain upon worldly people, viewing them with indifference, and even taking up the objects for his own enjoyment as they arise, remaining untainted. //69//

Baladeva: It has been stated that for one in the state of a seeker (*sādhaka*)—that is, for one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajña*)—the restraint of the senses is to be accomplished through effort.
However, for one in the state of perfection (*siddha*), that same discipline is natural; thus [the Lord] says, "That which is night," etc.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is of two kinds: that which is fixed on the solitary Self and that which is fixed on sense-objects.

The intellect fixed on the Self (ātma-niṣṭhā buddhiḥ) is here illustrated by the metaphor of night; it is like night in that it is non-illuminating. Just as people sleeping at night do not perceive the Self which is attainable therein, so all [ordinary] people do not experience it.
However, the self-controlled one (saṃyamī), having conquered the senses, remains awake in that state and does not sleep.
The meaning is that by means of her, one experiences the Self.

That state of wisdom (*buddhi*) in which the elements are awake—that is, in which they experience the enjoyment of objects—and in which they do not sleep, is "night" for the sage whose wisdom is established.
The meaning is that for him, it does not illuminate the enjoyment of objects.
To the question "Of what kind [of person]? he says: "Of one who sees.
This means: of one who directly experiences the Self and, even while experiencing objects drawn forth by past karma (*prārabdha*), remains indifferent toward them.
The meaning is that, according to the maxim of the dancer’s head and the jar, because the self is being perceived, there is no apprehension of any other aesthetic flavor (rasa).
"Filled [with water], yet remaining steady..."
Just as waters enter the ocean, so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who craves desires. //70//

Śrīdhara: Now, to address the inquiry as to how one can enjoy sense objects when there is an absence of vision toward them, he says: "Being filled... Just as other waters enter the ocean—which, though being filled by various rivers and streams, remains established in its steadiness and does not overstep its boundaries—so too do desires, that is, sense objects, enter that sage who has internal vision, yet he is not moved by enjoyments.
Remaining indeed unchanging, those who have been projected by their *prārabdha* karmas enter [into him]; he attains peace, which is liberation (*kaivalya*).
But one who desires objects of pleasure—one whose nature is the longing for enjoyment—does not. //70//
Madhusūdana:

For such a person of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*), even the cessation of all distractions is established as a matter of course; thus, he says "āpūryamāṇam" (being filled) along with an illustration.
Though being filled by all rivers, all waters arising from rain and other sources enter the ocean.

Of what sort is he "firmly established" (*acala-pratiṣṭha*)? It means one who has not transgressed the bounds of propriety (*anatikrānta-maryāda*). Alternatively, it expresses an excellence of profundity by stating that in him is the stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) of immovable things such as Mount Maināka and others.

Just as [the ocean remains] in a certain manner by way of being changeless (*nirvikāratvena*), so too does that person of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*) remain in that very same manner of being changeless.

While remaining entirely changeless, all objects of desire—sound and the rest—which are craved by ignorant people, enter him unavoidably due to the force of *prārabdha* karma; yet they are unable to cause any transformation in him. He, who stands like a great ocean, is the one of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*). He attains peace (*śāntim*), which is the cessation of all worldly and transcendental distractions caused by karma, and the cessation of the effects of ignorance that persist even after being sublated.
One attains [peace] through the power of knowledge.
One who desires objects—that is, one whose nature it is to long for sense-objects (*kāmakāmin*)—an ignorant person, does not attain the peace that has been fully described.
Rather, the meaning of the statement is that such a person remains forever submerged in the great ocean of affliction due to distraction by mundane and supramundane activities.

By this, it should be understood that the renunciation of the wise (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*), which is the very fruit of knowledge, belongs to the knower alone; and that his liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)—consisting in the cessation of all distractions and remaining unmodified even when experiencing objects through the force of past impressions—is thus described. //70//
Viśvanātha:
He says that freedom from agitation during the perception of objects is indeed "untaintedness" (*nirlepatā*) in the verse beginning with *āpūryamāṇam*.
Just as during the rainy season the waters of rivers flow here and there into the ocean—of what nature is it?
Even when being filled slightly, it cannot be filled even by that much water;
established in immovability and not transgressing its boundaries, in that very same way, desires—that is, sense objects—enter it, coming as things to be enjoyed.
Just as the ocean undergoes no change whatsoever whether water enters it or does not enter it.
In the same way, he who remains entirely undisturbed both in the enjoyment of desires and in their non-enjoyment is one whose wisdom is established;
[he attains] peace and knowledge. //70//
Baladeva, clarifying the intended meaning, says "āpūrya" (being filled):

Just as other waters arising from rain enter the ocean—which is being filled by its own very nature and yet remains established in its steadiness with its boundary untransgressed—but are unable to produce any change therein; so too [is the Lord].
In the same way, all desires—objects drawn forth by past karma—that enter one do not have the power to cause agitation; he attains peace.

The meaning is that even while sound and other objects remain within the range of his senses, he remains established in wisdom (*sthita-prajña*), finding satisfaction in the experience of the bliss of his own Self and perceiving not even a trace of modification.
However, he who desires objects and seeks after sense-pleasures does not attain the aforementioned peace. //70//
Having abandoned all desires, the man who moves about free from longing, without the sense of "mine," and without egoism— he attains peace. (2.71)

Śrīdhara: Because it is so, therefore [the text says] "having abandoned" (vihāya). Having abandoned—that is, having relinquished and disregarded—the desires already attained, and being free from longing for those not yet attained; because he is devoid of egoism (*nirahaṅkāra*), he is likewise free from the sense of "mine" (*nirmama*) regarding the means of enjoying them. Thus, becoming one whose vision is turned inward, he who "moves" (*carati*)—that is, he experiences enjoyments by the force of his *prārabdha* karma.
Wherever he may go, he attains peace. //71//
Madhusūdana:
Because it is so, therefore [the Lord says] "having abandoned.

This refers to all external things such as houses, fields, and the like, even if they have been acquired, as well as internal things in the form of mental projections (manorājya) which consist of mere latent impressions (vāsanā).

And while traveling on the path, having abandoned and disregarded the three kinds of desires consisting of the touch of grass and so forth, he remains free from longing even for mere bodily sustenance;
for he is devoid of egoism— that is, free from the conceit "I am this" regarding the body, senses, and so on—
or, alternatively, free from self-conceit based on causes such as possessing learning.
Therefore, being free from the sense of "mine" even regarding the mere maintenance of the body— such as the loincloth and covering necessitated by *prārabdha* karma—
that person who moves about, devoid of the conceit "this is mine," experiences enjoyments under the influence of *prārabdha* karma, or wanders wherever he may by chance.

Being thus established, the one of steady wisdom attains—that is, reaches by the power of knowledge—peace, characterized by the cessation of all the sufferings of saṃsāra and the removal of ignorance along with its effects.
This concludes the answer to the fourth question: what is the conduct of the one of steady wisdom. //71//
Viśvanātha:
But some, not placing trust in sense-objects, do not enjoy them at all;
thus he says, "having abandoned," meaning free from egoism (*nirahaṅkāra*) and possessiveness (*nirmama*), being devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and bodily concerns. //71//

Baladeva: "Having abandoned" means: having abandoned all desired objects that have been obtained, he moves about being devoid of the sense of "mine" even regarding the mere maintenance of the body, and being devoid of egoism—meaning devoid of the conceit of selfhood toward the non-self body—and he consumes only what is necessary for its sustenance.
"Wherever he goes, he attains peace"—this is the answer to the question, "Why should one go? //71//
This, O Pārtha, is the state of being established in Brahman; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Even at the time of death, by remaining in this state, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman. //72//
Śrīdhara: Praising the aforementioned steadfastness in knowledge, he concludes with the word "this":
"This is the state of Brahman," meaning the steadfastness in the knowledge of Brahman; it is of such a nature as described.
A person whose internal organ has been purified by the worship of the Supreme Lord, having attained this [knowledge], is no longer deluded;
he does not again encounter the delusion of saṃsāra.

For, even at the time of death—the end—by remaining in this [knowledge] for even a moment (lakṣa-mātram), one attains, that is, reaches, the extinction in Brahman (brahma-nirvāṇam), which is absorption into Brahman.
How much more, then, can it be said that one attains [the goal] by remaining established from childhood onwards? //72//
He who, through the instruction of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, lifted up his devotee Arjuna who was submerged in the mire of grief— he, Kṛṣṇa, is my refuge.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana:
Thus, under the guise of answering the four questions, all the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established have been described as duties for the seeker of liberation.
Now, praising the steadfastness in Sāṅkhya which is the fruit of Karma-yoga, He concludes with the words "This... (eṣā).
This has been described under the guise of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady.

And this "steadiness" (sthiti)—previously mentioned as "this wisdom regarding Sāṅkhya has been declared to you"—is characterized by the knowledge of the Supreme Self preceded by the renunciation of all actions; it is "Brahmic," meaning it has Brahman as its object, O Pārtha.
Having attained this state, no one whatsoever is ever deluded again;
for there is no possibility of the re-emergence of ignorance once it has been sublated by knowledge, since its production is impossible due to its beginninglessness.

Abiding in this state even at the time of death, or in the final stage of life, one attains *brahma-nirvāṇa*—that is, extinction in Brahman, or cessation [in Brahman], or extinction in the form of Brahman.
He "reaches" or goes to it without distinction.

What need is there to say that he who, having renounced even from the stage of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), remains for as long as life lasts in this state of Brahman, reaches the extinction of Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇa*)? This is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also). //72//

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Sutra of the Entire Meaning of the Gītā," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā) composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī. //2//
Viśvanātha concludes with the word "eṣā" (this):
it is *brāhmī*, meaning that which leads to the attainment of Brahman.
Even at the end of life, at the time of death; how much more so from childhood onwards? //72//
He has clearly explained knowledge and action, as well as devotion which is not yet manifest;
for this reason, this chapter is called the Śrī-Gītā-Sūtra.

Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary titled *Sārārthavarṣiṇī*, which showers the essential meaning for the hearts of devotees, this second chapter has been completed in a fitting manner for the virtuous. 2.
Baladeva: He praises the state of one whose wisdom is steady with the words "This... The term *brāhmī* means that which leads to the attainment of Brahman;
*anta-kāle* refers to the final stage of life.
How much more so for one who attains—that is, obtains—brahman from childhood;
the meaning is that he bestows that which is of the nature of the immortal, namely Nirvana.
[Objection: But how can one who is established in that [state] attain brahman?
If it is argued that its attainment is due to devotion to it being the cause, it is said in response:
because that [attainment] has devotion to it as its cause, and because devotion to it is the cause of that [attainment], devotion to it brings about its attainment. //72//
Through desireless actions, the man of knowledge becomes one who remembers Hari alone;
otherwise, it is indeed an obstacle—this is the determination of the second chapter.
Thus ends the second chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā Upaniṣad. //2//
